#3456. 10 Books Like ‘A Court of Thorns and Roses’ You Should Read Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Sarah J. Maas’ lush, romance-soaked series A Court of Thorns and Roses has blossomed into a sprawling, complex fantasy series with millions of dedicated fans, and with good reason. A complex heroine who keeps discovering new depths in herself, fascinating supporting characters who shift from antihero to antivillain in unexpected ways, creative and beautifully rendered world-building—the series has it all, while also being unapologetically romantic (and steamy).

The story of a huntress who is kidnapped by a fae prince and brought to the Spring Court as a prisoner, only to become a key player in all that fae drama, ACOTAR is special, but Maas can only write so fast. If you need more books with the same lush feel, here are 10 to get you started.

It’s no shock that one of Sarah J. Maas’ other series would be recommended for fans of A Court of Thorns and Roses, but there’s a specific reason you should jump into her Crescent City series, especially the third book, House of Flame and Shadow. The most recent ACOTAR book, A Court of Splintered Harmony, revealed that the events of House of Flame and Shadow tie directly into the events in Splintered Harmony, particularly with regard to the character of Feyre’s sister, Nesta. In other words, if you read Splintered Harmony and wondered why Nesta was being so weird, there’s a whole other book series you should dig into immediately.

If Feyre’s grit and determination are your favorite aspect of ACOTAR, Julie Kagawa’s Iron Fey series (starting with The Iron King) will be your next obsession. Meghan Chase has never felt ‘normal’ in her life, and she’s been haunted by her father’s disappearance since she was a child. When her brother also vanishes, she goes on a quest for answers, learns that she’s actually the daughter of a faerie king, and finds herself in a magical world that blurs in elements of Shakespeare’s A Midsummer Night’s Dream. Meghan is determined to save her brother (and herself), but a certain ice-cold fae prince captures her attention, even though he’s as dangerous as he is beautiful.

If you’re looking for some serious romance in your fantasy, Jennifer L. Armentrout’s A Blood and Ash series is a must. Poppy was chosen at birth to be the kingdom’s Maiden, isolated and untouched in order to be ready for her Ascension to ensure the land is protected from the evil force that took her family. But it’s a lonely existence—until Hawke is assigned as her sworn protector. Golden-eyed and beautiful, Hawke offers Poppy the connection she’s craved. When chaos erupts around her, Hawke takes the opportunity to spirit Poppy away. But Hawke has a secret, and Poppy is soon in danger of losing both her heart and the favor of the gods themselves.

If you love how A Court of Thorns and Roses takes the “enemies-to-lovers” trope and builds it into a deep, complex mesh of emotions and plot twists, you’ll love Shelby Mahurin’s Serpent & Dove series. When witch Louise le Blanc flees her coven, she takes shelter in the city of Cesarine, where magic is forbidden, and witches are unceremoniously hunted and burned. Louise’s life gets infinitely more complicated, dangerous, and steamy when she’s trapped into an unwanted marriage with Reid Diggory—who happens to be a huntsman of the Church, charged with tracking down and eliminating witches. And then Louise starts to realize that Reid is actually pretty darn hot.

If you’re looking for a romantasy that’s broadly similar to ACOTAR while being its own thing, read A.K. Mulford’s The Five Crowns of Okrith series, starting with The High Mountain Court. Remy is a red witch, which means she’s in hiding and ready to make a run for it if the fae get near. So when a group of fae shows up at her tavern, she makes for the exit—only to be captured by Prince Hale of the Eastern Court. Instead of striking her down, however, Hale asks Remy for help—he needs to locate two ancient magical artifacts created by red witches, and he needs her red magic to find them. Hale promises to set her free and even reunite her with the red witches still living. More importantly, Remy finds Hale irresistible and has a primal urge to stay with him, no matter what the cost.

Looking for a romantasy with a slightly different vibe from ACOTAR? Variety is the spice of life, after all—and The Fourth Wing delivers. Rebecca Yarros’ Empyrean Series made a huge splash when it debuted, and for good reason—it has everything, from a capable, intelligent heroine thrust into a dangerous scenario (in this case, a dragon rider academy where failure can be deadly) and forced to navigate alliances, conspiracies, and her own heart, which is pushing her towards a romance that might be as dangerous as the dragons themselves.

Love the moral complexity of ACOTAR, where everyone has at least a touch of darkness? Check out The Folk of the Air series by Holly Black. When Jude was a child, the father of her half-sister, the faerie Madoc, murdered her parents and took her back to the Faerie world with him. Raised as part of the gentry, Jude lives in a world where her mortal nature is hated and despised, but she battles for her place at court anyway while struggling with her love-hate relationship with her adoptive father and a growing bond with the titular prince, a relationship that is strictly forbidden. Jude is a fierce and extremely morally gray character, and one that fans of Feyre will adore.

Looking for more smart women at the center of beautifully-rendered fantasy stories? You’ll love Princess Lucero-Elisa de Riqueza of Orovalle, star of this series-starter by Rae Carson. Elisa was chosen for “Service” as a baby, when a godstone was placed in her navel by the gods, signaling that she was destined for greatness. But as a young woman, Elisa is self-hating and miserable. She’s never done anything even remotely great, and spends her time isolated, overweight, and reading military strategy books. One day she’s shocked to discover she’s been married off to the king of a distant land on the brink of war—and suddenly all that rage and book learning becomes invaluable as she struggles to survive an unfamiliar court and help her new homeland survive a dangerous onslaught.

If you loved Feyre’s journey as she discovered unknown reservoirs of power and courage inside herself, you should read Leigh Bardugo’s Grishaverse novels, starting with Shadow and Bone. As a child, Alina was tested by the Grisha and found to possess no magical ability. As an adult, she serves as a cartographer in the army. Charged with guiding the Darkling—the most powerful of the Grisha—across the dangerous and terrifying Shadow Fold, Alina is unexpectedly revealed to have incredible powers and is packed off to train with the Grisha. There, she must determine who her friends and enemies are, even while falling under the spell of the charismatic Darkling.

Emilia di Carlo and her sister Vittoria are very different—Emilia is bookish and shy, Vittoria outgoing and brash—but they share a secret: They’re both streghe, and have spent their lives learning to use magic. In this version of Italy, the Malvagi (the seven princes of Hell) haven’t been seen in a long time, but a terrifying accident summons the Prince of Wrath and leaves three witches dead, including Vittoria. Emilia swears to use her power to avenge her sister, but when her revenge is delayed and she’s forced to work with Wrath, unwanted feelings begin to tick up the spice level to an uncomfortable degree.

#3455. ‘Dig’ Review: Amy Poehler’s Talent-Rich Peacock Comedy Barely Scratches the Surface

The great benefit of having clout in Hollywood — aside from fame, fortune, and a standing reservation at any restaurant in town — is being able to say “no.” You don’t have to take any job that pays. You don’t even have to work year-round. And you certainly don’t have to chase silly trends, like, say — I don’t know — making a comedy that’s also a mystery that’s also a drama? Beloved, funny folks like Amy Poehler and Mike Schur, who earned a huge chunk of their influence through the indelible sitcom, “Parks and Recreation,” should be able to make anything they want! Any way they want! They earned it!

Far be it from me to know what exactly went wrong with Schur and Poehler’s new series, but something did, unfortunately, go wrong. Each 32-35 minute episode strains to wrap up plots that limp to the finish line. Narrative momentum only exists from the minor twists revealed in the final seconds — then the credits roll, the “up next” button lights up, and your natural curiosity over what happens next wins out over your desire to scroll for something better. Worst of all, everything is “light”: The tone is light, the jokes are light, the mystery is light, the drama is light, even the lighting is light. (It’s so bright, all the time, even at night!) Watching “Dig” is like bearing witness to dwindling interest: Whatever originally compelled the “Dig” team to adapt Kate Myers’ 2023 novel, “Excavations” gets spread so thin across the disparate parts of this broad adaptation that there’s almost nothing left.

Nothing, that is, but the stars. Poehler leads an affable cast (astutely assembled by casting directors Allison Jones and Emily Buntyn) as lead archaeologist Elise, a devoted digger (no, not that kind) whose decades in the dirt have earned her respect and admiration but also turned her cynical and closed-off. She’s an accomplished expert in the field who’s been waiting to run her own site for years, working diligently under the tutelage of beloved British professor Neville Wycombe (Hugh Laurie), but events have conspired to keep her from the top job.

The most obvious issue is also the simplest: Neville has repeatedly promised to retire, only to rescind that promise when it comes time to make it official. This year he swears he’ll step down for real, but Elise knows better than to buy-in, especially when her informal audition (giving the welcome speech to a group of undergrads they call Ugs) exposes her greatest weakness: She’s not an inspiring leader. “I know your default setting is ‘tough love,'” Neville tells Elise, “but please learn to give people some grace.”

That advice is put to the test when Dylan (Geraldine Viswanathan), Elise’s flaky former protégé, shows up at the dig site after abandoning her post five years prior without so much as a goodbye. Returning with a questionable back tattoo that reads “a traveler on the adventure of life” and without any luggage, directions, or direction (as in, for her life), Dylan is a messy 29-year-old trying to sort things out as she turns 30. Luckily, she meets the too-put-together-for-her-own-good Clare (Antonia Thomas), a 39-year-old head preservationist who’s secure in her calling, engaged to Dylan’s ex-boyfriend Gary (Jon Pointing), and always dressed to the nines. (Surprise, surprise: Clare comes from money.)

The two will learn from each other, just as they’ll each learn from Elise, but they should all take more cues from Patty Borkman (Fina Strazza), the 19-year-old intern who’s assigned to be Neville’s assistant. That’s, in part, because Patty is the youngest and eagerist of a central foursome neatly divided by decades (did I mention Elise is 49?), but more so because Patty — as you may have guessed by her last name — is a fizzy vat of quirky energy that Strazza impressively dissipates into a charming, fresh, coming-of-age character.

Patty’s voice sounds like a shy version of Cristin Milioti’s adult baby from “30 Rock.” She wears silly hats, can’t drive, and struggles to stick up for herself. She kinda, sorta believes she’s a demigod (after reading one of Neville’s books on Greek mythology as a kid), and she’s always been an outcast (for these reasons and more). Watching Patty come into her own — in ways both delightfully weird and universally endearing — is the most rewarding and compelling aspect of “Dig”; a strange, distinctive spark that could grow into a roaring fire if the series continues (and learns from its strongest asset).

But that’s a big “if.” The first season (consisting of 10 episodes) pivots around the four women finding a rare statue and making the questionable decision to keep it secret from Neville. At the time, they say it’s because their boss takes credit for everything, and they want something that’s just their own, but that contention doesn’t hold up to scrutiny as the season progresses because Neville doesn’t hold up to scrutiny as the season progresses. Neville is whoever he needs to be in any given episode — a mentor, an oppressor, a goofball, a stick in the mud, a nice old man, and a villainous monster — and while Laurie can pivot with the best of them, his inconsistent character development betrays a show that’s hesitant to commit to much of anything.

The love triangle between Gary, Dylan, and Clare fizzles out without any substantial conflict. Elsewhere, an inappropriate crush is introduced and tossed away without consequence. Great guest stars like Jason Mantzoukas (a local looter) and Max Greenfield (as a sketchy art dealer) feel like they were hired for arcs that ended up getting cut, while regulars (like Gary) can feel adrift in their ample, listless screentime. Premises primed for comic hijinks never get there, mysteries teed up for suspense are left slack, and relationships that should create a little friction when brought together instead find a way to slide off each other without anything sticking.

Poehler, at the center of it all, is a problem. While it’s theoretically interesting to see the former Leslie Knope take the opposite tact — playing another hard-working public servant (every artifact they uncover remains in Greece) only without the unbridled optimism — Elise’s glum demeanor limits her ability to crack jokes, stir passion, and generally light up a scene. Patty is the only outsized character in a bunch of overly composed normies, and while everyone gets a moment or two to strut their silly stuff, it’s not enough in a series where the humor is already spread so thin.

“Dig” has all the talent it needs to be whatever show it wants to be. The most obvious option would be a comedy, but I have faith in the cast and creatives to excel in other genres, too. They just need to pick one and, when they do, dig a whole lot deeper than this.

“Dig” premieres Monday, November 23 on Peacock. All 10 episodes will be released at once.

#3454. Why Lenore Dove Baird From The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping Looks So Familiar

In 2025, "Hunger Games" author Suzanne Collins released one of the most long-awaited stories in the entire franchise — the backstory of District 12 victor Haymitch Abernathy, "Sunrise on the Reaping." A film adaptation titled "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" immediately took shape, and after Joseph Zada was cast as a young version of Haymitch — before he's an aging, depressed, drink-swilling lout portrayed by Woody Harrelson in the four original films — the rest of the cast began to round out.

Immediately after I read the book, I wondered who might be cast as Lenore Dove Baird, the beautiful and wild girlfriend Haymitch is forced to leave behind in District 12 when he's essentially chosen to participate in the Games by mistake. I was then extremely pleased when Whitney Peak was cast in this important part, who's not only Haymitch's love interest but a vital link to the other prequel "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes" ... in that Lenore Dove is distantly related to that film and novel's heroine Lucy Gray Baird (Rachel Zegler).

So where have you seen Peak before she took on the role of Lenore Dove? I should say that, in general, Peak's star is still on the rise, but there's a reason she earned this role; not only is she extremely talented, but she's appeared in some pretty high-profile projects in recent years. From a major HBO reboot (that did fail, by no fault of Peak's) to some independent films, here's where you've seen Whitney Peak, who plays Lenore Dove in "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping," before.

After small roles in films like "Molly's Game" and TV shows like "The Chilling Adventures of Sabrina," Whitney Peak booked her first lead role courtesy of the "Gossip Girl" reboot that aired on HBO Max from 2021 to 2023.

As a huge fan of the ridiculous campfest that is the original "Gossip Girl" — which was adapted, very loosely, from a novel series written by Cecily von Ziegesar and ran on The CW from 2007 to 2012 — I was excited for this reboot, but sadly, it was a largely toothless and lackluster impersonation of the original. Still, Peak was very good! She plays Zoya Lott, a newcomer to the high-status New York City preparatory school who finds out that her late birth mother had another daughter. After Zoya and her half-sister, the wealthy and popular Julien Calloway (Jordan Alexander), make plans to meet up, they end up attending Constance Billard together ... but Zoya, who doesn't come from extreme privilege, struggles to fit in with Julien and her high society friends.

Again, this version of "Gossip Girl" is entirely too concerned with social justice crusades, whereas in the original show, the 20-somethings did insane stuff like sell each other for hotels. (Social justice is ... just not the point of a show like "Gossip Girl!") It was ultimately canceled after its Season 2 finale aired, leaving the story unfinished ... but it also freed Peak up for bigger and better opportunities.

In terms of her big-screen work, Whitney Peak has appeared in a solid mix of independent project and a few bigger movies — aside from "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping." In 2022, Peak showed up in the supporting role of Becca in the legacy sequel "Hocus Pocus 2," and I already mentioned that she was in "Molly's Game," which marked her film debut.

Elsewhere, Peak led films like the independent horror movie "Eye for an Eye," directed by Colin Tilley and adapted from Elisa Victoria's book "Mr. Sandman" — in that, Peak plays a young woman grieving the tragic loss of her parents who finds herself newly traumatized by a shocking, violent incident in her new home in Florida. Peak also appeared in the action thriller "Trap House" alongside Sophia Lillis, Inde Navarrette, Jack Champion, and Bobby Cannavale, as well as Tommy Wirkola's survival film "Thrash" with Phoebe Dynevor and Djimon Hounsou.

You can see Peak as Lenore Dove Baird in "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" in theaters now.

#3453. The Apple Watch Series 11 Is $100 Off in Walmart's Early Black Friday Sale

If you’ve been counting down to Black Friday and hoping for a deal on an Apple Watch, there’s no time like the present: Walmart recently launched its early Black Friday tech deals, and the rarely discounted Apple Watch Series 11 is currently $100 off, bringing the 42mm GPS model down to $299 (originally $399). The 46mm GPS model is $329 (originally $429), while the GPS + Cellular versions start at $399 and are also $100 off.

Though it has been supplanted by the Series 12, released earlier this fall, the Series 11 is still a great buy. It lasts up to 24 hours, making it a great option for everyday use and sleep tracking, and a 15-minute charge provides around eight hours of use. It has a strong selection of health features, including wrist temperature sensing, sleep score, ECG, heart-rate monitoring, and hypertension notifications, as well as detailed workout tracking. Compared with the Series 10, this aluminum model’s Ion-X display is twice as scratch-resistant. It’s also water-resistant to 50 meters.

While it doesn’t have the Series 12’s new processor or updated health-tracking features, the Apple Watch Series 11 is a great pick for your first Apple Watch or as an upgrade from an older model, such as the Series 8. Its large display, durability, and versatile staple features deliver the core Apple Watch experience at a more affordable price, especially if you don’t want Apple’s latest Audio Intelligence features.

Prime Day and Black Friday are the two best times of the year to get the best deals on most purchases. Of course, depending on what you're shopping for, you might find other opportunities throughout the year, but in general, Prime Day and Black Friday have the best sales.

Black Friday used to be bigger for major retailers and more expensive tech and appliances, while Cyber Monday was better for cheaper tech and gave smaller businesses a chance to compete online. Nowadays, though, the distinction is almost meaningless. Every major retailer will offer sales on both days, and the smart move is to know what you want, do your research, or refer to guides like our Black Friday and Cyber Monday coverage that have done all the vetting for you.

#3452. Brandon Sanderson’s Mistborn TTRPG Solves the Biggest Problem With Licensed Games

The wildly ambitious campaign takes generations

The wildly ambitious campaign takes generations

Licensed tabletop role-playing games provide players with a new way to experience their favorite franchises like Star Wars, Star Trek, and the Lord of the Rings. But those adventures always come with a big question about how player characters are supposed to make their mark on stories that already have their own legendary heroes. Rather than erasing canon characters or turning them into quest-givers, the wildly ambitious Mistborn Legacy campaign for the Cosmere Roleplaying Game allows players to forge legends as powerful as any of Brandon Sanderson’s characters.

Sanderson has written seven Mistborn novels set between two distinct eras. The first trilogy exists in a bleak time when most of the world is uninhabitable. The immortal Lord Ruler crushes all dissent and brutally oppresses most people. The second series kicks off 300 years later at a time when the world has been restored and transformed into something resembling a blend of the Wild West and the Gilded Age. Mistborn Legacy spans both these eras as the PCs work to ensure the Lord Ruler can’t return.

Brotherwise Games’ designers worked closely with Sanderson and his longtime collaborator Dan Wells to devise a way for the players to really matter in the story of Mistborn. They take the historical view that the concentration of wealth and power is problematic in every era, whether that’s the nobles in Era One or the railroad barons and weapons manufacturers in Era Two. The players are always acting from a position of weakness as they try to uncover the machinations of powerful interests that could undo all of the progress the heroes of Mistborn sacrificed to make possible.

The campaign introduces the Eternity Spike, an artifact created through mass human sacrifice that could imbue someone with power that rivals the Lord Ruler. It cannot be destroyed and is actively pursued by a secret society. Era One strongly evokes the original trilogy, as players take on the role of a crew of thieves infiltrating high society and making allies of urchins and revolutionaries. There’s a whole scene where the players have to impress people at a secret masquerade ball and try to untangle a love triangle, but there are also tough fights against twisted monsters and killers trained to negate the players’ magical powers.

Era Two leans more into that series’ pulp adventure sensibilities. The Gilded Trio resemble Indiana Jones villains as they search for ancient secrets that can lead them to a lost magical artifact. Era One can get quite dark, and while Era Two has its own twisted villains, it’s a lighter adventure involving illegal street racing and spending time on a university campus.

The sections are connected by a legacy system, with hooks for the party at large and each individual character archetype. The characters become legends akin to Sanderson’s characters like Vin and Kelsier, so the game master takes notes on what they did at key moments as they inspire future fashion trends and build organizations that stand the test of time. The book is filled with “legacy moments” that create special conflicts or opportunities in Era One depending on whehter your character is a convict, urchin, or veteran. After completing the Era One adventure, players create new characters with connections to other players’ previous characters. For instance, the storyteller in Era Two is working on the convict’s biography while the rookie is inspired by the veteran’s heroism.

Both parts are meticulously detailed, packed with maps, character art, and subsystems for mini-games and downtime planning. There are also detailed handouts for everything from party invitations to newspaper articles. Getting a group together to play through a campaign of this scale requires commitment, but GMs and players are rewarded by an extremely rich world filled with plenty of ways to make a mark.

Mistborn Legacy is best run by someone familiar with Sanderson’s series, but there are so many character hooks that it would be easy for Cosmere novices to slip into the game world. Even if you’re not already invested in the story of Scadrial, it’s easy to empathize with heroes trying to fight oppression and ensure that the future is bright for everyone. Rather than making players feel like they’re walking in the shadows of the series’ protagonists, Mistborn Legacy lets them preserve what they built while forging their own legends.

It’s officially Grand Theft Auto VI launch day. It really does feel surreal to say GTA 6 is a game you can play right now. It’s been a long road, but Vice City is now open to visitors.

To celebrate GTA 6’s historic launch, Tom’s Guide is bringing you live coverage of launch day, with the latest news, our first impressions as we start playing the game for ourselves, and, because it’s Black Friday shopping season, there are also plenty of great gaming deals that can upgrade your experience, letting you experience GTA 6 at its absolute best.

I know you’d probably rather be playing the game right now, but if you can’t get to a console just yet, stick around for all the latest updates and best deals on GTA 6 launch day.

Grand Theft Auto VI is now available for PlayStation 5 and XBOX Series X|S. https://t.co/8QXtlg7RmP https://t.co/SjphLTnbLQNovember 19, 2026

To quote super underrated British indie rockers Circa Waves, "it took a long, long time to get here, but we made it." Rockstar Games has just posted on its social accounts to note that Grand Theft Auto VI is "now available." Okay, so it's been playable in most regions for more than 12 hours now, but still it's a reminder that GTA 6 has arrived, the 13 year wait for a new GTA game is over, and Vice City is our to explore freely.

As noted, I'm only 90 minutes into GTA 6 — sadly couldn't stay up too late last night — but I want to hear how much time you've spend in Vice City already. Is anybody already at the 10 hour mark? Or do you just have a couple of hours in GTA 6 so far?

It's been over 24 hours since GTA 6 reviews went live, and it still holds a near-perfect 99 score on Metacritic. After 150 reviews, it's the current highest-reviewed video game on the platform. Some other titles have the same score, but not with this many reviews accounted for. It's remarkable that Rockstar Games actually delivered on the extremely high levels of hype! Based on my limited playtime, it deserves the 99, too.

I won’t lie — I’m biased as a GTA fan. This is more than a game. It’s a chance to look back at how far you’ve come over 13 years.

But one thing remains the same across both. That feeling of escaping to another living world that nobody but Rockstar can capture. I played four hours when it launched at midnight (currently on my third cup of coffee to keep going), and I’m truly floored by the scope of GTA VI.

Setting aside the fact it’s a beautiful-looking game with a stellar soundtrack and a Leonida that feels truly alive, the biggest thing that’s stood out to me so far is what I’ll call the “Red Dead-ification” of GTA.

I spoke to my boss about doing some day-to-day menial tasks and DIY in-game — such as fixing my roof at 2 am — and the reaction was “...why?” It’s a good question, and the answer is the same as Red Dead Redemption 2. As much as the world feels alive, you feel like a part of it with your own personal stories and supporting cast of people you actually care about.

A skeptic’s take would be to say Rockstar’s made an “adulting” educational game for millennials. But in reality, these small elements are significant in really making you emotionally invested in the characters, their personalities and their stories.

Playing GTA 6 into the early hours of today reminded me how useful a second controller can be. My first DualSense ran out of battery just 30 mins into my session, but because I had a spare fully charged one, I could swap over. No need to pause playing or to play with a wired connection. If you need a spare DualSense, or just a shiny new one, PS5 DualSense controllers are $54 at Amazon (down from $74).

If for some reason you haven't already bought GTA 6, I bet you feeling the FOMO right about now. There's still time to join the party over in Vice City ahead of the weekend. You can either purchase the game digitally on the Xbox and PlayStation Store, or you can grab a "code in box" edition, which comes with a nifty poster (pictured above). I'm far too early to make a definitive judgement on GTA 6, but so far it's blowing me away.

I stayed up past my bedtime last time to play GTA 6 as soon as it unlocked at midnight. I've only played roughly 90 minutes of the game, but I'm already overwhelmed, and seriously impressed. Graphically the game is stunning, but it's the rich detail of the world that has grabbed me out of the gate. Vice City is a place I just want to wander. I didn't even complete any mission beyond the prologue, I just walked the streets, taking in the sounds and signs of this overwhelming location.

The wait is over, Grand Theft Auto VI has arrived. Millions of gamers are taking their first steps in Vice City, and to celebrate, we're talking all things GTA 6 today in this live blog. I'll have news, first impressions from across the Tom's Guide team, some interactive polls (I want to hear your early thoughts, too), and plenty of early Black Friday deals so you can upgrade your gaming setup for the hours of play ahead.

#3450. Film Independent’s New President Wants to Build an L.A. Powerhouse — and Shake Up the Spirit Awards

Major change is afoot at Film Independent, the Los Angeles nonprofit that supports indie filmmakers. Not merely a restructuring of departments over the coming years or a revamping of its centerpiece offering, the four-decades-old Spirit Awards, but something more expansive, place-based, and integrated.Since the tragic passing of Josh Welsh, a beloved figure in the indie community who served as Film Independent’s president for 12 years, many felt a leadership vacuum at a time when the L.A. film industry was in severe crisis, from productions rapidly departing the city to studio mergers.

Juan Devis, appointed the new president in April, now envisions Film Independent to become something akin to a nonprofit studio, and equally, a pivotal cultural institution in Los Angeles, to be considered in the same breath as LACMA, the guilds, or the Academy Museum. A day after announcing John Early and Kate Berlant as the new hosts of the Spirit Awards, Devis, in his first public interview since his appointment, spoke to IndieWire about his all-encompassing vision and gave exclusives on the latest promotions following a significant restructuring.Devis’ office sits in the same corner of Film Independent’s headquarters in Miracle Mile as Welsh’s, and though it shares a similar calm, shaped by majestic 270-degree, ninth-story views of the Hollywood Hills to South L.A., Devis has made it bespoke with mementos from his childhood. His father’s paintings circa 1979 hang on the back wall. In Bogotá, Colombia, where he grew up, his father was a painter, his mother a social worker, and Devis a Star Wars buff. Related Stories ‘Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma’ Comes to VHS in Special Pan-and-Scan Edition from Mutant ‘Epic Zombie Christmas,’ Family Comedy About Senior Citizens and Teenagers Making a Horror Film, Begins Production

Gleefully showing me miniature slides of scenes he recreated from the franchise’s toys he owned or borrowed, Devis reminisced about how, as an eight-year-old, he’d direct his family to reenact the movie from a script he recorded on a vintage audio cassette. He cast his father as Darth Vader, his sister as Princess Leia (before the revelations of “The Empire Strikes Back”), and himself, of course, as Lucas Skywalker.This obsession with film would lead Devis to major in it at Emerson College in Boston, return to Colombia to shoot his thesis, and find himself working in Los Angeles for New Regency on the Warner Bros. lot, driving up and down Barham Blvd and taking meetings at the Peninsula. He didn’t connect with the glamour of it all, and was eager to reconcile his “indie kid” notion of film with what he was seeing in L.A. In the early ‘90s, that meant the race uprising, the Northridge earthquake, O.J. Simpson, and studios eager to replicate the success of Robert Rodriguez’s “El Mariachi.”

Devis would spend 15 years at PBS, connecting, in his words, “storytelling with placemaking” and pioneering interactive documentaries, while serving on the boards of nonprofits like Arts for LA and as a California Arts Council member. When he got the phone call about his potential interest in becoming president of Film Independent, he saw a deeply “civic” role for storytelling that Devis felt was missing in the turbulent media landscape.Prior to accepting, Devis did his homework. He spoke to board members whom he is friends with, looked at their social media, and asked about the branding and positioning of the Spirit Awards (which he has never attended) vis-à-vis all the other “amazing programs supporting independent filmmaking both locally and globally.”Devis said he ran a collaborative workshop with staff leadership, asking them to break down everything they do. Film Independent does everything from development, funding, and production to distribution, education, and celebration, but these activities weren’t quite talking to each other.

For instance, the organization provides more than two dozen grants and donor-named fellowships across many scopes and areas. The #FiPresents folks offer an array of programming, including live reads such as the recent “Secretary” led by Jane Schoenbrun, suggesting the org’s expertise in exhibition. Numerous labs, from the Screenwriting, Fiction Producing, and Episodic Labs to robust international initiatives such as Global Media Makers, reach far to find underrepresented artists, taking them through development and mentorship. Fast Track is a four-day finance market that connects the film teams to funders. And the annual Forum and the triennial Sloan Summit convene folks from all aspects of the industry, making them key events on the nonprofit’s calendar.“I realized that Film Independent actually supports the entire life cycle of independent makers,” said Devis, “but they don’t see their programs and activities in that way. [Everything] is very siloed. So I started to really litigate that. For example, the [Sundance 2026 feature] ‘Union County’ found two-thirds of its funding through Fast Track. Project Involve’s shorts have turned into features and shows. Yet we don’t see ourselves as holding value in that regard. We simply create the conditions for these [films] to happen, and they go off on their own.”His solution? “If we are able to accordion out these [activities], to start to look at a vision of an interconnected organization that is supporting the entire life cycle, to look at how we can actually serve the filmmaker intentionally in each of these areas, then we are creating a different proposition. That is one of the main shifts we are doing right now. It’s looking at ourselves much more as a potential nonprofit studio.”Becoming something akin to a nonprofit studio is a huge cultural and institutional shift, so surely there must be resistance, since the staff has been functioning efficiently in their silos. Devis suggested that, generally, everyone is on board. “Staff needs to understand that we need to operate in a different way. As I talk to independent filmmakers, they [already] need the support in these areas, and they’re not getting it. It is a shift away from the [individual] lab mentality to the [full] life cycle. It is a shift in the culture of how we see the value we provide to the filmmakers, to our partners, and to the ecosystem in general.”The Humana Foundation grant is a pilot program to operationalize this shift. Five shorts will be selected from a submissions call, and each will receive $100,000 to develop stories about seniors’ contributions to society. Devis said, “We could have easily said, ‘Why don’t we create a lab to develop intergenerational stories about aging?’” But the goal is for Film Independent “to produce these shorts and other films down the line, identify director-producer teams, develop the IP, and figure out how to distribute it.” That’s how Devis positions the proposal to funders.In the competitive landscape of similar organizations like Sundance, the American Film Institute, or Gotham Institute, Devis argues Film Independent is singular in its goal of becoming like a nonprofit studio. Maybe ITVS, he suggests, but that is tied to documentary making and distribution via PBS. “Our landscape is completely open.”In this regard, IndieWire can exclusively reveal a series of promotions resulting from the three-to-five year restructuring strategy Devis has initiated.Kate Walker D’Angelo, previously senior director of Development, has been upped to executive vice president of Strategy and Institutional Advancement, which Devis said is a crucial top-level position, in part because of all the work Film Independent is doing with the government right now, and how it will continue to collaborate on the OTIS College Report on the Creative Economy with the goal of ultimately influencing policy. Walker D’Angelo will continue to lead Philanthropic Fundraising and Partnerships, with new responsibilities including oversight of Community and Membership, and Marketing and Communications.Returning to the idea of “life cycle,” Devis also applies it longitudinally. Proud of Film Independent’s Youth Program for middle and high schoolers, Devis said, “Youth are such an integral part of the industry because that’s where filmmaking begins.” Devis wants to propel an integration not just across the vertical — i.e., from development and financing to producing, distribution, exhibition and celebration — but also across filmmakers’ lives. They already host labs for emerging filmmakers, which for many is around age 27 or 28. “We are helping these filmmakers enter the ecosystem. So it doesn’t make sense to me to separate our youth lab programs from what we used to call artist development.”One implication of this shift is a greater emphasis on curation. “Can we identify projects that are ready to be moved to other areas, those which need packaging, additional funding?” Devis asked rhetorically. To this end, another major move will combine what were previously siloed as “artist development” programs and labs, “international” programs, “education” initiatives, and “youth” programs into one department headed by Angela Lee, who has been promoted to vice president of Creative Development and Production.This is a remarkable integration, given how unique (and relatively less publicized) Film Independent’s international programs have been. Initiatives like the Global Media Makers (GMM) Residency are funded by a State Department grant (e.g., the 2026 Residency, which concluded in October, invited nine filmmakers from Malaysia, plus folks from other Asian countries). Devis acknowledged that “we are very lucky to have this grant. It is very unusual. But those things are very volatile, right? I have to think about the sustainability of these programs. I have been in the nonprofit sector for a very long time. The worry is when you rely on one source to keep you going.”

The big question: Where do the Spirit Awards fit into this grand reconfiguration?Devis is very excited and optimistic about this prospect, since for him, the annual event, which will enter its 42nd year in 2027, is “the best place to tell our story. I don’t want to separate the Spirit Awards from Film Independent. They are the head of the sphere of so many things we do, and they should be a reflection of our values, programs, intentions, and aspirations.”“And they should not be just an awards show.”In their first move from the legendary beach tent in Santa Monica to the Hollywood Palladium about a mile away from where the Oscars are held, the 2026 Spirit Awards show garnered tepid to more harshly critical reviews, not just because of the venue. Devis is aware of the reception, even though he hadn’t yet been appointed president. The problem, he said, is that the Spirit Awards ended up being “just another stop” on the “Lazy Susan” that is the “exhausting” awards circuit, losing everything that made them unique.“I think we need to return to when [the Spirit Awards] were a party, a true celebration. This involves a healthy dose of disruption. I actually think we shouldn’t fight the fact that we’re at the Palladium. We’re in the heart of Hollywood. The film and TV business in L.A. and in California has taken a very big hit. We need to celebrate our resilience in the place it all began. Everybody was very sad we moved from the beach and that people could bike to get there. Luckily enough, I never went to any of those and don’t have that reference. But I can imagine what this party could be at the Palladium.”Here, Devis spoke with the pride of being an Angeleno of more than three decades. “One of the first things is to embrace the idea of LA. I truly believe independent films are small businesses. We [the Spirit Awards] are the small business of the ecosystem, right? We’re in the neighborhood where the cool restaurant just opened up, with the bookstore, the bodega, and the Armenian-owned [enterprise]. That’s job creation. That’s entrepreneurship. That’s community building.”Devis has already begun implementing this vision for the Film Independent Spirit Awards. “One of the first things I did when I got the job was to call the city and say we want to close Sunset Boulevard. We want to have fans, and the city be a part of the celebration. Then, I invited Roman Coppola to be a fresh editorial voice, and it has been a super fun journey. I also think John [Early] and Kate [Berlant] are just the perfect hosts of the moment. We want to do something spectacular, even if it’s not perfect, right? We want to ‘undust’ ourselves from expectations we shouldn’t hold, that we should be a ‘proper’ awards show. What made the Spirit Awards shine is the opposite,” bringing up the example of the 2020 segment featuring Gay Men’s Choir of Los Angeles from Jordan Firstman that ended in an obsessed crescendo to queer icon Laura Dern.

Earlier this summer, fresh off the news of Film Independent’s biggest grant ever — $2.55 million from the Perenchio Foundation — the organization announced two new nomination categories: Best International First Feature, which Devis said reflects his commitment to capture the immense breadth of international cinema, and a new Digital Creator Award as a part of its Emerging Filmmaker Grants. “New formats and platforms extend the definition of “independent,” he said, claiming that the sensation of “Obsession” was just coincidental to the announcement of this award.Moreover, the Berlin Film Festival was added to the list of qualifying festivals, and the Robert Redford Environmental Vision Award was announced in June to recognize a narrative film or TV work engaging with environmental issues in an innovative way. Not announced yet because he’s still pondering it, Devis also wants to celebrate below-the-line workers at the Awards, since they are pivotal to L.A.’s film ecosystem.In fact, Los Angeles is the true cornerstone of Devis’ overarching vision, connecting, it would seem, his past to the organization’s future and fueling his dreams to foster integrated life cycles for local and global filmmakers across their life spans.The way to do that? Here, Devis thumped his desk with his knuckles, speaking with excitement and pride.“I want Film Independent to become a really important cultural institution for the city. Going back to this idea of small businesses, creatives, and the economy it generates, [we need to] celebrate who we are. MOCA celebrates contemporary artists. LACMA has a potpourri of things. So does Lucas. The Academy Museum does their thing. We need to move away from seeing ourselves as a trade organization and claim our space as a cultural institution.”Big, bright dreams. Devis’ repositioning of the nonprofit to function as a studio, along with the major restructuring and promotions, forms the basis for drawing a line from a shift in management strategy to a stake in cultural and institutional influence. The LA Film Festival may not come back, as some still hope it does, but Film Independent already has the Forum, the Changemaker Awards, youth screenings, prestige screenings, live reads, filmmaker conversations, and, of course, the centerpiece Spirit Awards. Devis said they are exploring how to bring these different live events under one tent, so to speak.To that end, another major promotion involves appointing Rachel Bleemer and Shawn Davis (the longtime Spirit Awards EP) as joint vice presidents of editorial and cultural experiences. Devis said they’ll be brilliant because they complement each other, and also signals a plan to reestablish their former partnership with LACMA.Finally, Valecia Phillips will lead Film Independent’s finance and operations department, even as Devis foreshadows a “digital ecosystem and innovation department” to leverage their existing streaming service, Vision Media, with potentially an app and a digital marketplace for the public. The goal is to hire somebody by 2027 Q1.Indie film as a category is famous for supposedly dying multiple deaths, with folks clutching pearls or taking to the soapbox with each new cycle of systemic change. Devis, as a Film Independent newcomer, wants to armor it with generative life cycles — entire movies, entire careers — while embedding the force of his staff, partners, and stakeholders in the cultural ecosystem of Los Angeles. His vision makes for a compelling case study of how to adapt, lead, and reposition during a prolonged industry crisis.Thursday, November 19, would have been the late Josh Welsh’s 64th birthday. One can imagine Welsh, remembered fondly for his hobby as a guitarist in his band Meatyard, signing off and even stringing along to Devis’ tunes.

#3449. The Further Mis-Adventures Of Cliff Booth Review: Fincher And Tarantino's Mean-Spirited Hollywood Sequel

There was a time in my life when a movie made by David Fincher and Quentin Tarantino would be the biggest cinematic event ever. Not to get all film bro on you, but Fincher and Tarantino were very important filmmakers to me in my youth. That's not to say they aren't still important to me now ... but the luster has faded a bit. Fincher has spent the last few years making movies specifically for Netflix, and while those films — "Mank" and "The Killer" — have their charms, they pale in comparison to his previous work, so much so that I'd say the last great movie was "Gone Girl" in 2014 (for what it's worth, Fincher's exclusivity with Netflix is now over).

As for Tarantino, while he tends to make everyone's eyes roll when he gives a new hot take-laden interview, I still think he has the juice. However, the "Pulp Fiction" auteur has decided that he will only direct 10 movies and then hang up his filmmaking spurs. Because of this, Tarantino seems hesitant to direct a movie again, since that hypothetical movie would be his last. He came close to making "The Movie Critic" only to drop the idea entirely, and now he's working on directing his first stage play, "The Popinjay Cavalier."

But his previous film, "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood," might just be his best. It's certainly near and dear to my heart, as I find it inherently rewatchable. It's a funny, sad, surprisingly sweet hang-out movie that doubles as a slice of alternate Hollywood history. Tarantino has now returned to the world of "Hollywood" with his new script, but again, since he doesn't want to direct his tenth and final movie just yet, he's handed the project over to Fincher.

All of this is a long-winded way of saying that everything about "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" should, in theory, appeal to me, a movie nerd who still considers Fincher and Tarantino to be among the greats. But Fincher's not-so-stellar Netflix output coupled with Tarantino's weird insistence on not directing the movie himself muted my enthusiasm a bit, as have some lackluster trailers. On top of all that, Fincher and Tarantino have vastly different movie making styles. Would a union between the pair even work? I'm pleased to say the answer is "Yes." Sort of. While I was cautious about "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth," it eventually won me over. But it's not quite the movie I think anyone is expecting, and that's going to catch a few folks off guard.

"Once Upon a Time in Hollywood" introduced us to washed-up actor Rick Dalton, played by Leonardo DiCaprio, and his trusty stunt man sidekick Cliff Booth, played by Brad Pitt. Pitt turned in a funny, scene-stealing performance that landed him an Oscar, but Cliff seemed destined to be a supporting player in Rick's life. "Cliff Booth" turns him into a leading man, and I'm not entirely sure that's a good idea. Because without Rick Dalton by his side, what is Cliff Booth? I think the case can be made that Cliff Booth is a very charming psychopath. He's certainly not against brutally murdering people, and while he's highly capable and smooth as silk, there doesn't seem to be a whole lot going on in Cliff Booth's head. Rick and his internal struggles were part of what gave "Hollywood" its heart. Without him around, "Cliff Booth" ends up frequently feeling cold and cruel.

Pitt's Cliff became so lovable and likable in the first movie that I can't help but think Tarantino, always one to subvert expectations, is deliberately hammering home the point that for all his charms, Cliff is not exactly a good guy. He's a cypher; an idealized version of machismo — a men's pulp magazine hero brought to life. He lives fast and hard, likes drugs and booze, constantly risks life and limb, flirts with every woman he encounters, can kick everyone's butt, and still finds time to chill out and watch TV with his dear old dad. And yes, he occasionally murders people. Is "Cliff Booth" an attempt by Tarantino, or maybe Fincher, to remind us that this guy isn't nearly as cool as he seems?

In "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth," it's 1977, and Cliff's movie stunt days seem to behind him, especially since Rick Dalton has moved to Australia, where he's currently starring on a popular Aussie TV show. Cliff keeps busy, though, working an assortment of odd jobs. He runs the projector at the New Beverly Cinema, he works as a bartender making all sorts of elaborate margaritas, he participates in a demolition derby, and he even occasionally appears in an X-rated movie or two.

On the side, however, Cliff also works as a fixer for some of his old Hollywood friends. If they get into a jam that they can't go to the cops about, Cliff is willing to step in and work something out — for a price. And sometimes that results in a body count.

Cliff has become a legend due to his fight with Bruce Lee and the time he killed those damn hippies who broke into Rick's home (it's also worth noting that in "Hollywood," people suspected Cliff of murdering his wife, although that incident isn't mentioned here). At the end of the day, Cliff comes home to the apartment he shares with his dad Gus (Peter Weller) to watch old movies and TV. Weller's Gus is the warmest part of this surprisingly cold movie, and the banter between Cliff and his father is laid-back and believable in a way that made me wish the entire movie was just the two of them shooting the breeze.

"Cliff Booth" is in no hurry, but eventually a shaggy Hollywood crime thriller plot emerges. The logistics of what's going on are hilariously convoluted, but Cliff is hired by manic actor Charlie Peters (Scott Caan, looking eerily like his late father in nearly every frame) to help get him out of some trouble. Cliff doesn't exactly like Charlie, but he does like Charlie's wife Toni (Carla Gugino), whom he had a love affair with over a decade ago. And Cliff really likes Charlie's agent, amazonian goddess Karen Crosby, played Elizabeth Debicki.

The flirty relationship between Cliff and Karen is meant to be sweet and romantic, but while Pitt and Debicki are both quite good in their respective roles (Debicki is particularly funny, bugging her eyes out at all the ludicrous things that happen), they don't have much chemistry. There's the glimmer of something interesting in how Cliff reveals he's a masochist who gets off on the idea of Karen slapping him around, but this angle is ultimately treated as little more than a throwaway gag.

While "Cliff Booth" has the same hang-out movie vibes as "Hollywood," there are bursts of brutal violence that left me uncomfortable. Tarantino is no stranger to violence, and the big finale of "Hollywood" is drenched in blood. But here is where the styles of Fincher and Tarantino seem to clash the most. Tarantino's violence is almost always hyper-stylized and over-the-top. Influenced by countless splatter flicks and kung-fu movies, Tarantino shoots his violence in ways that are so ludicrously graphic that they become funny in a twisted sort of way.

Fincher, however, has a more realistic approach, which results in a handful of brutal scenes — most notably when the film's villains, a pair of gangsters from the Philippines (played by Matt Groove and JB Tadena) butcher an entire family during a home invasion. This moment has no bearing on Cliff's story, and seems to only exist to show us how bad these bad guys are. Which is fine, in theory, but Fincher stages it in such a cruel, unpleasant way that when he tries to lighten the mood in the following scenes, it rings hollow.

There's a conversation worth having here about movie violence, I suppose. Which is the more questionable approach: depicting these moments in an unrealistic over-the-top fashion, or making them as real (and therefore upsetting) as possible? Again, I can't help but think that Tarantino is intentionally trying to flip the script and deliver something harsher after the good vibes of "Hollywood." The '60s are over, and here we're at the tail-end of the '70s, nearing the '80s. It makes sense for the vibes to be drastically different. But intentional or not, this contrast between Fincher and Tarantino makes "Cliff Booth" more mean-spirited than expected.

Midway through the film, Tarantino's script gives Karen a meaty monologue about movies. Before becoming an agent, Karen was a budding film critic, and in her professional opinion, movies should entertain above all else. While she thinks movies can be artistic, she doesn't think of them as art. It's 1977, and the movie everyone is talking about is "Star Wars," which Karen thinks proves her point: audiences don't want a fancy cinematic meal, they want movie fast food. Even "The Godfather" is little more than pulp in her estimation.

I don't think a lifelong movie nerd like Tarantino actually believes this (and I don't think Fincher does, either), but this little speech must be here for a reason. Are we meant to just sit back and enjoy the ride of "Cliff Booth" and not think too much about what's unfolding here? Or is the film itself trying to prove Karen's theory wrong? For all it's moments of comedy, there's a cold darkness lurking beneath "Cliff Booth" that keeps it from being fully entertaining. It's as if Fincher and Tarantino don't quite have a grasp on the material.

Regardless, "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" is Fincher's best movie in years — since "Gone Girl," really. While I do think he and Tarantino don't quite mix as well as we'd all hoped, the material has energized the filmmaker to craft a great-looking movie with several standout set pieces (I particularly liked a montage, told entirely via press photographs, showing Karen attending the premiere of "Looking for Mr. Goodbar").

Still, I can't help but wish Tarantino had just gone ahead and directed this himself. If he had, I think the tonal clashes might've been smoothed out considerably. "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood" felt like something of a masterpiece to me when I first saw it, and the film's hefty runtime was a blessing rather than a curse — I wanted to spend as much time in this world with these characters as possible.

But that world is nowhere to be found in "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth." Tarantino clearly didn't want to tread the same ground all over again when he banged out this script, and there's nothing wrong with that. But if everything is so different this time around, why would we want to check back in with Cliff at all, then? Especially without Rick by his side? "Cliff Booth" builds towards a memorable, brutal, action-packed climax before just sort of giving up and rolling credits. It's as if, in the end, everyone involved realized that old "Hollywood" magic was finally gone.

"The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" will be released exclusively in IMAX on November 25, 2026 for a two-week engagement before streaming on Netflix December 23, 2026.

#3448. These Are the Best Ways to Encrypt Your Email

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

As this in-depth explainer from Adaptive Security describes, most emails are encrypted in transit via Transport Layer Security (TLS), which prevents anyone from reading your message as it travels from server to server. However, encryption is temporarily stripped at each server: content is received and processed in plaintext and then re-encrypted when it leaves, meaning it could be read, logged, and distributed by the server provider.

Emails are also typically encrypted at rest—for example, while sitting on Google's servers and in a Gmail recipient's inbox. But this only prevents someone with physical access to the server hardware from reading messages, as Google still holds the encryption key and can access stored data. And, as PCMag points out, Google is scanning your messages to a degree, and it (along with other email providers) can and will hand emails over to law enforcement and government agencies in some cases.

If you have an account with a major email provider like Gmail, Outlook, or Apple Mail, you can add a third-party tool that layers an encryption protocol like OpenPGP on top of your existing account. PCMag recommends PreVeil, SecureMyEmail, and Virtru (which is limited to Gmail users in Chrome) for those who want to keep their current emails. Mailvelope is a browser add-on (and therefore a desktop-only tool) available in Chrome, Firefox, and Edge, though it can also be installed on other browsers, like Brave, that are built on the same architecture. FlowCrypt integrates with Gmail and Google Workspace on desktop and mobile.

Note that enterprise users of Google Workspace and Microsoft 365 have access to true end-to-end encryption without third-party add-ons. Gmail's Confidential mode and Outlook's Encrypt feature, available to all users, are not E2EE equivalents, as Google and Microsoft, respectively, still manage the keys.

For those who are willing to start fresh with a new email address (or who have a custom domain), providers like Proton Mail or Tuta offer native end-to-end encryption. The caveat: by default, this is only between users on the same service, so from one Proton user to another. If you want to send an end-to-end encrypted email from Proton to a Gmail user, for example, you have to set up password protection (and share the password via another secure channel) or use a PGP-compatible tool like those listed above. You can also Proton's Gmail integration does allow for end-to-end encryption, but only if both Gmail parties are using the Proton integration.

#3446. Does Brad Pitt's Cliff Booth Movie Have A Post-Credits Scene? A Spoiler-Free Guide

Brad Pitt is back as Cliff Booth. The character he first played in Quentin Tarantino's "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood" is back for his very own spin-off with the aptly-titled "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth." Pitt won Best Supporting Actor for his work at the confusing, chaotic, cathartic 2020 Oscars. So having him back in that role is a big deal. But does his return as Cliff end when the credits roll? Or is there more to it?

Tarantino only wrote the script this time, with Pitt's friend and frequent collaborator David Fincher ("Fight Club," "Seven") taking over as director. Neither of these filmmakers are known for including post-credits scenes in their movies, but it's the sort of thing we can never really rule out these days. Especially since this spin-off is being made for Netflix. To that end, the "Cliff Booth" movie marks the end of an era for Fincher and Netflix, as the director has opted not to renew his deal with the streamer. So this is a swan song of sorts. One that viewers will be paying very close attention to.

We're here to offer up a spoiler-free guide when it comes to the movie's credits scene situation. Seriously, we're not going to spoil anything meaningful at all, merely arming viewers with essential information to enhance the viewing experience. So proceed without fear. With that out of the way, let's get to it.

Yes, "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" has one credits scene that audiences very much need to be aware of. It's more of a mid-credits scene that appears around 30 seconds (maybe a little more) after the credits initially begin. Without getting into details, this is a fairly important scene and something that viewers will want to stick around for. Whether you're seeing it in a theater or streaming from home, keep this in mind.

This is one of the biggest new titles coming to Netflix in December 2026, which should help end the year on a high note for the streaming service. The sequel/spin-off takes place in 1977, eight years after the events of "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood." Cliff is no longer working as a stuntman, instead spending his days as a projectionist and bartender. But he also works as a "fixer," solving situations for Hollywood's great and, sometimes, not so good.

#3445. 10 Privacy Hacks Every Mac User Should Know

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Enabling the macOS Firewall (which is off by default) adds a layer of protection against external devices on your wifi network, as well as unauthorized apps from initiating a connection to your device. Turning on Stealth Mode prevents your Mac from even responding to these requests, essentially making it invisible to anything that's scanning a network you're connected to. This makes it more difficult for hackers and malware to know your device exists, much less attack it. This can interfere with certain essential activity when you're on your home network, but it's a valuable security setting when on public wifi. You can leave Firewall on all the time and enable Stealth Mode only as needed. Go to Settings > Network > Firewall, flip the toggle, then hit Options to manage Stealth Mode.

Images and screenshots contain metadata, such as timestamps, device and hardware details, and, in the case of photos, physical location. Much of this information is stripped automatically when you share files to social media or via encrypted messaging apps, but if you're sending them via text or email, posting to forums, or sharing over AirDrop, metadata remains intact. You can easily remove metadata from your images right on your desktop. Select the file and hit control + click to bring up an options menu, then go to Quick Actions > Convert Image. Uncheck the box next to Preserve Metadata, then hit Convert. (This is also useful for quickly converting HEIC to JPEG without opening a separate app.)

If you're using iCloud to store photos, files, and device backups, your data is encrypted on Apple's servers and in transit. Apple still holds the decryption key, which is useful if you somehow get locked out of your account and need help recovering it, but for sensitive data—including device backups—end-to-end encryption is the most secure way to ensure no one but you can gain access. Advanced Data Protection is an opt-in setting for iCloud that encrypts your information end to end. You'll need to set up an alternative recovery method, such as your device passcode with two-factor authentication, a recovery contact, or a recovery key. Be careful, though: If you lose access to this recovery method, you will lose your data. You can enable Advanced Data Protection on your Mac under System Settings > [Your Name] > iCloud > Advanced Data Protection > Turn On. Note that some iCloud data, including passwords and payment methods, are already end-to-end encrypted by default.

#3444. ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ Review: David Fincher’s Breezy Tarantino Spinoff Is a Disappointing Compromise Between Great Directors

The scratchy “vintage” Netflix logo says everything so well that the rest of the movie almost feels like it’s belaboring the point: “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” is a story about a town where half the people are dreaming up the future, the other half are desperate to mythologize the past, and all of them are stuck together in the ugly compromise we call the right fucking now.

Then again, “story” might be too strong a word for the unbothered zen noir that Quentin Tarantino has spun off from his 1969-set hit “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood,” which memorably ended with former TV Western star Rick Dalton and his longtime stuntman Cliff Booth saving Manson Family victim Sharon Tate from the cruel fate that befell her in real life. Los Angeles was built on the promise that history could be rewritten, and that anyone who made their way onto a studio lot could print the legend, but the present is another beast altogether. It’s feral. Unforgiving. It has to be survived before it can be shaped into a story worth telling, even if that isn’t much of a story at all. Related Stories Film Independent’s New President Wants to Build an L.A. Powerhouse — and Shake Up the Spirit Awards ‘Dig’ Review: Amy Poehler’s Talent-Rich Peacock Comedy Barely Scratches the Surface

After decades of trafficking in ultra-fetishistic nostalgia (and continued years of refusing to close the book on his own legend), Tarantino has scripted a conditional surrender to the forward march of time — a film whose modest and spectacularly unbothered protagonist invites his egomaniacal and constantly agitated creator to make a certain peace with the inevitable fact of being left behind. And though it was initially Tarantino’s plan to direct that film himself, handing the reins of this breezy showbiz throwback to modern Hollywood’s most unsentimental technician forces “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” into a muted but fascinating tug-of-war between the past tense and the future perfect (even if that scratchy “vintage” Netflix logo articulates the same tension with a greater clarity of purpose than any other part of this perverse collaboration).

Pleasant enough for a movie so dark, and strangely relaxed for a movie so deeply self-conflicted, “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” is ultimately a story — there’s that word again — about someone changing with the times without letting the times change them in return. It takes place over the span of a few days in the summer of 1977 (even though it builds to the October premiere of “Looking for Mr. Goodbar,” which I suppose might have happened a few months earlier in this parallel universe), when “Star Wars” is the biggest force on Earth and the tough guys of yore are being phased out by the very different kind of daring that New Hollywood brought to the table. Once upon a time, Cliff Booth did his business supporting Rick Dalton on the big screen — reborn here as the lead of a David Fincher film, he’s reintroduced working the projector at the New Beverly Cinema like the hyper-chill uncle Tyler Durden never had (digital cigarette burns and all).

If “The Further Mis-Adventures” doesn’t belabor the reel change from one generation of movies to another, that’s because Cliff doesn’t either. He’s just happy to be there — still hot, cool, and at total peace with himself despite an increasingly violent reputation (a state of mind Brad Pitt might relate to). The world around him is a lot uglier than it was eight years ago, as the vibrant celluloid memory palace of Tarantino’s film has faded into the computational muddiness that Fincher has come to mistake for the truth, but that “don’t mean shit” to Cliff.

Drab cinematography and bad disco aren’t enough to unsettle a guy who lied about his age so that he could join the Philippine resistance as a teenager during World War II. A guy who spontaneously killed his own wife in the span of a shrugged-off flashback, and beat up Bruce Lee as part of a controversial backstory that Tarantino can’t quite bring himself to disavow. Besides, Cliff doesn’t want for glory — he delights in sharing a small apartment with his TV-obsessed dad in Marina del Rey (Gus Booth is played by a winsome and wonderful Peter Weller), and always demurs when someone insists that they know him from somewhere, which is all the time. Manning the booth at a half-empty Fairfax grindhouse might seem like a fall from grace, but — as “Anora” favorite Karren Karagulian learns the hard way in the movie’s self-contained opening scene — underestimate Cliff Booth at your own peril.

Of course, that isn’t Cliff’s only job. If anything, the gig at the New Bev is just a convenient front for his far more lucrative work as a Hollywood fixer, which sees him apply his curious but unyielding moral code to a wide variety of situations — even if Fincher’s movie only has the bandwidth to illustrate a small handful of them. Tarantino might be drawn to the discursive plotting of an Elmore Leonard paperback, but after watching any number of Netflix TV shows that should have been shortened into movies, it’s a cruel irony to see two of our greatest filmmakers slush their talents together into a movie that should have serialized into a long-running TV show, complete with a new guest star every week.

Alas, that’s not the world that streaming hath wrought, and so we have to settle for shape-shifting content that seems equally ill-suited to both small and big screens alike, the elasticity of its intended presentation reflected by the ambiguity of a plot that drifts from a casual hangout session to a brutal crime-thriller and a sweetly abrasive romance without ever becoming much of anything. These different energies ultimately collect around a manic and lunkheaded TV actor named Charlie Peters (a very game Scott Caan, channeling his father), who’s compensated for being short by doing all of his own stunts.

Ordinarily that would give him little reason to link up with Cliff Booth, but it turns out that old Charlie got a little too drunk in Manila one night and put a hit out on his wife, Toni (Carla Gugino), who once made her own sad bid for stardom. After sobering up and falling back in love with his bride, Charlie hoped to call the whole thing off, but the two psychotic Filipino hitmen who just landed in L.A. (Matt Groove and JB Tadena as ruthless brothers Mr. Verdusco and Mr. Verdusco) refuse to go home without being made whole, and so it’s up to Cliff to make everyone happy.

Sounds easy enough, but then we get to the most crucial part: Cliff Booth has a crush. A big one. Or maybe tall would be a better choice of words. Her name is Karen Crosby, she’s Charlie’s exasperated agent, and she’s played by a luminous Elizabeth Debicki (sporting her native Australian accent), who’s charmed by Cliff’s modesty and the slight embarrassment of his machismo. He knows exactly who he is in a town where everyone is busy pretending to be somewhere else, and the drawling magic of Pitt’s performance — which he continues to wear like a second skin — is that he always seems to be content with living in the moment at hand. It’s all a big goof, which is exactly why he’ll kill you for getting in the way of a good story.

Karen, on the other hand, is a former critic who resents Hollywood for the same reason that Cliff is so at home there, and their mutual ability to see each other through the spectacle of it all is a perfect template for how Tarantino and Fincher might have found some common ground. Tarantino gets off on memorializing a world gone by (brace for long conversations about Ralph Meeker’s body fat, along with an extended deep-dive into the nuances of network TV in the ’60s), while Fincher tolerates it as an excuse to play with the tech required to make it look like Johnny Carson is talking to Charlie Peters.

Although slapdash and forgettable by Tarantino’s standards, the writing naturally wants to swim in this strange trench of Tinseltown history. The direction, by contrast, seems motivated by finding the most efficient path to shore. Fincher lives for the thrill of solving things only he would see as problems in the first place, and that mindset proves as contradictory to Cliff Booth’s laid-back, leathery ethos as it is perfectly aligned with the Swiss-watch precision of the hitman in “The Killer.”

Tarantino sees this as a séance, Fincher as a math equation, and while the tension between those approaches can be rich in theme, it’s often dull in function. Neither of these name-brand auteurs is willing to let go as much as the movie they’re making together insists they should, so “The Further Mis-Adventures” ultimately dilutes them both instead of sparking some kind of unexpected kismet between them. It’s no wonder that the scenes between Cliff and Karen accomplish exactly that, as each of them surrenders to the lack of control they share with each other. (A dynamic illustrated through the chaos of an Infinity Racing sequence that ends with the movie’s driest visual joke, a too-rare instance of Cliff making good on his insistence that he’s “a little funny.”)

The film is too watchable for that to sting as much as it could, but the small handful of electric scenes where those dueling energies feel complementary — the climactic sitdown between Cliff and the Verdusco brothers comes to mind — are forced to carry the weight of so much wasted potential. Don’t give me Yahya Abdul-Mateen II as a football-player-turned-Blaxploitation-star if you’re just going to kneecap him like that! Don’t let Karen deride American movies as “hamburgers” if you’re going to make us settle for steak tartare.

Of course, “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” had a similar hard-on for delayed gratification, and for evoking a world that it didn’t have time to more fully explore before it disappeared forever. But that movie was living on borrowed time, this one is striving to live outside of time altogether. “In Hollywood,” Gus says, “two things matter: shelf life, and shelf space.” Neither of those things matter to Cliff Booth — or to the company distributing his mis-adventures. He just wants to make the best of the moment at hand. It can be a lot of fun to watch him try, but it still feels like he’s forced to settle for the present in the end.

Netflix will release “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” in IMAX theaters on Wednesday, November 25. It will be available to stream on Netflix starting Wednesday, December 23.
