#3443. If Your Google Pixel's Camera Is Suddenly Broken, Here's the Fix

Updates are generally good for your devices. The latest Chrome update, for example, patches an actively exploited security vulnerability, while Apple's latest updates stop people from seeing iMessages they shouldn't have access to. In most cases, it's beneficial to update your tech to the latest software version whenever possible.

Sadly, updates aren't all perfect, as Google Pixel users are discovering this week. As reported by Android Authority, Google's November update apparently shipped with a bug that breaks some Pixel 10 and Pixel 11 cameras. Seeing as Pixels are rather famous for their shooters, this is a decidedly unfortunate glitch.

Here's the situation: Following the November update, some users are opening their Pixel Camera apps to find an error that reads, "Something went wrong. Close and open the Camera app again," with a "Learn More" link to, well, learn more. Others aren't receiving the error, but are instead running into a blank Camera viewfinder, as if the lens is totally covered. What's more, some users are reportedly saying that the issue is present on third-party camera apps, not just the Pixel Camera app. That would imply this is an issue with the camera system-wide, not just the Pixel Camera app itself.

To be clear, it doesn't seem like this is a universal issue. It's not like all Pixel users are now running with broken cameras. But based on the forum complaints Android Authority discovered, it seems reasonable to assume that this glitch isn't limited to just a handful of unlucky Pixel owners.

Luckily, there is an apparent workaround here, though it's not totally obvious. Some users are having no luck restarting their Pixels, while others report that a factory reset wasn't enough to restore camera functionality.

What does appear to work, however, is shutting your Pixel down and waiting five minutes or so. It's not clear why, but giving your Pixel a chance to "breathe" seems to shake the glitch and bring back your camera. As Android Authority reports, that fix comes from "Diamond and Gold product experts" on Google's Support forum.

If your Pixel's camera is giving you grief following the November update, this workaround is definitely worth a try—especially since more drastic measures don't actually seem to do anything. As the issue does seem to be rather widespread, I wouldn't be surprised to see Google issue a patch in the coming days. But until then, turning your phone off for five minutes may be a decent compromise.

#3441. Before He Played Sylvester Stallone in ‘I Play Rocky,’ Star Anthony Ippolito Fought Hard for His Own Big Break

I don’t think I was supposed to hear Anthony Ippolito when he exclaimed, “20 minutes?” right before this interview, as he was given the amount of time this interview would last. Though, it kind of hit me, if you’re not used to doing interviews — and there’s no way Ippolito can be at this young stage of his career — 20 minutes is a long time to make conversation with a total stranger. Especially, as he is quick to point out, after a barrage of quick, three-minute interviews.

Ippolito has been in films and television before — kind of famously now, he played Al Pacino in “The Offer” — but none of those were roles in which he’d have to do press. Let alone playing the lead role in a major motion picture in which everyone wants to talk to him. Oh, and that lead role is as … Sylvester Stallone. Related Stories ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ Review: David Fincher’s Breezy Tarantino Spinoff Is a Disappointing Compromise Between Great Directors Film Independent’s New President Wants to Build an L.A. Powerhouse — and Shake Up the Spirit Awards

In “I Play Rocky,” yes, Ippolito plays Stallone at the make or break point in Stallone’s career. Stallone had written “Rocky,” a very in-demand script. Not in demand was the idea of Stallone playing Rocky — as MGM offers more and more money to Stallone in an effort to get him to not play Rocky. (If you don’t know, Stallone stuck to his guns, played Rocky, and is now a very wealthy and famous actor.)

Directed by Peter Farrelly, Ippolito says he sent in multiple tapes trying to land this role — which does seem to be in the same spirit as the film itself. Though, Ippolito said, when he was actually going through the casting process, that’s not at all what he was thinking, even though it may seem that way now.

Ahead, he tells us (yes, over the course of 20 minutes) the Stallone movies he used to prep for playing Stallone, what is was like to talk to Stallone before filming, and why he loves Stallone and Dolly Parton together in “Rhinestone.” Also, if he had to play Stallone again in another movie, he does have another “I Play” installment in mind…

The following interview has been edited and condensed for clarity and length.

IndieWire: You seem excited about this being 20 minutes?

It’s a little strange, I’ve been having three-minute increment conversations with somebody. So, yes, I am excited.

OK, so how many Stallone movies did you watch? Did you stick to that era? His voice kind of evolves by the late ‘80s.

Yeah, I really tried to stay focused on a period of time. I don’t know the exact number. More so, from the stuff I was looking at I was watching it over and over again, rewatching. With the exception of a few.

Well, “Rocky Balboa.” It’s one of the best movies of the franchise.

For people who haven’t seen that one in a while, it’s very sweet.

It really is. It really is. And he does some excellent work in it. And I think it’s really powerful that he was able to come back many years later, after the fifth one, and make this incredible movie.

From closer to the “Rocky” era, I kind of love him in “The Prisoner of Second Avenue.” Jack Lemmon thinks he stole his wallet…

It’s just scene after scene of Jack Lemmon chasing Stallone through Central Park trying to get his wallet back…

But then Jack Lemmon realizes he left his wallet at home and wound up being the one who mugged Stallone.

But he was mistaken for a mugger and this was part of his issue, right?

It’s funny watching it now, because it’s so obviously Sylvester Stallone. So it’s amusing the whole role is just him being chased.

I agree with you and I found that throughout a lot of the stuff I was unearthing throughout this process.

In that, if he hadn’t become famous, I’d still look at him and think, “what an interesting looking dude,” and wonder what happened to him.

Speaking of that, there were times during “I Play Rocky,” knowing full well what happens in real life, and I’m still like, “Maybe just take the money. That’s a lot.”

It’s really remarkable. Especially when you convert the amount from what it was then to what it would be now.

I know you made a video for your audition which involved an old punching bag and gloves. What were you saying in it?

Oh, well, there was certain dialogue I was coming up with, or thinking of coming up with. And I hadn’t had my hands on too much of the script at this point. So I was just trying to capture his physicality and his movement as a boxer. I was just really passionate about the project. I wanted to put myself out there in a way. And, thankfully, I was able to get my hands on the script a bit later on.

So are you doing lines from “Rocky”? Or just stuff you came up with on your own?

I ask because that’s a time when you haven’t gained the weight yet, so you’re not in the physical condition you are when filming. So I feel you had to really sell this dialogue? Which obviously worked.

Yeah, I mean … it was difficult to come up with that part of it. I had given myself inspiration with some parts of the original film, and some parts from what I felt would work for dialogue from what I was understanding of the story. And then once I was able to get the script, then I was able to just put scenes on tape. And then continuously send them stuff until they relented.

Oh, there was more than one? You just kept going?

Well, that’s the spirit of this movie. Did you feel that way when you were sending them in? “Well, that’s what Stallone did.”

Hm … maybe? You know, it seems that way kind of now?

Right. But at that time, I was just like, “I probably seem crazy to everyone who is on the other end of this.”

Yeah, but I wasn’t thinking about that part for some reason, I guess.

Which is probably good, if you were getting ahead of yourself it doesn’t work out the way it did?

I know you spoke to Stallone before filming. A year ago, he was saying he knew nothing about this movie. When and how did that change?

Peter Farrelly tells a funny story about that. He had actually met with Stallone prior to that and discussed his level of involvement. And they discussed how Stallone would kind of not be necessarily in the trenches with us, just for the sake of Peter not wanting people to feel like Stallone had his hand in it in a way that it was shaped…

And historically Stallone never does that. I say that sarcastically because I’m well aware he has a specific vision for any movie he’s involved in…

Right. Right. So, Stallone went back after that and told somebody he has no idea about it. And Peter was like, “What are you doing?” And Stallone said, “You told me to separate myself.” And Peter was like, “Not that far, man!” So, I guess that was just a bit of a communication breakdown.

So in Stallone’s mind, he was doing a favor by saying that?

I’m not sure, but I was able to speak with him about a month before we started shooting. And I’m very grateful he was willing to take the time

What was that like? Was he in good spirits or was he apprehensive?

He was in great spirits about it. I was nervous, as you could probably imagine.

Yeah, and not only that, I had done so much of my own research. So, up to that point, it was really built up as this really big thing in my head. So, I was just really, really excited to meet him and to listen to him. He was really, really generous and disarming and very willing to share what that period of time was like for him.

What did he tell you that you don’t know already?

Oh, man. Well, he discussed with me building the character of Rocky as a writer. That’s where it became really interesting to me. Because he had studied filmmaking and writing while being an usher. So, hearing his perspective and his kind of clinical breakdown of how he approaches a script and of a character? It was hugely informative in developing and my understanding of this side of him as a writer.

From that, what changed on how you approached playing him? How does that conversation inform what we see?

You just really understand that this thing is his baby. And it really makes more sense that these numbers going so high during these negotiations because the script is that good. And so well written. Yeah, he’s a terrific writer and I think he proved that to Chartoff and Winkler with “Paradise Alley,” first.

My only experience with him was at the afterparty for “The Family Stallone.” He shows up at this restaurant in Little Italy and it’s like the Red Sea parting. Everyone stopped talking and made room so he could walk by. When he got near me I said, “Hey, Sly,” which I immediately regretted. He stopped, looked at me, and gave me a little nod.

He then walked off and I thought, “You know, good enough.”

Are you glad that you said it now? I feel like I would be.

But you keep bringing up meeting Wim Wenders. I know you’re a fan of his, is there something maybe happening?

I got to meet him at the Zurich Film Festival.

I know you like his movies, are you going to work with him?

I just think he makes great films, he’s made great films and he was a really, really sweet man and we got to speak. That’s pretty much it.

I feel that way about so many. Well, Scorsese obviously. Richard Linklater, Derek Cianfrance, Tim Burton.

That’s an eclectic group. “Place Beyond the Pines” and “Beetlejuice” are very different movies.

Very different movies. Well, I like that, You can go in so many different directions. And I appreciate directors and filmmakers who are singular.

And that is kind of the thing about Stallone, too. Did you look at the movies Stallone directed?

Honestly, well, I know he directed all the “Rocky” movies other than the first and fifth ones. And I understand he directed more stuff past that as well. But I hadn’t specifically looked at stuff he directed for this.

How far back did you go back to watch with Peter Farrelly’s films? Did you go back to “Dumb & Dumber”?

I’ve seen so much of his stuff already. So there’s not one that jumped out at me, but also, obviously, “There’s Something About Mary.”

It really is. I think he really killed it with that one. I mean, he has such an incredible sensibility. And he’s always aware of something on set. If there’s a moment to be discovered, to make a meal out of it, he’ll find it.

I always think about, “Unless someone comes up with six-minute abs.”

On social media a lot of people are doing their own “I Play …,” then insert any other Stallone movie type posts. If you had to play him again, what movie would you want to do?

Like, “I Play Cobra,” would be interesting. I do love “Cobra.”

You know, I guess I’m not the right age for this, but “I Play Rocky Balboa” would be very interesting…

Well, it’s the first one I remember. I would have had to have seen the ones prior? To the point I’m in the theater for “Rocky Balboa.”

Well, not necessarily. The first one I saw was “Rocky III”…

Because it was the one on cable all the time. Then I was told, “Oh, you know, the first one is a lot different.”

Yeah, I was pretty young, but I do remember seeing “Rocky Balboa.” And I just think there’s something interesting about the fact that, similar to how he’s fighting the boxing commission at the time to let him fight, because they think that he can’t, or shouldn’t — I think he was having a similar dialogue with the studio at the time. About him making the movie in the first place.

It’s interesting, even at that point, they still didn’t think they could take a chance on him making a “Rocky” movie.

I guess, yeah. It’s strange, but history does repeat itself.

Ah, OK, it’s not streaming, so it’s a little harder to find. It’s just interesting this is only a few years after “Rocky” and now he’s on stage singing with Dolly Parton. It’s kind of fascination what that one decision did for him…

It’s very true. And I think Dolly Parton is spectacular in that.

How good is she in that? Right? I mean, she has such a warmth to her. I mean, yeah. She’s just incredible in the movie and it makes it so fun. The two of them! They are dynamic.

You could also make “I Play Nick Martinelli.”

So what are the lessons you personally took away from playing Stallone? I can’t help but think there are lessons here for actors starting out.

I agree. Well, he really overcame so much and he didn’t have too many people in his corner at the time. I mean, thankfully, he had Sasha who was there for him, who AnnaSophia Robb plays in the movie. And she’s so great in it. And as much as you want to see Stallone persevere, and be kind of a lone wolf through this? For actors there’s meaning in that, and there’s a lesson to be learned in that.

But there’s also a lesson to be found in Sasha. Because you need that person sometimes in your life. Or sometimes it’s good to be that person for people — to remind people to believe in themselves. Because, no matter what, Stallone overcame so much, but of course he doubted himself. And if you don’t have at least somebody who is there, willing to be that person to remind you to believe in yourself, it’s a tough road.

Amazon MGM Studios will release “I Play Rocky” in select theaters on Friday, November 6, before going wide on Friday, November 20.

#3440. 11 Best Historical Fantasies Since Outlander

It's been five years since the last new Outlander book released, and historical fantasy readers will likely be waiting a bit longer for Book 10. The series has had an impressive run, with the first book released back in 1991. Interest in Diana Gabaldon's time-traveling work of historical fiction remains strong, but it's far from the only phenomenal historical fantasy book out there.

Publishing has changed quite a bit since Outlander first hit the scene in 1991. Not only has the TV series brought a whole new level of attention to Outlander itself, but historical fantasy as a genre has continued to grow and expand. There are so many excellent books that blend magic and historical settings, giving Outlander ​​​​​​fans plenty of reading material between books.

Since Claire first journeyed to the past, we've seen countless stories that blend historical settings with fantasy elements. Some, like This Is How You Lose the Time War, feature their own wibbly-wobbly time travel goodness. Others stay tethered to one historical setting, but infuse it with magic and mystery. Regardless of what you're looking for, there's a historical fantasy book that will tide you over until the next Outlander book and beyond.

Like Outlander before it, this Hugo Award-winning novel has been adapted for TV, giving the story a whole new level of popularity and cultural relevance. But before BBC brought its characters to the screen, Jonathan Strange & Mr. Norrell had already captivated readers with its charming rival magicians and fast-paced storytelling. And believe it or not, this was Susanna Clarke's debut novel!

Jonathan Strange & Mr. Norrell is set during the Napoleonic Wars, in a world where magic is thought to be a thing of the past. But Mr. Norrell reveals that magic is alive and well in him, followed not long after by Jonathan Strange. What follows is a story steeped in magic, humor, and compelling world-building that brings its alternate historical setting to life. With over 4 million copies sold, this is an absolute must-read in the historical fantasy space.

You can purchase Jonathan Strange & Mr. Norrell here.

The Napoleonic Wars, but with dragons, is one of those pitches that doesn't sound like it should work. Yet somehow, His Majesty's Dragon proves that it does. In this alternate history, Britain and France duke it out atop the backs of dragons. A New York Times bestseller and winner of the Locus Award, this is the beginning of Novik's beloved Temeraire series.

In this first installment, readers meet Captain Will Laurence, who suddenly finds himself thrust into the world of dragons and their riders. It offers a fresh take on the bond between dragon and rider, giving readers beautiful writing, engaging characters, and a page-turning plot. Masterfully blending historical fiction and fantasy, His Majesty's Dragon is a must-read for historical fantasy enthusiasts and dragon lovers alike.

You can purchase His Majesty's Dragon here.

When it first released in 2011, it felt like The Night Circus was everywhere. And given its New York Times bestseller status, that was at least partly true. The book pulls on the star-crossed lover trope, adding in a mysterious traveling circus and rival magicians for a story that spans time, place, and genre.

Set in the late 1800s to early 1900s, The Night Circus spans much of the lives of its core protagonists. Two rival magicians each select and train a young pupil, destined to one day battle one another. As their stories unfold, they fall in love, despite the circumstances that would pit them against each other. Packed with romance, longing, and wonderfully surreal magic, The Night Circus feels like a fairytale and a Shakespeare tragedy all rolled into one.

Before it became a viral social media sensation, This Is How You Lose the Time War snagged a Hugo, Nebula, and Locus Award for best novella. It's not easy to craft a compelling time-travel story in a short space, but El-Mohtar and Gladstone pulled it off in this historical sci-fi/fantasy hybrid.

Told through letters between rival agents on opposite sides of the titular time war, this story is part epic time-travel saga, part love story. Though more heavily science fiction than fantasy, this book defies exact genre confines with its magical, lyrical adventure through space and time. Lyrically written and surprisingly action-packed, This Is How You Lose the Time War continues to captivate readers who love historical fiction, fantasy, and sci-fi... not to mention a good star-crossed love story.

You can purchase This Is How You Lose the Time War here.

Practical Magic is, of course, an iconic story about witches, sisterhood, and love gone wrong. So it's not surprising that the prequel, released in 2020, became an instant bestseller. But many readers also consider this the best book in the entire series due to its combination of stunning prose and powerfully rendered characters. Magic Lessons offers a trip back to the 1600s to uncover how the Owens women became cursed in the first place, shedding light on the magical legacy that would bring us the beloved movie.

Maria Owens is a compelling protagonist, a young witch abandoned first by her birth family and later by her first love. By the time she lays the curse that will devastate generations of Owens women, Hoffman deftly makes you understand exactly what brings her to that place. It is beautifully written, full of nuanced characters and just the right touch of magic.

Whether you were browsing the bestseller lists or scrolling Bookstagram, The Invisible Life of Addie LaRue was impossible to miss. Released in 2020, this book landed a truly staggering number of Best Books mentions and continues to pop up in bookish circles to date. Schwab's impressive writing and the book's heartbreaking, time-traveling premise are central to this book's ongoing longevity.

Our story begins in the 1700s, when Addie LaRue first makes the deal that lets her live forever, but be remembered by no one. Spanning both time and location, this is a unique story of identity, connection, and longing. It's a page-turner in the truest sense, but also crafts an ironically unforgettable character in the titular Addie. If you've yet to pick up this historical fantasy, it's still well worth revisiting.

You can purchase The Invisible Life of Addie LaRue here.

This historical fantasy is set in an alternate version of the late 1800s. It centers on sisters who join the suffragette movement to help women gain a fraction of power, but wind up working to reawaken the lost magic that made them powerful all along. During its release year, it snagged several Best Books of the Year nominations and hit the New York Times bestseller list, and for good reason.

The Once and Future Witches is a beautifully written, compelling story that grips you from start to finish. A powerful homage to feminine power and the men who seek to crush it, this book is steeped in magic and packed with plot twists you won't see coming. If you love Outlander for Claire's spirited efforts to stand her ground in her past and present, you'll root for the sisters who strive to reclaim lost magic and the old ways in this historical fantasy novel.

You can purchase The Once and Future Witches here.

Though it's often classified as more traditional historical fiction, there's no denying the tinge of magic in Emilia Hart's stunning debut, Weyward. Set across three different generations of women haunted by their links to witchcraft, this book was an instant bestseller and winner of two Goodreads Choice Awards.

The story takes place in three timelines, set in the 1600s, 1940s, and modern day. Each woman faces unique challenges that harken back to the Weyward women's magical roots. The fantasy elements here might be a light touch, but this is nevertheless a beautifully crafted story about female power and resistance that is right at home on any historical fantasy reader's shelf right alongside Outlander.

There's a reason readers were beside themselves when Penner finally confirmed a sequel to The Lost Apothecary. This book is part historical fiction, part mystery, and part magical realism, weaving a story that left many readers desperate for more. Its status as a historical fantasy is debatable, as our apothecary is more of a traditional healer than a full-on witch, but the book very much reads like a story of witches.

The Lost Apothecary uses a dual-timeline setup, with part of our story in 18th-century London and the other half following a present-day historian. As Caroline uncovers Nella's past, the two women's stories become linked and echo off one another in surprising, magical ways. A beautifully written and bestselling debut, The Lost Apothecary is a must-read for Outlander fans and anyone who loves a good story about women's wrongs.

You can purchase The Lost Apothecary here.

She Who Became the Sun is the first book in the Radiant Emperor duology. It was both an international bestseller and a finalist for several major fantasy awards during its release year. Set in an alternate China during the rise of the Ming Dynasty, this book follows a young woman who takes her brother's identity to join the rebellion against the Mongols.

This story is an epic reimagining of history, one steeped in political intrigue and questions about fate, family, and identity. Its writing is memorable and poetic, tempering the absolutely devastating, epic story that doesn't pull punches. Its magic lies largely in its reimagined history, but She Who Became the Sun is nevertheless both a solid epic fantasy and a powerful work of historical fiction.

You can purchase She Who Became the Sun here.

#3439. Five Hacks Every Apple Watch Series 12 User Should Know

The latest Apple Watches have a lot of new features that older watches don't, so I figured it was time for a new list of hacks. While our general Apple Watch and fitness tracking hacks are still golden, Series 12 devices offer new features like native step counting, a Readiness app, an upgraded heart rate sensor, an AI-based version of Siri, and "audio intelligence" that can replay and summarize real-life conversations, within limits. Here's how to get the most out of them.

The Series 12 can finally count steps natively, a task that for some reason is only arriving now, and is restricted to just the newest Apple Watch models. Enjoy it! To add a step counter to your watch face, long-press on the clock screen to edit it, tap on a complication (that’s what Apple calls those little icons and numbers that appear on some watch faces), choose Activity, and then tap Steps.

You don’t need this creepy feature listening in to everything, but it can be nice to have it as a backup on occasion. A button in your Apple Watch’s Control Center can turn the feature on and off. Keep it off except when you have a structured conversation that you’ll want to refer to later. This feature is currently in beta (which you can try now if you want to), but is expected to be available to everyone later this year.

It's worth turning off the default setting not just because of the creepiness factor, but also because the recaps work best when there is a single subject of conversation, with a clear start and end, and just one context. If you leave recaps running all the time, your doctor’s appointment will get mixed in with your grocery shopping, YouTube watching, and everyday chatter.

To finish off a recap and make it useful, take a look at the recap shortly after the conversation, tap the three-dots menu, and hit Edit. You’ll be able to adjust the notes and add your own important details. Siri won’t identify speakers and seems to shy away from including certain details, like people’s names. You can add in what it missed and also create your own bullet points so that everything gets noted down while it’s still fresh in your mind.

This one isn’t specific to the Series 12, but if you haven’t gotten on board with the pinch and wrist flick gestures yet, now is a great time.

First, the wrist flick: If a notification is on your screen, or you’re otherwise looking at something you’d rather be done with, just flick your wrist away from you and then back toward you, as if there were a crumb on the watch face and you wanted to knock it off. This will bring you back to the watch face and close whatever you were looking at.

The double pinch is another useful one, although Apple calls it double tap. This is confusing because you aren’t double tapping the watch, you’re tapping your thumb and forefinger together while wearing the watch. You don’t need to touch the watch face at all. So, when you get a notification or a call, look at it on your watch, and pinch your thumb and forefinger (of the watch hand) together twice. The watch detects the pinch from subtle movements in your wrist, and it will open the notification. You can then use the wrist flick to close the notification. Performing a double pinch when no notification is on screen will bring up your smart stack. You can then double-pinch to move to the next card in the smart stack, or single-pinch to open that card and see its details.

If you want to learn even more gestures, go into the Watch app, and select Accessibility and then Hand gestures. You can remap a whole-fist “clench” to do the same thing as pressing the digital crown, for example, or to open the control center or Siri.

A little rude, perhaps, but helpful: With the new AI-based Siri, sometimes answers to questions can be long-winded. If Siri launches into a novel-length response and you’re not interested in hearing all that, just put your palm over the screen. You’ll instantly be transported back to your watch face, and the Siri response will stop.

If you still want to see those longer responses without having Siri read the whole thing to you, you can set this up on your phone, and the settings will carry over to your watch. On your iPhone, go to Settings and tap Siri, then Responses. Select Silent responses instead of Spoken responses. You can then read through her answers, or skim them, as you prefer.

#3438. ‘The Gilded Age’ Renewed for Fifth Season Following Ratings Boom

Fans of “The Gilded Age,” rejoice! There are still more luncheons to plan, more balls to savor, and more opera opening nights to fight over. Yes, the HBO original series has been renewed for a fifth season.

The move follows a surge in popularity that began with the show’s drama-filled third season, which saw Bertha (Carrie Coon) and George Russell’s (Morgan Spector) relationship strain, and has continued with the fourth season, which has dealt with their marriage troubles, the wedding of Peggy Scott (Denée Benton), and a visit from Grover Cleveland.

Clearly, it’s working. Viewership for Season 4 has grown week over week, HBO stated in a press release. Episode 3 hit a season high of 4.3 million U.S. cross-platform viewers and episodes are averaging 5.9 million viewers and growing. That outpaces the prior season by nearly 20 percent. Related Stories ‘Dig’ Review: Amy Poehler’s Talent-Rich Peacock Comedy Barely Scratches the Surface ‘The Altruists’ Review: Netflix’s Slight Sam Bankman-Fried Series Tells a Strange, Crooked Love Story

The turnaround is striking because “The Gilded Age” was very much on the bubble for most of its first two seasons. Bringing 19th-century high-society to life is expensive, and the show initially struggled to become a ratings powerhouse despite being co-created by Julian Fellowes of “Downton Abbey” fame. In interviews, the cast admitted that they often feared they would be canceled. But audiences have shown up in a big way, and Fellowes and his co-creator Sonja Warfield recently told IndieWire that they have more stories to tell beyond this season.

“We have a Season 5 in us if we’re allowed to do it,” Fellowes said. “But when you write a TV series, you have to finish every season so that it could be the end, because one day it will be.”

In its three eligible seasons, “The Gilded Age” has earned 15 total Emmy nominations, including Outstanding Drama Series and Outstanding Directing for a Drama Series, as well as a Screen Actors Guild Award nomination for Outstanding Performance by an Ensemble in a Drama Series.

“The Gilded Age” cast includes Christine Baranski, Cynthia Nixon, Louisa Jacobson, Taissa Farmiga, Harry Richardson, Blake Ritson, Ben Ahlers, Ashlie Atkinson, Dylan Baker, Kelley Curran, Jordan Donica, Jessica Frances Dukes, Amy Forsyth, Jack Gilpin, Simon Jones, Celia Keenan-Bolger, Ben Lamb, Audra McDonald, Brian Stokes Mitchell, Debra Monk, Hattie Morahan, Donna Murphy, and Kristine Nielsen.

“The Gilded Age” is a co-production between HBO and Universal Television, a division of Universal Studio Group.

#3437. Guy Ritchie’s ‘The Gentlemen’ Officially Returns With Brand-New Release

Hannah covers horror, sci-fi, and games at Collider, where she writes news and features, reviews new releases, and interviews the people who make them. She’s helping build out Collider’s gaming coverage, with Pokémon as one of her specialties. If she isn’t writing about a monster, she’s probably watching one on a tape from her VHS collection.

Hugh Grant turns up at Charlie Hunnam’s house in The Gentlemen with a screenplay, a price in mind, and every intention of staying for a drink. Grant’s Fletcher is a private investigator who thinks the dirt he’s dug up on a London drug empire would make a terrific movie, while Hunnam’s Raymond works for the man who runs that empire.

The man whose retirement plans inspired all that creative writing is Mickey Pearson (Matthew McConaughey), an American who figured out that the British aristocracy had two things he could use. They owned enormous estates, and quite a few of them could use the money. Growing marijuana on their land made Mickey rich enough to retire. His mistake was letting anyone hear that he wanted out before Jeremy Strong’s prospective buyer had signed on the dotted line.

Guy Ritchie’s The Gentlemen will get its first U.S. 4K SteelBook on December 15, 2026. The Amazon-exclusive edition from Lionsgate Home Entertainment pairs the movie on 4K Ultra HD with a standard Blu-ray, and preorders are open now. The movie first came to 4K in April 2020, and a Blu-ray SteelBook followed in Germany that summer. This December’s release gives U.S. collectors a domestic edition with both discs in one case. You can preorder on Amazon now.

If you bought The Gentlemen on 4K in 2020, the reason to make room for another copy is the SteelBook itself. All three video extras from that release are back, including “Best Gentlemanly Quips,” which has three minutes and nine seconds to choose between Colin Farrell politely correcting the boys in his boxing gym and Grant making himself a little too comfortable in Hunnam’s kitchen. The disc also finds 46 seconds for a “Glossary of Cannabis,” in case Mickey’s line of work was your introduction to any unfamiliar vocabulary. A 96-second behind-the-scenes featurette and a photo gallery round out the extras.

As for the movie itself, the set includes the full 113-minute feature on both 4K UHD and Blu-ray. The 4K disc keeps Ritchie’s 2.39:1 widescreen framing and adds HDR10 to the mix, with English Dolby Atmos and 7.1 Dolby TrueHD audio. There are Spanish subtitles and English SDH, the latter something audiences will be thankful to have when Fletcher gets going.

The Gentlemen releases on 4K UHD and Blu-ray SteelBook December 15, exclusively at Amazon.

#3435. Pedro Pascal’s Last Of Us Season 3 Return Gets Definitive Update

Pedro Pascal's Joel may be dead, but his presence lives on in The Last of Us season 3.

Adapted from the Naughty Dog game of the same name, the HBO series has chronicled the journey of Ellie, a young woman with an immunity to a fungal virus that wiped out the world who strives to survive in the post-apocalypse, all while bonding with Pascal's Joel, a courier with a tragic past. Staying true to its source material, The Last of Us season 2 saw the death of Joel, with Ellie subsequently setting out on a quest for vengeance against Kaitlyn Dever's Abby and her group.

During a recent interview with The Hollywood Reporter for his work on The Terminal List and Dexter: Resurrection, Gabriel Luna opened up about his work on The Last of Us season 3. As the conversation shifted to Pedro Pascal and Joel, a definitive update was given that the former lead star will not return for the HBO show's final season, though Luna assures that "the spirit of Joel runs through everything" and praises Pascal for the presence he brought to the set that is still being carried forward:

Gabriel Luna: Pedro committed such an extraordinary performance to the screen, and you know the audience is certainly holding that flame for him. All the characters are too. In every action, in every life Tommy takes and in every round fired, there is that longing for his brother. I know Bella feels the same way about Ellie and the character’s grief. So, in the world of the show and in our memories of the great time we spent working together, we just carry him with us. But I always say Bella Ramsey is a great general, and we’re in great hands with them at the helm.

It shouldn't come as too much of a surprise that Pascal won't be returning as Joel for The Last of Us season 3 for a few reasons. For starters, with the show's final season set to adapt the second half of Naughty Dog's 2020 sequel game, the plot is now shifting to making Abby the primary character in order to showcase her life before and after killing Joel and the deadly standoff with Ellie and Luna's Tommy in the season 2 finale.

Additionally, Pascal has remained steadily busy all year with a variety of productions. In addition to doing press for the highly-anticipated Avengers: Doomsday, the four-time Emmy nominee was busy with the Todd Haynes-helmed De Noche and Tony Gilroy-helmed Behemoth!, both of which he rescued from being scrapped after their original leading stars departed their productions. He's also expected to return for Avengers: Secret Wars, which is tentatively slated for an early 2027 filming start.

That being said, while his current status may be a definitive absence from the final season, there are still a few ways Pascal could return in The Last of Us season 3. As established in season 2, there are still plenty of gaps to fill with Joel and Ellie's relationship in the five-year time jump from season 1, though it did tackle the ones featured in the sequel game. With Neil Druckmann not co-showrunning the new season, there is a chance Craig Mazin could venture into original territory to do so.

The Last of Us season 2, episode 6 is made up almost entirely of flashbacks across a sprawling timeline. When do all the flashbacks take place?

One of the other most likely ways Pascal could still return for The Last of Us season 3, which still has a quarter of its production remaining, is as a vision to Ellie or Abby. Those familiar with the game know the direction the story is taking both of its characters on the way to an emotional showdown, and Joel's presence in some capacity could be what's needed to keep one or both of them from going into darker territory.

The Last Of Us is a television adaptation of the acclaimed video game series, set in a post-apocalyptic world where a smuggler named Joel (Pedro Pascal) is tasked with escorting a teenage girl, Ellie (Bella Ramsey) across the ravaged United States. Along their journey, they confront various threats from both infected creatures and hostile human factions.

#3434. 10 Hacks Every watchOS 27 User Should Know

Khamosh Pathak is a freelance tech journalist with over 13 years of experience writing online. An accounting graduate, he turned his interest in writing and technology into a career. He holds a specialization in user experience design from ISDI Parsons in Mumbai, where he sought to deepen his understanding of UX, consumer devices, and interplay between software and technology.

Khamosh has written thousands of how-tos and guides on every major platform (iOS, macOS, Android, and Windows). He got started writing how-tos and guides for Guiding Tech, where he also published several e-books. His work has also been seen at MakeUseOf, How-To Geek, and PCMag. He is truly passionate about brewing good coffee.

watchOS 27 introduces a solid set of upgrades to your wrist—assuming your Apple Watch supports it. While the newest update isn't Apple's most feature-filled, it does include a number of changes that improve the way you exercise, track your health, and locate missing items. That's especially true for anyone with the latest Series 12 or Ultra 4. If your Apple Watch supports watchOS 27, you should know about these 10 hacks:

With watchOS 27, Apple changed what double-pressing the Digital Crown does. Instead of opening the app switcher, it now triggers Audio Intelligence—if you have an Apple Watch Series 12 or Ultra 4. If you don't have access to those features, the gesture now does nothing.

It seems Apple realized the mistake, however, as evidenced by watchOS 27.2. When you're using an app while running this latest update, press and hold the bottom part of the watch's screen, and you'll trigger the app switcher. You can now jump to a different app, or close an app that isn't working. Sadly, this only works when you're already in an app, and not when you're on the Home Screen, but it's certainly better than nothing.

While you can load up multiple complications on your Apple Watch, they aren't exactly dynamic. That's why I'm a big fan of the Smart Stack widgets on the Apple Watch, which update dynamically to show contextual information. Now, with the new Siri Modular Face, you can access dynamic widgets on the Home Screen. If you've just parked your car, for example, you'll see a widget showing its location; likewise, if you have an upcoming calendar appointment, it will be front and center.

To use the Siri Modular watch face, tap and hold on the screen, go to the end of the list, tap the Plus button, and find and add the Siri Modular watch face. Once you do, you'll start seeing dynamic widgets when you wake up your watch. Don't expect much personalization from this watch face, however. You can customize the colors and add three small complications, but that's it.

The double-tap gesture is one of my favorite Apple Watch features. By tapping your thumb and index finger together twice, you can do things like answer a call or reply to a message. In watchOS 27, Apple took the gesture one step forward. You can now use the double-tap gesture to scroll through your widgets; if you perform a single tap, it then opens the highlighted widget or the shortcut. This means you can open and browse the weather app, or start a workout, without ever touching your Apple Watch's screen.

Your Apple Watch's new Music Recognition app has native Shazam integration. What's more, Shazam will record your request even when you're offline and away from your iPhone. The moment you reconnect, the service will identify the songs, which you can see in the Shazam app on your iPhone or Apple Watch.

It seems like Apple has a library of songs it uses for offline recognition, because in my testing, it was able to recognize a Coldplay song instantly, even when in Airplane mode. To use it, you can either open the Music Recognition app, or you can add the widget for faster access. Scroll up on the Home Screen, go to the bottom of the screen, tap the Edit button, then the Plus button, and add the Music Recognition widget.

Apple Watches have traditionally lacked a live step count widget or complication. To find your step count, you had to go to the bottom of the Activity app, or rely on third-party apps. But even still, these apps never showed live data. You’d always have to wait a couple of seconds to see the updated stats.

Now, if you own the latest Apple Watch Series 12 or the Ultra 4, you can add a live step count widget or complication to the Apple Watch face or the Smart Stack. This will show you your precise step count at all times. To use it, go to the bottom of the Smart Stack, tap the Edit button, then tap the Plus button. Here, find and add the new Step count widget.

Siri is no longer a voice assistant that you use for one-off tasks. With Siri AI, you can now carry on multiple conversations with context and memory. It's not as robust as ChatGPT or Claude, but you can use Siri AI for brainstorming, researching, and jotting down ideas for later.

The Siri AI app on the iPhone shows all your conversations, and so does the Apple Watch. This means you can continue your Siri AI conversations and view past chats on your Apple Watch. To use it, press the Digital Crown once, then tap the Siri app icon in the center. This will open up all your conversations instead of calling upon Siri. Tap a conversation to continue your chat on the Apple Watch. Of course, anything you do here will be reflected in the Siri app on your iPhone.

The new Find My app on the Apple Watch shows a single map for finding people, devices, and items. This means you can now locate your family members who are sharing their location with you, as well as AirTags or other Find My items from the watchOS app.

After opening the app, you can use the Digital Crown to zoom in or out of the map. Use touch to pan around. The map doesn't show all items and people at once, though. Tap the Menu button at the bottom-right corner, and then switch between People, Items, or Devices. If you have multiple items, you can scroll through them using the Digital Crown.

While it's not a Whoop-level feature, the Apple Watch now includes a Readiness score. Instead of individually looking at your training load, sleep score, and vitals, you now have one number that gives you the whole picture.

The Readiness score ranges from 0 to 10 and is based on your recent fitness activity, sleep data, and background health monitoring. If you have a score of 8 to 10, your Apple Watch thinks you can push yourself, or "go for it," as it says; if it's below 5, the watch thinks you should consider lighter activity. This feature, though, is only available on Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. You can use the new Readiness app on your Apple Watch to see this data, but you can also access it on your iPhone in the Fitness app's new Readiness section.

Low Power Mode isn't your only option when it comes to extending the battery life for your Apple Watch. watchOS 27 offers a special Max Extended Workout mode just for long workouts. With it, your Apple Watch disables some features, like splits and alerts, and reduces the frequency of GPS and heart rate readings, in the hopes of extending your battery throughout your entire exercise. To use it, go to the Workout app and select the workout you want. Tap the Goals button in the top-right corner, and choose the Extended option. Then, switch to the Max Extended option and start your workout.

The Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 come with a set of Audio Intelligence features that use the microphones on the Apple Watch, paired with AI models (both local and cloud-based), to identify sounds, music, and record conversation. Thanks to this new feature, one of the iPhone's accessibility features also makes its way to the Apple Watch.

Sound Recognition can alert you when it hears sirens, alarms, doorbells, and more, even when your iPhone isn’t around. To set this up, go to the Settings app on your iPhone and navigate to Accessibility > Sound & Name Recognition > Sound Recognition. Here, enable the sounds you want to monitor, and make sure to turn on the Detect using Apple Watch toggle.

#3433. Don’t Forget the Other ‘Heat’ Movie, Which Gave Burt Reynolds One of His Best Noir Roles

40 years ago, the crime drama “Heat” opened in France and received positive reviews from Paris critics. No, not the “Heat” directed by Michael Mann that starred Robert De Niro and Al Pacino and would go on to become a revered classic — that came nine years later. The “Heat” that played in Europe in 1986 starred Burt Reynolds, was directed by multiple journeyman helmers, and was almost immediately forgotten only months after it limped into U.S. theaters in March of 1987.

American reviewers dismissed “Heat” with casual cruelty, but as so often happens in film history — think Jerry Lewis, Michael Cimino’s “Heaven’s Gate,” or Brian De Palma’s “Mission to Mars” — the French got our cinema right where our own critics got it embarrassingly wrong. “Heat,” in which Reynolds plays an aging mercenary held prisoner by a crippling gambling addiction, is not only one of Reynolds’ most interesting films but one of his most personal, and a top-tier entry in the canon of the subgenre that is “Burt Noir.” Related Stories Before He Played Sylvester Stallone in ‘I Play Rocky,’ Star Anthony Ippolito Fought Hard for His Own Big Break ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ Review: David Fincher’s Breezy Tarantino Spinoff Is a Disappointing Compromise Between Great Directors

From early on, one of the most interesting things about Burt Reynolds was the tension between his affable onscreen persona — the smiling, charming fellow who had major box office hits with crowd-pleasers like “Smokey and the Bandit” and “The Cannonball Run” — and the visible agitation simmering underneath. Reynolds was one of the premier talk show guests (and occasional guest hosts) of the 1970s and early 1980s, a guy who could always be counted on to tell a funny, self-deprecating anecdote that made the audience feel like a part of his inner circle.

But Reynolds always gave the sense that there was a chip on his shoulder — that he was mad about not being taken seriously enough, or being taken too seriously, or losing out on the best parts to his friend and competitor Clint Eastwood and other stars. (Never mind the fact that Reynolds lost out on most of his potentially successful roles — “Terms of Endearment,” “Die Hard,” “Pretty Woman” — because he turned them down, not because anyone took them from him.)

Early on, Eastwood let his controlled rage be a defining trait of his star persona; Reynolds generally tried, and failed, to cloak his under chuckling humility. Many of Reynolds’ best performances exploit this tension, from John Boorman’s “Deliverance,” in which Reynolds’ male bonding fishing expedition descends into a horror, to Paul Thomas Anderson’s “Boogie Nights,” in which the actor’s initially nurturing father figure turns dark and violent when tested.

Reynolds’ memoir, “But Enough About Me,” offers a fascinating glimpse into the contradiction between his healthy self-regard (hilariously exhibited in passages in which he disparages two of the best directors he ever worked with, Anderson and Peter Bogdanovich) and his persistent self-loathing (demonstrated in his candid appraisals of his many terrible personal and professional decisions). The latter informs an ongoing, if intermittent, cycle of Reynolds movies of which “Heat” is a key example: movies I define as “Burt Noir,” in which the actor plays supremely confident men of action tormented by regret and the knowledge that they’ve failed to live up to their potential.

The first, and possibly best, example of Burt Noir is the 1975 cop drama “Hustle,” in which Reynolds plays a Los Angeles detective surrounded by moral decay and corruption. Reynolds and director Robert Aldrich got to make “Hustle” after their commercial success with “The Longest Yard,” and they immediately squandered whatever mainstream goodwill that comedy had bought them with a film so grim and pessimistic it made James Ellroy look like Fred Rogers.

In “Hustle,” Reynolds is surrounded by evil both banal and terrifying, and he meets almost all of it with a weary resignation — aside from one desperate, possibly pointless act, he doesn’t even try to fight the men to whom he knows he is morally, intellectually, and physically superior. The movie reeks with sadness in spite of being marketed as a muscular action movie — though it is a muscular action movie, as is a later and more commercially successful Burt Noir, “Sharky’s Machine.”

That movie, in which Reynolds plays a cop who falls for the prostitute he’s got under surveillance, further explores the sense of moral outrage that marked “Hustle” and Reynolds’ directorial debut, “Gator,” and it gives Reynolds another of his tortured heroes who alternates between spurts of violent action and long passages of almost complete impotence — a combination that reaches its apotheosis in “Heat.”

A clue to what Reynolds is up to in terms of deconstructing his persona comes in the opening of “Heat,” a 12-minute prologue that doesn’t have much to do with the rest of the film other than breaking down Reynolds’ heroic image for audience members who still see him as a conventional leading man. Reynolds’ Nick Escalante tries to pick up a woman in a bar in the ugliest, aggressive way possible, and it’s confusing for the audience — why has the guy who was such a sweet charmer to Sally Field, Goldie Hawn, Jill Clayburgh, and Julie Andrews in earlier movies turned into such a misogynistic pig?

Even more confusing is what follows, when the meek twerp the woman is dating shows up and beats the hell out of Reynolds in the parking lot. We learn, later on, that the whole thing was a set-up — the guy hired Nick to fake everything so he could look like a hero in front of his girlfriend. But in the audience’s mind, the seed has already been planted; subconsciously we can never quite see this guy as a straightforward hero, and that’s the way Reynolds and screenwriter William Goldman want it.

The film progresses as a kind of hangout movie familiar to anyone who loves Quentin Tarantino’s “Jackie Brown” or “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth”; there’s a relatively solid genre movie structure running underneath everything, but Goldman takes plenty of time for character-developing digressions that give the whole movie a rich sense of melancholy texture.

Escalante’s tale of attempted moral redemption in the form of his efforts to help the victim of a sadistic young gangster avenge her beating moves from sharp wit (in the form of the best dialogue Goldman ever wrote — which is saying something when you’re talking about the guy who wrote “Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid”) and contemplative scenes of self-examination to shocking bursts of expertly choreographed violence and wistful romance.

It’s all given added layers of irony and resonance by the Las Vegas setting, which seems to mock Escalante’s dreams of hitting it big and escaping to a peaceful retirement in Italy, and Goldman’s choice to set the movie at Christmas, which only mocks Escalante more cruelly. Although “Heat” is one of Goldman’s least well known films (a movie that is easily forgotten amidst the more honored “All the President’s Men,” “Marathon Man,” and “Misery”), it’s one of his most beautifully written, with badinage as snappy as it is revealing and a weaving plot whose emotional effects really sneak up on you.

So why were American critics so dismissive? As is so often the case, they mostly seemed to be reviewing the chaotic circumstances of the production more than the movie that actually resulted from them. “Heat” was a famously troubled movie, whose misfortunes made their way into the press long before the film actually hit American screens. Its beginnings were auspicious: Goldman, one of the most respected writers in the business, was adapting his own novel (with a clause in his contract that said he couldn’t be rewritten), and Robert Altman was set to direct.

Then, only days before shooting, Altman quit the project after his favored cinematographer, Canadian cameraman Pierre Mignot, was denied an H-1 Visa to work in America. Altman claimed that over the course of eight pictures he had developed a style and way of working with Mignot that he didn’t want to abandon, and certainly didn’t want to have to reinvent in a matter of days with another director of photography. Whether or not this is the whole story is anybody’s guess — it was reported that the real reason Altman left had to do with creative differences between him and producer Elliott Kastner, and that Mignot merely gave him the excuse he was looking for to walk.

Goldman suggested Reynolds, who had helmed “Sharky’s Machine” and other fine pictures, take over directing himself, but Burt said he wanted to focus solely on his performance. Thus began a game of directorial musical chairs that would be widely reported and which gave “Heat” the patina of a disaster in the making. Reliable craftsman Dick Richards came on first, only to leave the production after getting into a fistfight with Reynolds on the set. In spite of lawsuits flying back and forth, Richards returned to the set, only to leave again when he fell off a camera crane and ended up in the hospital.

On the days when Richards was out second-unit director and stunt coordinator Stan Barrett took on directing duties, and some of the most electrifying moments in “Heat” can be attributed to him. Barrett had worked as Reynolds’ stunt double for more than 20 years and had a great sense of how to capitalize on the actor’s physicality and image, and the set pieces he directed for “Heat” — like a hotel room fight between Reynolds and some thugs — are beautifully staged and filled with brutally effective and original instances of sudden and shocking violence.

DGA rules at the time prohibited Barrett from taking over the reins for more than five days, since the guild forbade any preexisting member of a troupe from replacing the director — a rule, ironically, that was created when Reynolds’ friend Clint Eastwood fired director Philip Kaufman from “The Outlaw Josey Wales” and replaced him with himself. With only eight days of filming left on “Heat,” television stalwart Jerry Jameson (who had directed Reynolds years earlier on “Dan August”) stepped in and finished the picture.

The experience doesn’t seem to have been a happy one for many of the principals involved, especially Richards, who gave interviews begging people not to blame him for what he saw as the film’s failures. A DGA arbitration determined that Richards was responsible for 40% of the film — more than any of the other directors on the project — and thus should have the credit. Not wanting his name on the movie, Richards eschewed his usual credit for “Directed by R.M. Richards” and tried to wash his hands of the entire debacle as soon as he could.

With the movie’s own director badmouthing the film in the press, “Heat” never really stood a chance. Yet the movie that exists doesn’t show signs of any of the production’s dysfunction, aside from a slightly abrupt and abbreviated finale (one of several that was shot). In the end, Goldman and Reynolds, more than any director, are the true auteurs of “Heat,” and the consistency of their conception of Nick Escalante as an honorable, self-destructive, romantic, tortured, possibly doomed hero gives “Heat” a lingering emotional resonance and power that still works 40 years later.

Burt would continue his forays into Burt Noir both in film (“Malone,” “Rent-A-Cop,” “Physical Evidence”) and television (“B.L. Stryker,” “Hard Time”), but he never played this kind of character better than he did in “Heat.” The movie was remade, incidentally, in 2015 by “Con Air” director Simon West as “Wild Card.” That version didn’t connect with critics or audiences either, in spite of Goldman once again writing the screenplay. At this point it’s fair to assume that “Heat” is just a doomed project, which is a shame — since it also happens to represent one of Goldman’s finest artistic moments.

#3432. Andrew Garfield Officially Transforms Into Sam Altman in New ‘Artificial’ Trailer

By now, many people know Sam Altman because he has become almost synonymous with ChatGPT and OpenAI. Since ChatGPT burst onto the scene several years ago, it has become one of the most valuable tech companies in the world after pioneering AI as we know it. But while many might have known about the app and its parent company, OpenAI, for a few years, Altman spent decades steering it as it sought to make one of the biggest technological advancements in history. Like many companies, OpenAI has faced a lot of problems, chief among them leadership wrangling.

When OpenAI was launched, its goal was to become a venture geared towards the flourishing of humanity. It was a non-profit organization that relied on funding from the ultra-wealthy to keep its research and breakthroughs going. But at some point, its funders had a different vision, leading to internal struggles that saw Altman removed as CEO before returning. OpenAI is now a public benefit company that does business with other companies and the US government. Despite some problems with ChatGPT, Altman and his team have adopted the same mission as other AI companies: growth at all costs. They think AI will, at the very least, replace human labor, and if they really succeed, annihilate humanity.

Enter Artificial, a drama film directed by Luca Guadagnino that turns back the clock and explores how we got here. The film explores the two-decade AI race that has upended the world as we know it, for good or for worse. When a computer scientist and AI pioneer, Professor Geoffrey Hinton, makes a breakthrough they are certain will alter humanity forever, Sam Altman, Elon Musk, and the most prominent figures in Silicon Valley race to become part of their vision. As the technology becomes more powerful and more valuable than anyone ever imagined, a battle wages over who should control the tech that could change the fate of humanity," the film's official description explains.

The film was written by Simon Rich, with celebrated director Guadagnino behind the camera. Andrew Garfield is having his second The Social Network moment, leading the cast as Altman. Other cast members include Yura Borisov (Anora), Monica Barbaro (One Night Only), Cooper Hoffman (The Long Walk), Jason Schwartzman (Asteroid City), Ike Barinholtz (The Studio), and Mark Rylance (Wolf Hall). Artificial is being distributed by Neon after Amazon MGM dropped it following the signing of a $50 billion deal with OpenAI. Neon is bringing the film to select theaters on December 25 before it streams on January 8. The trailer embedded in the YouTube video above previews the film's events and characters.

#3431. The Thing Meets Brokeback Mountain In This Award-Winning Sci-Fi Author's 2027 Book

Since John Carpenter’s The Thing (1982), few works of horror media have been quite so successful at capturing the uncanny terror of being isolated on icy terrain.

Adapted from the 1932 sci-fi novella Who Goes There? by John W. Campbell, that filmmade full use of its Antarctic setting, turning the mere possibility of what lives out on the ice into the ultimate boogeyman. With nowhere to run and nothing on the horizon but more snow, the tight-knit group of researchers at the center of The Thing became strangers as paranoia—and a malevolent entity—invaded their base, turning colleague against colleague in a fight to stay alive.

In all great works of horror-on-ice fiction, the frozen landscape has a way of becoming a character in and of itself, one that is as much of a villain to the characters as any supernatural entity. Luckily, the reigning queen of literary sci-fi is following in that tradition with her next novel.

Julia Armfield’s Up to the Light, which releases on March 30, 2027, will be a treat for anyone who loved her debut novel, Our Wives Under the Sea (2022). This one is similar in both premise and structure: it’s told in two timelines, predominantly by two soulmate narrators, in the period leading up to and after a potentially supernatural disaster.

In 1994, best friends and expert mountain climbers Petal and Liam join an expedition led by Jim, a wealthy, vain documentarian, to scale Mount Varda, Western Europe's highest summit. If successful, their eight-person crew would be the first to reach the summit. In 2005, only Petal, Liam, and Jim remain—as does Jim’s best-selling, highly disputed memoir about their doomed expedition, excerpts of which are interspersed between Liam and Petal’s narration.

In true Armfield fashion, however, the supernatural disaster is only one part of the story. It takes nearly two-thirds of the novel for her mountain climbers to actually begin their climb, but the delay doesn’t feel like a letdown. Long before a single character sets foot at the base, the mountain is already a character in its own right. It produces strange visions, emits phantom sounds, and even changes shape overnight. There’s also the looming phantom of previous failed expeditions, particularly a doomed climb from 21 years earlier that resulted in the deaths of its entire crew. The mountain, like a haunted mansion, seems to cast out unwanted visitors.

Up to the Light was pitched as "Into Thin Air meets The Haunting of Hill House by way of Brokeback Mountain." Though that last comparison seems out of left field, it's a welcome twist as the story takes shape.

It may take most of the novel for Armfield to set up the disastrous climb, but she wastes no time building out a slow-burn romance. (So slow-burn that revealing the two characters involved would involve a mild spoiler.) Somewhere, amid all the haunted mountaineering, Armfield finds time to craft an achingly romantic rivals-to-lovers arc that, along with another beautifully written platonic relationship, gives the book its emotional core.

Armfield’s sci-fi has always been horror-adjacent, but Up to the Light is perhaps her only novel that truly belongs in that category. She reworks some of her favorite tropes from Our Wives Under the Sea and Private Rites—shared hallucinations, characters whose physical bodies seem to be disappearing bit by bit, an entity too cosmic for any one narrator to fully articulate—but dials up the scares to a new level.

The horror in this novel feels akin to Mike Flanagan’s in The Haunting of Bly Manor—chilling, but also so emotionally resonant that the worst terror comes not from jump scares, but from anticipating the next devastating loss.

Still, this book is terrifying. Among the climbers, there’s a constant, looming memory of the lost crew from 20 years earlier, and a creeping feeling that somehow, they’ve each been here before. Where the researchers in The Thing grew openly suspicious of each other, these climbers are too nervous to even mention the strange happenings that abound on this mountain.

But there is also real environmental terror to contend with: the increasing risk of freezing to death or running out of oxygen, the constant prospect of avalanches and storms, the looming threat of death-by-falling, and the very real possibility of simply getting lost in the snow and never returning. When it all comes to a head, Up to the Light transforms itself in a second from slow-paced literary fiction to an all-out bloodbath.

Up to the Light ​​​​​​releases on March 30, 2027. You can pre-order it here.

#3430. I Analyzed the Seven Biggest AI Chatbots to Determine How Safe They Are for Kids

David Nield is a technology journalist from Manchester in the U.K. who has been writing about gadgets and apps for more than 20 years.

He has a bachelor's degree in English Literature from Durham University, where he also spent a term as editor of the award-winning student newspaper Palatinate. His journalism career started in print media, where he contributed to and edited several technology magazines and bookazines sold in the U.K. and internationally. More recently, he has worked as a freelancer for some of the biggest technology publications on the web, covering everything from on-the-ground reporting about product launches, to detailed explainers and how-to guides on apps, gadgets, and platforms. His expertise covers broad areas of consumer tech, including smartphones, laptops, wearables, and AI.

AI safety for both adults and children is under greater scrutiny than ever before, with a growing number of questions and concerns appearing around how beneficial or otherwise these conversational bots actually are for our mental well-being—even without considering their energy use, ethics, or economic implications. At the same time, an increasing number of apps and services are becoming age-gated in a growing number of countries around the world, as governments realize that letting kids loose on AI apps, social media platforms, and the web at large might not be the best idea for their ongoing development and prosperity.

The big AI apps, such as ChatGPT and Gemini, are right in the center of these trends, and the companies behind them are taking steps that they promise will keep children safe. If you want to know what youngsters in your family may be getting exposed to, and what you can do about it, here's the rundown.

OpenAI's ChatGPT has one of the more comprehensive setups in terms of parental controls. The minimum age for users is 13, and if you're under 18, you need to have parental consent to open an account—age is predicted via several signals, including what times of day you use ChatGPT and what you talk about.

Accounts for under-18s automatically become ChatGPT for Teens accounts. There's more of a focus on learning and study (with a dedicated study mode), as well as "age-appropriate safeguards to help reduce exposure to sensitive or potentially harmful content." There are built-in protections for "harmful topics," including sexual, romantic, or violent roleplay, graphic violence, and self-harm. These work on top of the safeguards for all users that limit chats about physical harm and illegal activity.

These ChatGPT for Teens accounts can also be linked to a parental account—but while parental consent is required for under-18s to use the service, ChatGPT clearly says that teens do have the option to break the link if they want. If you do persuade your kid to keep your accounts connected, you can set time limits on when the AI bot can be used, and tweak some of the sensitivity settings. However, you can't view any conversations.

To set up parental controls from ChatGPT on the web, click your profile icon (bottom left), then Settings > Parental controls > Add family member and follow the instructions. It's also worth bearing in mind that ChatGPT app can also be used for free, anonymously, in any web browser, though OpenAI says users accessing the AI this way are subject to the default under-18s limits (and can't save chats or access an archive).

Gemini is tied into everything else Google does, and follows the broader rules for Google accounts: No under-13s, unless you're part of a family group and using an account managed by an adult. You can manage your family through the Family Link portal on the web, though as far as parental controls specific to Gemini go, you can only enable or disable access to the AI (settings like screen time apply across all enabled apps).

For all under-18s (partly identified through age estimation), whether or not they're part of a managed family group, Google applies some additional protections. They include preventing the AI from taking on a persona, guarding against emotional dependence on the AI, and discouraging bullying and other forms of harassment. There are also safeguards to limit chats about age-restricted substances like alcohol or vapes, and mental health issues like eating disorders.

These protections for minors are applied in addition to the usual guardrails in Gemini for everyone. The guardrails should lead you away from conversations about self-harm, suicide, violence, and illegal activities, and offer quick links to support in times of crisis. However, Google itself admits that these filters aren't perfect.

As with ChatGPT, there's a loophole of sorts in that anyone can start chatting with Gemini, for free inside a web browser, with no checks at all. These conversations can't be saved and come up against usage limits fairly quickly, but they're only protected by the general restrictions for all accounts, not the ones specific to minors.

Meta AI will show up in several apps that young people and children are likely to use, including WhatsApp and Instagram, as well as having its own separate app on the web and on phones. The standard restrictions for Meta's social media accounts apply to its AI too: A minimum age of 13, and restrictions for all under-18s. Like many other platforms, it uses some AI magic to flag up accounts being used by minors.

If you're under 18 and on a Meta Teen account, you'll come up against blocks if you try to get Meta AI to engage in sexual or romantic roleplay, or discuss alcohol or substance misuse. Chats on topics such as eating disorders and self-harm will prompt the AI to offer guidance towards relevant support services.

Meta offers a comprehensive parental control setup for its apps, including Meta AI, but connecting a parent account isn't compulsory for teens. This is handled through the Meta Family Center portal, and parents can get reports on the general topics that kids are chatting about with AI—though they don't get the exact transcripts or prompts. Any self-harm or suicide discussion can trigger an alert to the connected parent account.

All users, under 18 or over 18, get support and crisis intervention responses when chatting about suicide and self-harm, and there are strict limits on discussing illegal and harmful acts, including drug use and cyberbullying, as well as sexual and adult content.

Apple users have to be 13 or over to have an account, which is required to access Siri AI—anyone younger needs to have an account created for them by an adult, and these accounts can only get at the basic, older Siri. Date of birth must be declared when opening an Apple account, with tighter checks rolling out in many parts of the world.

Anyone over the age of 13 can have an Apple account and use the Siri AI app, with or without a connected parent account, as it stands in most U.S. states. This means the well-being safeguards are essentially the same for teens as they are for adults: There are safeguards around self-harm, suicide, sexual and violent content, and illegal commands. It's one of the more conservative AIs when it comes to what it will talk about.

The new and improved Siri AI can be managed to some extent by the new parental controls available in iOS 27 and Apple's other software updates for 2026—Apple has clearly seen the way the wind is blowing—but this is optional for teens. It depends on whether or not you can corral your kids into a Family Sharing group.

If your teens are in your family group of users, then the standard Screen Time rules apply for controlling app usage limits and device access (in iOS Settings, tap your name, then Family to get at them). There are also options for disabling certain Siri AI features, such as the writing tools or the image creation capabilities.

Like Gemini/Google and Apple/Siri, Copilot is tied into the wider Microsoft ecosystem, and access for under-18s can be managed through it. Users must be 13 or older to hold a Microsoft or a Copilot account—and again, there's some underlying tech in place to detect anyone who might be deliberately lying about their age.

If you've got a teen using Copilot, you can manage their access through the standard Microsoft Family Safety portal. You're able to enable or disable Copilot access, set times during which Copilot can and can't be used, and disable certain features like image generation or voice mode. Parents can't read the Copilot chats of their kids, though.

Parental supervision is optional—a teen aged 13–17 can use Copilot without linking their account to an adult one. Microsoft says users identified as under 18 won't see personalized results or ads, and will get age-appropriate responses regarding risky or harmful content, though there's not much detail on what that entails.

More generally, content around self-harm, violence, adult content, harassment, and harmful or illegal activity is banned on the AI platform. Any prompts about suicide or drugs will bring up support options rather than answers, whether you're an adult or a young person using the service.

Out of the bigger AI chatbots out there, Grok is very much the worst at protecting minors. It can be accessed through X or as its own standalone app, and while its terms of use indicate there's a minimum age requirement of 13, a recent report by Common Sense Media says the platform's age checks aren't effective.

Ultimately that means that minors have the same access to Grok as adults, if they want it—an AI platform that combines "weak safety guardrails" and "a range of extremely harmful content" that includes "explicit sexual content, mental health risks, violent content, and inappropriate responses to... offensive content" (that's the Common Sense Media Report again).

Yes, this is the AI chatbot that has previously had a problem with deepfake porn imagery, and which has traditionally taken a rather casual attitude towards safety concerns, led by SpaceXAI CEO Elon Musk. While illegal and harmful content is supposedly banned from Grok, its own FAQs admit that certain chats can result in "dialogue that may involve coarse language, crude humor, sexual situations, or violence."

There is actually a Grok Kids Mode that limits the kind of content that can be shown and the conversation topics that can be added, but it requires users to self-declare themselves as minors and is easy to bypass. The advice from Common Sense Media seems to be the way to go with Grok: Do not let your teens access it.

Claude's approach to child safety is straightforward: You can only register for an account if you're over 18. It is possible to lie about your age when signing up, but like the other platforms, Anthropic looks at various "signals" in behavior to spot minors—if your account gets flagged, you have to verify your age using an option like face age estimation or Yoti.

There's no free web access to the chatbot, like there is with ChatGPT and Gemini, so if you're under 18, you're locked out from the service unless you know the behavioral tricks to get past Claude's detection systems.

In terms of more general well-being protections on Claude, any chat around self-harm or suicide will guide users towards helplines and other resources for support. Conversations about illegal activities, disallowed speech, and explicit sexual content are banned from the platform. In recent months, Anthropic says it's also reduced AI sycophancy.

That's something of a whistle-stop tour of the big seven AI chatbots, but if you're a parent, it should give you some idea of what's out there and how easy it is to access. Besides the parental controls built into these AIs (or not), you also have the settings available at the platform level—Android, iOS, Windows, macOS—to restrict the use of any potentially harmful apps.
