#3429. Taylor Sheridan’s ‘Tulsa King’ Officially Sets Season 4 Finale Date

Taylor Sheridan fans may have to wait a little longer for the third season of Landman, but another of his popular shows has officially set a date for its most important episode. It was thought for most of the year that Landman would make it back to streaming for Season 3 before the end of the year, but several production delays led to the new release date being pushed back into 2027. Taylor Sheridan regulars have had several other shows to help hold them over before Landman Season 3, though, including the long-awaited third season of Lioness, the dark ops spy thriller starring Zoe Saldaña. Despite dominating streaming throughout the duration of its third season and even weeks after its finale, the series has still not been officially picked up for Season 4 — its fate remains undecided.

One of Sheridan’s shows that doesn’t have the same issue is Tulsa King, the gritty crime thriller starring Sylvester Stallone that’s currently in the heat of its fourth season. Paramount doubled down on the future of Tulsa King weeks ago, announcing that the show had already been renewed for a fifth season, which will also be the first season of the show set in New York. Stallone also told Collider earlier this year that he would like to see the show run for six seasons, but before making it this far, it has to get through its fourth season, which premiered on Paramount Plus on October 16. With another 10-episode order like the past two seasons, Paramount has confirmed that new episodes of Tulsa King will be released until the Season 4 finale on December 18, just nine days before Christmas.

The show that claimed the most of your answers is the world you were built for. If two tied, both are shown — you're complicated enough to straddle two Sheridan universes.

You are a Dutton — or you might as well be. You understand that some things are worth protecting at any cost, and that the modern world's indifference to history, to land, to legacy, is not something you're willing to accept quietly. You lead from the front, you carry your family's weight without complaint, and when someone threatens what's yours, you don't escalate — you finish it. You're not cruel. But you are absolute. In Yellowstone's world, that combination of ferocity and loyalty doesn't make you a villain. It makes you the only thing standing between everything that matters and everyone who wants to take it.

You thrive in the chaos of high-stakes negotiation, where the money is enormous, the margins are thin, and the wrong word in the wrong room can cost everyone everything. You're a fixer — the person called when a situation is already on fire and needs someone with the nerve to walk into it. West Texas oil country rewards exactly what you are: sharp, adaptable, unsentimental, and absolutely clear-eyed about what people want and what they'll do to get it. You're not naive enough to think this world is fair. You're smart enough to be the one deciding who it's fair to.

You are a Dwight Manfredi — someone who has served their time, paid their dues, and arrived somewhere unexpected with nothing but their reputation and their wits. You adapt without losing yourself. You build loyalty through respect rather than fear, though you're not above reminding people that the two aren't mutually exclusive. Tulsa King is for people who are still standing when everyone assumed they'd be finished — who find, in an unfamiliar place, that they're more capable than the world gave them credit for. You don't need a throne. You build one, wherever you happen to land.

You carry the weight of a system that is broken by design, and you do it anyway — because someone has to, and because you're the only one positioned to do it without the whole thing collapsing. Mike McLusky's world is for people who are comfortable operating where there are no good options, only less catastrophic ones. You speak every language: law enforcement, criminal, political, human. That fluency makes you invaluable and it makes you a target. You've made your peace with both. Mayor of Kingstown belongs to people who understand that keeping the peace is not the same as being at peace — and who do the job regardless.

Before Tulsa King, the only one of Taylor Sheridan’s shows that had received an official spin-off is Yellowstone, which has other shows like Marshals and Dutton Ranch to continue its story. Now, Tulsa King is expanding next month on December 18 with Frisco King, the new series starring Samuel L. Jackson, who was first introduced in Tulsa King Season 3. This is the same day as the Tulsa King Season 4 finale. Paramount released the first official trailer for Frisco King earlier this week, which also confirmed that Sylvester Stallone will be featured as a guest star in the first season of the show. Asa Germann from Gen V will also recur in Season 1 alongside Jackson.

Check out new episodes of Tulsa King every week on Paramount Plus and stay tuned to Collider for more updates and coverage of Taylor Sheridan’s future projects.

#3428. How to Check Your Flight Status After the FAA Canceled the Ground Stop for All Airports

Update, 8:41 p.m.: The Federal Aviation Administration announced it has ended the ground stop.

On Friday afternoon, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ordered a nationwide ground stop for all airports in the United States. If you're planning to fly this afternoon or evening, or you have friends or family doing the same, you're likely concerned about tracking flight statuses. While there's still a lot we don't know, there are tools to help track flights at this time:

There are a number of options for tracking flights, whether you have your flight number or not. If you have the flight number, the fastest method is to Google it: Google will display a live tracker of your flight at the top of the results page. You can also head to the airline's official website to track your flight: United Airlines, for example, has a flight tracker where you can either enter your route information or your flight number. Most, if not all, airlines will have a similar tool you can use.

Alternatively, you can use a site or service that tracks all flights. FlightAware is one such site and has a flight tracker that lets you search flights—so long as you know the origin and the destination. If you have the flight number, your iPhone can help: You can enter your flight number into Spotlight search to see a live tracker, or you can text a contact your flight number, then tap the link that appears under the number to see a tracker of the flight.

At this time, the exact reason isn't totally clear. According to the agency, “The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following communication issues impacting multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers,” but the FAA hasn't said what caused those communications issues or when they expect to lift the grounding. The grounding order comes one day after a massive Microsoft outage that disrupted service for users of Outlook, Teams, and other Microsoft products. It also comes one day after Ars Technica reported that the FAA was rolling out an AI-powered tool to help manage air traffic across the country.

This is only the third time in U.S. history that the FAA has made such an order—once after 9/11, and again in January of 2023 due to a pilot alert system issue; the latter ground stop lasted around 90 minutes.

Jude Law and Andrew Garfield will star as Siegfried Fischbacher and Roy Horn in the upcoming series Wild Things, and Apple TV just announced the premiere date and shared a teaser video.

Created by John Hoffman, Wild Things tells the true story of the iconic Las Vegas magician act Siegfried and Roy, who regularly incorporated tigers and lions into their performances. Back in 2003, a tiger attacked Horn on stage, bringing the duo's long-running stage show to a close.

The Wild Things teaser begins with a shot of the Las Vegas Sphere. Images of Law and Garfield as Siegfried and Roy appear on the exterior's LED display, along with a clip of the duo walking on either side of a white tiger. The video ends with the tiger growling and the April 16 premiere date reveal. Throughout the teaser, Siegfried says in a voiceover, "We will give you the most spectacular event anyone has ever seen." Roy then adds, "Siegfried and Roy, masters of the impossible."

Garfield, Law, Leckart, Brian Grazer, Tony Leondis, Kathy Ciric, Will Malnati and director Matt Shakman serve as executive producers as well. #3424. Sunrise On The Reaping Soundtrack Guide: Every Song & When They Play

Warning: Contains spoilers for The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping!Despite its dystopian sci-fi setting, The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping includes multiple songs, with its full soundtrack even bigger than the movie lets on. The Hunger Games movies have always incorporated music, with Katniss Everdeen singing throughout the first four films and Lucy Gray Baird's songs heavily featured in The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes.

While Sunrise on the Reaping shifts the story to a 16-year-old Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada), the District 12 tribute is hardly someone to break into song. Nor are there any major needle drops. The movie instead utilizes the Covey and known District 12 songs to sprinkle in some music as Haymitch's life and the 50th Hunger Games unfold.

In typical Hunger Games fashion, the songs speak directly to the story and larger themes. Multiple are performed by Haymitch's Covey girlfriend, Lenore Dove Baird (Whitney Peak). And while there's only five songs heard from the start to finish of Sunrise on the Reaping, the movie's complete soundtrack includes a lot more Hunger Games-inspired music.

"The Raven" by Whitney Peak: Sunrise on the Reaping gets the music going from the very beginning. As establishing shots of District 12 are shown to get audiences accustomed to how it looks 24 years before Katniss' story began and some prep for the 50th Hunger Games reaping, the movie introduces the vocal performance of Peak's Lenore Dove. The movie brings "The Raven" back shortly thereafter, as Lenore is singing it in the meadow when Haymitch comes to see her on the morning of the reaping.

"The Goose and the Common" by Whitney Peak: Lenore is responsible for the next song in Sunrise on the Reaping, which occurs while the 2nd Quarter Quell is underway. Haymitch is poisoned by water and only survives by eating a charcoal tablet, leaving him to lay on the ground and recover. As he looks to the sky, birds fly overhead and he hears Lenore singing "The Goose and the Common."

"The Old Therebefore" by Scot Greenan: Sunrise on the Reaping's soundtrack doesn't resume until after the 50th Hunger Games are over. After Haymitch returns to District 12, the locals gather for a funeral to honor the fallen tributes: Maysilee Donner, Wyatt Callow, and Louella McCoy. The funeral concludes with Scot Greenan's Burdock Everdeen singing "The Old Therebefore," which was originally performed by Rachel Zegler's Lucy Gray Baird in The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes.

"Deep in the Meadow (Lullaby)" by Jennifer Lawrence: One of the last songs in Sunrise on the Reaping comes as part of the epilogue, which jumps beyond the events of Mockingjay and shows Haymitch celebrating the sun rising on his birthday without a reaping. After a short exchange with Katniss and Peeta Mellark, featuring Jennifer Lawrence and Josh Hutcherson back in their iconic roles, Woody Harrelson's version of Haymitch is shown in the meadow outside District 12. Lawrence sings a new rendition of "Deep in the Meadow" as Haymitch remembers his time with Lenore.

"Draw You Out" by Noah Kahan: Once Sunrise on the Reaping's credits begin, the movie shifts to another song, "Draw You Out" by Noah Kahan. The song was written exclusively for the Hunger Games movie and plays over the early credits that highlight the film's main cast members.

Those five songs are not the only ones on Sunrise on the Reaping's soundtrack, though. Lionsgate and MCA recruited a massive collection of artists to curate an entire album of songs that are almost exclusively written, performed, and produced specifically for the film. The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping — The Album includes 29 songs, which have a total length of 1 hour and 40 minutes. The full song list is below:

The Sunrise on the Reaping soundtrack is currently available to listen to in several ways, as it was released a full week before the movie even hit theaters. The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping — The Album can be heard in its entirety on Amazon Music, Apple Music, Spotify, and YouTube Music.

Beyond the digital options, the studios have ensured that there are multiple physical copies to acquire and collect. There are eight limited edition vinyl variants: First Pressing Pretty With A Purpose 2LP, District 12 Edition Volcanic Ash 2LP, Capitol Edition Elegance Is Authority 2LP, a Target exclusive Wild Sunflower 2LP, an Amazon exclusive Sweetshop 2LP, an Indie Store exclusive Sage Mist 2LP, a Barnes & Noble exclusive Songbird Sky 2LP, and a Walmart exclusive Meadowgold 2LP.

#3423. Quentin Tarantino’s First Movie in 7 Years Is Officially a Near-Perfect Hit

Quentin Tarantino's last movie debuted to rave reviews and boffo box office seven years ago, in 2019. And while he's still hemming and hawing over his tenth and reportedly last movie in the director's chair, he's set to return to theaters next week with a new film. That movie just had its Hollywood premiere earlier this week, and the reactions are in.

The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth is a sequel to Tarantino's last film, Once Upon a Time in Hollywood, focusing on the onetime stuntman of the title (Brad Pitt). Tarantino penned the script, but he didn't direct: that honor went to David Fincher, in what will be the final act of his groundbreaking contract with Netflix. Tarantino had previously penned a number of films that were helmed by other directors, including True Romance, Natural Born Killers, and From Dusk Till Dawn, but this is the first time it's happened in 30 years.

And now, the reviews are in, and it's looking like this adventure is well worth undertaking. The movie has an 89% Fresh rating on Rotten Tomatoes, which puts it in the upper echelon of films for both Tarantino and Fincher. In fact, it outdoes its predecessor, which currently holds an 86% Fresh rating. That should bode well for the film: its predecessor grossed $410 million USD at the box office and garnered 10 Oscar nominations, winning two (Best Supporting Actor for Pitt and Best Production Design).

ScreenRant's Graeme Guttman raved about the film, calling it a hangout movie that takes a look at a darker side of Los Angeles than its predecessor:

...the reason Further Mis-Adventures works so well is, in part, because Fincher is able to visually tap into the sadness of the character and the time period at the heart of the film. Sure, Cliff is wily and spirited and Hollywood is booming, but there's an underlying sense of melancholy that follows him around town: in interactions with his father, in the way he pursues Karen, and even in his relationship to the world of film, which he so clearly loves even if it doesn't always love him back.

Jake Kleinman at Polygon smells a sequel, and thinks this could be part of an extended franchise for Tarantino:

...it's easy to imagine a world where we get to keep hanging out with Cliff for even longer. Like Benoit Blanc returning to solve each new Knives Out mystery, Brad Pitt's fixer could easily resurface a few years from now for another misadventure, ideally with Tarantino still writing the script.

Collider's Robert Brian Taylor, meanwhile, doesn't agree with the critical consensus: he calls it "a surprisingly shrug-worthy affair."

The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth is a lark, a throwaway, a side quest. If that's all you want out of it, you'll find things to enjoy here. But if you're hoping for something on the level of Once Upon a Time... in Hollywood (or any of Tarantino or Fincher's masterworks, really), I'd suggest realigning your expectations.

Rare for a Netflix release, The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth is getting a worldwide launch in theaters: it will hit the big screen for two weeks only, starting on November 25, before coming to the streamer on December 23.

Nevermind turned thirty-five last month and the arguments started up again immediately, which is what these four records do. Here is yours, what it says about you, and the case for it being the best album on the list.

You are the beautiful disaster who keeps everybody together anyway. Rumours was made by five people who were all breaking up with each other in the same room and refusing to stop working, and it came out sounding like the sunniest record of the decade.

You are the one who went quiet and came back with a theory. Dark Side is an album about time, money, pressure and losing your mind, built so carefully that it still sounds like it was finished yesterday.

You are the main character and you have never pretended otherwise. Purple Rain is an album, a film and a complete personality delivered at once, by somebody who decided he was going to be the most interesting person alive and then simply was.

You want it on your own terms or not at all. Nevermind is the record that dragged the underground into the middle of the mainstream and then spent the rest of its life uncomfortable about having done it.

Now bereft of his actor pal Rick Dalton (Leonardo DiCaprio, who is not in the movie), Cliff Booth is now a theater manager and Hollywood fixer living with his elderly father (Peter Weller). Pretty soon, he gets mixed up with a TV star (Scott Caan) and his wife (Carla Gugino), a high-powered talent agent (Elizabeth Debicki), a football star turned Blaxploitation actor (Yahya Abdul-Mateen II), and some sadistic Filipino mobsters.

The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth will be released in theaters on November 25 for a limited engagement, then will stream exclusively on Netflix on December 23. Stay tuned to Collider for future updates.

#3421. Google Killed Its Dark Web Report, but You Can Still Monitor Data Breaches

Google’s Dark Web Report used to be the only consumer-focused platform that let users scan major data breaches, dark web marketplaces, and private forums to see if their personal information had ended up in the hands of hackers. But the company discontinued the service at the start of 2026, with new scans stopping on Jan. 15 and all accounts deleted on Feb. 16.

Google says it sunsetted Dark Web Report because, although the information it provided was generally useful, the service failed to provide “helpful next steps” for users whose data was found on the dark web. Google promised a new service that would provide more actionable intel, but that service has yet to materialize, and there haven’t been any further announcements about it yet.

Dark Web Report may not have been perfect, but it was the only early warning system of its kind that was available for personal use and let users run scans free of cost. Now that it’s gone, however, there are plenty of other services that offer the same service at varying costs and levels of effectiveness. Let’s talk through the nature of the insight that Google's reports offered, how it collected that information in the first place, and what options exist in the market to replace it.

Google launched the Dark Web Report in March 2023 as a premium feature available to Google One users, but later extended it for free to anyone with a Google account and moved it to the "Results about you" dashboard.

You'd set up a monitoring profile with your name, date of birth, physical address, phone number, emails, and Social Security Number if you lived in the U.S. After that, you could head to the dashboard anytime you wanted to run a free scan across dark web forums and marketplaces, publicly disclosed corporate data breaches, and other hidden online spaces to see if any of your personal information had shown up there. It was easy to use—but not a lot of people knew it existed in the first place.

It’s unclear what prompted the internal decision at Google, but in the absence of concrete next steps, it is reasonable to think the reports could create panic for the uninitiated. There’s no way to remove your information from the dark web once it’s already in circulation there. Still, having an early warning so you could reset 2FA or self-lock your SSN isn’t without merit.

But perhaps more importantly, most people with Google accounts didn’t know and hadn’t heard of the Dark Web Report’s existence. Google has likely taken it as a hint that users want more active remediation tools than simple alerts, which is why it’s now directing users to the Password Manager, Passkeys, and “Results about you” dashboard instead—though, again, the company hasn't followed through on a direct replacement for Dark Web Report, despite teasing such a feature.

Many of the top dark web scanners draw from the same well of information, scanning against major data breaches and dark web spaces. Several also offer breach notifications that send you email alerts when your details show up in a periodic scan. However, none of that is worth paying for because Have I Been Pwned or Mozilla Monitor cover those features quite well for free. Even the default password managers from Google and Apple come with some ability to monitor leaked credentials.

There isn’t an easy way to scrub your information from the dark web once it ends up getting leaked. But you can take steps to protect sensitive information or financial data once you know there’s been a leak. If a password has been compromised, reset it immediately. Also, enable 2FA on the affected account for added security. Even better, switch to a passkey if that account supports it. If not, authenticator apps are a safer way to receive 2FA codes than standard SMS.

If your Social Security number has been leaked, freeze your credit with Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion. You can do this by contacting each agency separately. Freezing your credit will prevent unauthorized credit withdrawals and protect your credit score from abuse by attackers. If one of your credit or debit card numbers has ended up in a breach, call your bank to freeze transactions on that card immediately.

Finally, get in the habit of using email aliases instead of sharing your actual email address with every platform and service provider. Addy.io and Proton’s SimpleLogin are both popular services that let you generate temporary email aliases that point to your inbox.

#3418. New Legend Of Zelda 40th Anniversary Collection Officially Confirmed For 2027

The Legend of Zelda may have celebrated its 40th anniversary in 2026, but that doesn't mean the festivities won't continue in 2027. Thanks to the latest financial results from Nintendo, we have official confirmation that additional 40th anniversary releases will happen next year, and they will stretch beyond the movie and merchandise we know about already. For Zelda fans who are already looking ahead to see what's next for the beloved franchise, this is great news.

This year is already ending on a strong note for The Legend of Zelda. The Ocarina of Time remake launched on Switch 2 earlier this month, becoming the best-selling physical game of the year and receiving accolades from critics and players alike. This year has also seen the release of some music collections and apparel over the summer, as well as a new LEGO set back in March. Thankfully, it looks like 2027 might be an even bigger year for The Legend of Zelda and its fans.

Nintendo has shared its second quarter financial results and corporate management policy for 2026, and within the 47-page document, Shuntaro Furukawa, President of Nintendo, outlines some surprising news for 40th anniversary releases for next year, even though the 40th anniversary is technically over as soon as the calendar year moves into 2027.

Furukawa states that going into next year, Nintendo "will pursue a variety of initiatives to celebrate the 40th anniversary of The Legend of Zelda. In addition to games, we will expand opportunities for consumers to experience its world through the movie, music, character merchandise, and more."

Furthermore, Nintendo "will make the series even more appealing by offering different ways to enjoy it, both for those who cherish its earlier titles and for those discovering it for the first time.”

While the overview doesn't mention specific releases, it at least confirms that more 40th anniversary items are coming in 2027. And it sounds like that will include more than next year's movie and merchandise. Of course, beyond a new mainline Legend of Zelda game, there's at least a couple of big releases that would get Zelda fans hyped.

For years now, fans have wanted HD remasters of Twilight Princess and Wind Waker on the Switch (and eventually the Switch 2). Thus far, neither game has gotten a re-release since the HD remasters arrived on the Wii U. While Wind Waker at least showed up on the GameCube library for Nintendo Switch Online, it wasn't necessarily what most fans were hoping for. Considering all of this, the timing would be right to release both HD remasters in 2027 as part of the continued 40th anniversary celebrations.

Right now, we don't have any specifics on what else Nintendo is planning for The Legend of Zelda in 2027. #3417. Four Things You Can Do With Google Maps' New 'Ask Maps' Feature

Google has given its AI-powered "Ask Maps" feature a major upgrade, adding tools for trip planning, real-time route guidance, appointment finding, and saved-list search. The updates begin rolling out today on Android and iOS.

Google launched Ask Maps last March as an AI assistant designed to handle questions and requests more complicated than simply searching the word "bar" or "groceries." Instead of performing simple keyword searches, the idea behind Ask Maps is that you can describe several specific requirements at once, and Maps will find places that match them all. For example, you could ask for a restaurant with outdoor seating for a certain number of people, and "Ask Maps" will factor in your past searches and give you results. Of course, AI assistants have a habit of making things up, so even with today's roll-out, you'll want to double-check your sources before you drive an hour to the wrong restaurant.

To me, this is the most useful new feature launching today. Whether you're planning a day trip for holiday shopping or something more ambitious, like a three-day road trip with coastal hikes and oceanfront dining, Ask Maps will put together a day-by-day schedule. Each plan includes insider tips and numbered map pins for every stop, so you can see the whole route at a glance. Once you're happy with the plan, you can share it with friends and family or export it to Google Docs on desktop.

When it's time to head out, you can ask Maps to pull up your itinerary, or look for the "itinerary" badge in your chat history. You'll see real-time details such as live traffic conditions, whether a place is currently open, and even the vibe at your next stop.

Plans can change on the fly, too. Ask Maps to add a scenic viewpoint or a lunch spot along the way, then tap to get directions to your next stop straight from the itinerary.

Here's what else you can use Ask Maps to do, starting today.

Pulling up directions now surfaces "Know Before You Go" tips for your route. These include where to park or charge your car, along with real-time conditions like weather, potential delays, and tolls.

Ask Maps is also gaining some agentic capabilities. Allegedly, you can just ask, “Find me a 4 p.m. nail appointment near me,” and Ask Maps will show you open slots across nearby businesses. In addition to finding appointments, Google says this agent will be able to call local businesses on your behalf—stay tuned while I wait for the upgrade and test this one out myself.

If you keep lists of saved places, Ask Maps can now search them for you. Ask something like, "Which spots saved in my lists have availability for 5 in the next 30 minutes?" Ask Maps looks across your lists and checks live availability, so you can pick a place and go.

These updates start rolling out today on Android and iOS. Travel itineraries and saved-list search are available everywhere Ask Maps is offered. "Know Before You Go" route tips and appointment finding are launching first in the U.S., with more regions coming soon.

#3416. Jason Bourne Meets ‘Minority Report’ in Peacock’s Near-Perfect 8-Part Sci-Fi Thriller

Minority Report painted a chilling vision of the future, with the precognitive dreams of three psychic children leading police officers to arrest people before they could commit any potential crimes. It was also a propulsive action thriller, thanks to Steven Spielberg's expert hand and Tom Cruise's driven performance. Though therehave been plenty of science-fiction/action movies and television shows, none have come close to capturing the intensity of Minority Report (not even its short-lived TV sequel series). Peacock finally came close with The Copenhagen Test.

The Copenhagen Test follows a similar setup to Minority Report but also throws in a little of The Bourne Identity's signature mystery. Intelligence analyst Alexander Hale (Simu Liu) is accused of being a mole in the mysterious organization he works for, even though he protests his innocence. The truth is a little more complicated: someone has implanted technology in Hale's brain, transmitting everything he sees and hears. To catch the culprit, Hale decides to throw himself into field work, though he soon finds himself questioning who he can really trust.

Looking at all the talent attached to The Copenhagen Test, you'd probably mistake it for a high-concept science fiction blockbuster ​​​​​​rather than a streaming series. Simu Liu is joined by a cast including Melissa Barrera, Sinclair Daniel, Brian d'Arcy James and Mark O'Brien; all of them play characters who have a close connection to Alexander Hale, though it's up in the air if they're a friend or foe to him. In addition to taking the role of leading man, Liu also executive produces The Copenhagen Test alongside horror legend James Wan. Wan had previously produced the short-lived horror/sci-fi series Teacup for Peacock, and The Copenhagen Test met the same fate when Peacock canceled it after one season.

The Copenhagen Test also has an advantage: there's plenty of action to balance out the ongoing mystery. Not only is this a chance for Liu to once again show off his martial arts skills, but it also taps into the trend of military and spy shows as major standouts on streaming. Prime Video has more or less cornered the market thanks to shows like Reacher, The Terminal List, and Jack Ryan; Hulu has Paradise; and Apple TV+ has been delivering sci-fi hit after sci-fi hit. The Copenhagen Test lands squarely in that wheelhouse, giving Peacock another twisty thriller alongside All Her Fault.

Though comparisons might be made to The Minority Report and the Jason Bourne films when watching The Copenhagen Test, it turns out that the creators had another movie in mind — specifically, The Truman Show. The Jim Carrey dramedy centers on Truman Burbank, a man unaware that his entire life has been orchestrated as part of an extremely popular reality show, and given that The Copenhagen Test features a man whose body has literally been hijacked by cameras, the comparison is very apt.

The Copenhagen Test also featured plenty of hands-on creative input from Simu Liu, according to series creator Thomas Brandon. Brandon and co-showrunner Jennifer Yale went into detail about how Liu was involved in nearly every aspect of the creative process:

"Simu actually joined our writers' room for the first two weeks...He loves the creative process. He wasn't just an executive producer in name. He'd focus on relationships between other characters, not just his own. He was so thoughtful about the story as a whole."

The fact that Simu Liu is willing to dedicate himself to a project long enough to give notes on a script screams "passion project." While most fans might be looking forward to Liu reprising his role as Shang-Chi in Avengers: Doomsday, this should be on their radar, as it's a worthy successor to Minority Report.

All eight episodes of The Copenhagen Test are streaming on Peacock in the U.S.

Playbill is apologizing after posting a casting call for a musical about George Floyd ... admitting the listing should have never appeared on its website in the first place.

The theater publication came under fire after advertising for singers to appear on a cast album for "George Floyd the Musical," a dark comedy project from a company called Busted Broadway.

#3414. Marvel Officially Announces Captain America’s New Codename For Steve Rogers’ Next Era

Steve Rogers loses his Captain America title and replaces it with an ominous three-word moniker. Unlike Tony Stark, who has retained the Iron Man mantle almost permanently throughout his whole superhero career, Steve Rogers' historical legacy as Captain America has spawned dozens of official and unofficial replacements. Sam Wilson and Bucky Barnes are Steve Rogers' direct successors, and Sam himself has cemented himself as a definitive Captain America on the same level as Steve.

In the comics, following Steve’s apparent death in 1945, the US government quietly recruited William Nasland and later Jeffrey Mace to wear the uniform and preserve public morale without revealing the original Captain America’s loss, while Isaiah Bradley endured secret super-soldier experimentation as a Captain America tragically forgotten by history. Later decades introduced impostors like William Burnside, the obsessed 1950s Cold War fanatic who surgically altered his face and took a flawed serum that made him violent, alongside Roscoe Simons, a brave young Cap admirer briefly given the shield by Falcon before the Red Skull murdered him.

Steve Rogers has even been replaced by himself, back when Captain America's infamous Captain Hydra clone supplanted him in Secret Empire, and now by his own monstrous evolution.

Six months after Marvel first unveiled the Infernal Hulk's army for the upcoming Hulk War, the monster's nightmarish Avengers finally get their official names. Iron Man becomes "The Iron Thing" and Spider-Man becomes "The Arthropod," while Captain Marvel transforms into "The Ebon Sphinx" and Jubilee into "The Angler," with Vision evolving into the mind-bending "Diaboli Ex Machina." The darkest redesign in the Infernal Hulk's Avengers is probably Captain America, who's crucified and carried by four zombie soldiers, bearing the name "The War Dead."

The first image featuring the Infernal Hulk's Infernal Avengers revealed a crucified Captain America standing above the already large Iron Thing, Diaboli Ex MAchina, and Infernal Hulk, only surpassed in height by Spider-Man's colossal Arthropod transformation. It also included a couple of undead soldiers mysteriously clad in all red. Now, the Infernal Avengers character sheet designed by Nic Klein provides a closer look at "The War Dead," revealing that the four soldiers carrying Steve Rogers' body are actually bathed in his blood.

The Infernal Hulk has already proved nearly unbeatable with nothing but the Eldest-possessed body of the Hulk. Now aided by even bigger creatures like the muscular Iron Thing and the grotesquely large Arthropod, the Infernal Hulk seems truly unstoppable. The flying Ebon Sphinx also seems particularly dangerous in battle, and the Angler's energy-based body makes her the most unpredictable monster. Likewise, Diaboli Ex Machina may retain all of the Vision's overpowered abilities and none of his restraints.

Captain America may be single, but he sure has a lot of kids in the multiverse.

Captain America's body doesn't appear to undergo a transformation of any kind. Instead, Steve Rogers is pierced in the chest and the back by two spears, with an additional spear going through each hand decorated with skulls. Cap seems to be unconscious or dead, while the undead soldiers carry the whole weight of the platform supporting him on their shoulders. There's very little The War Dead may be able to do during battle, but his design is without a doubt the most gruesome of the Infernal Avengers.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Sharon Horgan had a string of British hits (including a couple we'll talk about here), before scoring stated successes with Divorce, Shining Vale, and Bad Sisters. She's quickly rising in the ranks of TV super-producers, the acerbically funny HBO Max rom-com Youth (in which she also stars) being just the latest.

This earlier series created by and starring Sharon Horgan is a family sitcom that feels far more believable than most, seeing Irish primary school teacher Sharon (Horgan) hooking up with American ad exec Rob (Rob Delaney) over the course of a week, only to discover that she's pregnant once he returns home. They don't really have feelings for each other, but decide to give it a go at being a couple, eventually falling into marriage just before the birth of their child. There are lots of jokes and plenty of acerbic dialogue, but this isn't Married... with Children. Sharon and Rob can be a bit nasty to each other and to their sloppy friend group, but there's also something rather sweet in the show's conviction that having someone to be a mess with can be one of life's great joys. Stream Catastrophe on Prime Video.

A little more of a high-concept here, but nevertheless an effective show about reimagining yourself in middle age. Younger follows Liza Miller (Sutton Foster), a recently divorced woman in her 40s who finds that age is a barrier to reentering the publishing industry she left years earlier. After a compliment convinces her that she could pass for a younger woman (poor thing), she manages to convince the right people that she's just 26 in order to land an entry-level job. Seven seasons of misadventures ensue, but much of the show revolves around the twisty-turny relationship between Liza and Josh (Nico Tortorella), a tattoo artist in his twenties. Stream Younger on Netflix.

Bridget Everett stars as Sam Miller, who struggles to find her new direction after moving back to her hometown to care for her dying sister. (Don't worry: There's plenty of comedy in the drama, and it's not as heavy as it sounds.) She's solidly middle-aged and starting over, kinda—making new friends in a familiar environment where she has to confront the past and the future alike. Luckily, her love of singing—and a community of goofy oddballs—are there to help. It's another story of a person of a certain age, trying to rebuild their life following an upheaval. Stream Somebody Somewhere on HBO Max.

When all else fails: Start a punk band. This drama from Sally Wainwright (Gentleman Jack) sees five women start a punk band as a lark, just a fun way to kill some time by entering a local talent context. The women realize very quickly, though, that they're very, very pissed off—about the workplace for women, menopause, a diminished dating pool, caring for aging parents and grown children—all of it tied up in the ways in which we treat women, and particularly middle-aged women. The band is a way to reclaim their voices, which doesn't erase or negate any of their problems nor drama (and there's plenty here), but gives them a platform with which to make some noise about it. Stream Riot Women on Britbox.

More of a traditional sitcom, not that there's anything wrong with that, this one builds a lot of goodwill with the performance of Leanne Morgan, its lead and co-creator (alongside Susan McMartin and Chuck Lorre). She plays the show's lead: a Knoxville, Tennessee wife and mom, who finds herself suddenly single in her 50s after her husband of 33 years leaves her. It's a genial, old-school hang-out show with a phenomenal veteran supporting cast that includes Kristen Johnston, Ryan Stiles, and Tim Daly. Stream Leanne on Netflix.

Michele Buteau, who also co-created the series) stars here as a fashion-forward stylist who'd devoted herself to the wrong guy for way too long. As the series opens, Mavis Beaumont is ready for a fresh start, putting herself and her career first—which does not preclude falling into a number of romantic entanglements. As she says more than once, she's going to take on the fashion world with a "body-positive attitude, cute v-neck, and some lip-gloss." Stream Survival of the Thickest on Netflix.

Certainly the goofiest take here on the idea of starting over in mid-life, this is very much a traditional three-camera sitcom, albeit one with a stacked cast of TV legends. Writer Melanie (Valerie Bertinelli), beautician Joy (Jane Leeves), and soap diva Victoria (Wendie Malick) wind up spending a wild night in Cleveland after a plane to Paris is diverted, discovering in the process that, while they're seen as over-the-hill back in Los Angeles, they're all Ohio 10s—though the sassy caretaker of their house, Elka (Betty White), might not agree. Stream Hot in Cleveland on Paramount+.

She'a s hair younger than Alex, but Fleabag (she's only ever referred to as "Fleabag") is trying to rebuild her life after a bad breakup, with extremely mixed results. This very dark comedy-drama follows a free-spirited, deeply angry single young woman living in London and sharing her romantic ups and downs via confessional asides to us, the audience. She falls, rather reluctantly, for "The Priest" (Andrew Scott)—while she's a confirmed atheist, and he's obviously not, the show doesn't turn aside from the general messiness of the situation. Phoebe Waller-Bridge won separate Emmys as the star, creator, and writer of the series. Stream Fleabag on Prime Video.

Maisel was one of Prime’s first truly buzzy original series, a comedy-drama from Amy Sherman-Palladino (Gilmore Girls) about the title’s Midge Maisel (Rachel Brosnahan), a long-time New York housewife of the late 1950s who discovers a talent for stand-up comedy. Inspired by the real-life careers of comedians like Totie Fields and Joan Rivers, the show is warm and welcoming, with great performances and dialogue; it also achieves something rare in being a show about comedy that’s actually funny. Stream The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel on Prime Video.

The big life change in this earlier Sharon Horgan hit is a little different: Julia Johnstone's mother had been a big help in taking care of Julia's children, but she's not going to do it anymore, leaving this working mom (Anna Maxwell Martin) to take the full brunt of childcare for the first time (her husband in the picture, but not much use). She joins up with other working moms involved with a local support group, including shallow Amanda (Lucy Punch), star of her own ongoing spin-off. Stream Motherland on Prime Video and Britbox.

#3410. What THAT Lucy Gray Reference In Sunrise On The Reaping Means For Her Hunger Games Fate

Warning! Spoilers for Sunrise on the Reaping (book and movie) ahead!Suzanne Collins' Sunrise on the Reaping included a mysterious reference to Lucy Gray Baird that provides some clues regarding her fate in the Hunger Games franchise. The question of whether she lived or died served as the final big mystery of The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes, and that was, of course, the entire point. Audiences were meant to ruminate on this and develop their own theories regarding Lucy Gray's ending. Though Haymitch's Hunger Games prequel mentioned the character a handful of times, one particular Lucy Gray reference stands out.

At the end of the Sunrise on the Reaping book, Haymitch searched desperately in the woods surrounding District 12 for Lenore Dove Baird's grave. He was finally led to a small Covey cemetery by Burdock Everdeen. Haymitch found three graves, each engraved with lines from the poems the deceased had been named for. One grave was, of course, dedicated to Lenore Dove. The other two belonged to Maude Ivory Baird and Lucy Gray Baird, both characters in The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes. This only presents Hunger Games readers with more questions.

At the end of The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes, Lucy Gray Baird attempts to escape Coriolanus Snow, who shoots after her through the trees. Snow was unsure whether any of his bullets had found Lucy Gray, and he was forced to flee the woods to seek care for his snake bite.

As far as Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes ever revealed, Snow remained uncertain about whether Lucy Gray lived or died all the way to his death. The fact that this songbird had a grave in District 12 in the year of the 50th Hunger Games could suggest that she had died, but it's really not that simple.

Lucy Gray's gravestone said only " - yet some maintain that to this day she is a living child; That you may see sweet Lucy Gray upon the lonesome wild." This is a line from the poem Lucy Gray by William Wordsworth, which the Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes character was named for.

It's possible that Tam Amber and Clerk Carmine found Lucy Gray's body in the woods after Snow returned to the Capitol and buried her in the Covey cemetery. This would mean that she truly had been shot at the end of Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes. It's also possible that the two Covey men searched but couldn't find Lucy Gray, so they dedicated an empty grave to her, assuming that Snow had killed her.

Additionally, the grave in Sunrise on the Reaping could indicate that Lucy Gray returned to the District 12 years later and was buried in the woods following the death of a different cause.

All the grave in Sunrise on the Reaping does is confirm that Tam Amber and Clerk Carmine have said their goodbyes to Lucy Gray. Whether they did so while possessing her actual body or they simply established an empty grave for her is uncertain. Still, Lucy Gray's grave was an important feature of Haymitch's prequel story. Whether she lived or died, it's clear through President Snow's actions in Sunrise on the Reaping that Lucy Gray left an impression. The mystery of her fate haunts him, and he takes this out of District 12 as a whole.

For this very reason, Lucy Gray's fate remaining a mystery is critical. Her tragic and mysterious fate quietly fuels rebellion, so Sunrise on the Reaping providing an answer would have been a mistake. Still, it was just as important that this Hunger Games prequel emphasized Lucy Gray's role in the overarching story. The grave was the perfect way to do so. It didn't solve the mystery one way or another, but the stone demonstrated that, despite Snow's efforts, Lucy Gray was remembered. She may have lived or died, but her legacy came for the Capitol in the end all the same.

The Sunrise on the Reaping movie takes a different approach to Lucy Gray, with most of the book's references to her omitted from the adaptation, including the grave, as well as Haymitch seeing a video of her singing on TV. This is perhaps to streamline things and keep the focus a little more squarely on Haymitch and Lenore, as Tam Amber is also cut.

Instead, we simply see Haymitch reading Lenore's stone, and while it's feasible Lucy Gray's is nearby, it isn't shown on screen. This might also have been done to avoid confusing those who've only watched the movies, rather than having general audiences think she's dead.

The one mention of Lucy Gray in the movie comes from President Snow, during his interaction with Haymitch in Plutarch Heavensbee's library. This itself does fit into the mystery of the character, however, as it confirms that in the movie timeline, much like the books, Snow himself has no idea what happened to her. Whether there'll ever be a return from Rachel Zegler or a recast, older version remains to be seen, but after Sunrise on the Reaping it seems unlikely there'll be any more clarity on Lucy Gray's fate in the future.

My feelings were low-key hurt when one of my friends called me “The King of Gift Cards” last year after I passed them a wrapped-up box containing…you guessed it, a gift card!

And this time, I’m veering away from my penchant for picking up a bunch of gift cards and throwing them at my friends and family like it’s a massive giveaway.

In particular, I’m going the extra mile to make sure I give my father something he truly cherishes. He doesn’t really ask for much around the holidays, but I still want to give him something extra special. Shopping for my mom is so much easier since she tells me exactly what she wants, but it’s a bit harder to do that for my dad.

With ChatGPT and Gemini in my corner, I used both chatbots to see which one could bring up the best gift recommendations. And one of them came out ahead a bit more than its competition.

Since I know my dad’s two main interests, I included them in my prompt alongside a few of his other faves to make sure both chatbots generated the most appropriate gifts possible. This is the prompt I ultimately went with:

“My father is a drummer and a vinyl collector. His favorite artists are Jimi Hendrix, James Brown, The Beatles, The Monkees, A Tribe Called Quest, and Prince. Show me the 7 best gift recommendations I should consider getting him for Christmas this year.”

ChatGPT certainly understood the assignment, as it combed the internet and came back with a wide selection of books and records worth throwing onto my dad’s gift wishlist. As for items geared toward his profession and hobby as a drummer, the chatbot brought up one product that should be right up his alley. Alongside each of its picks, it attached them to different categories and listed their prices so I could have as much information about all its listed items as possible.

As for the gifts that were geared towards his music-based profession, both ChatGPT brought up one item while Gemini mentioned two recommendations. It was a close race, but I ended up siding with Gemini more during this latest AI tool faceoff. ChatGPT’s list is strong, no doubt. #3406. You Can Try WhatsApp's New Disappearing Text Messages Early

Like Snapchat messages, WhatsApp's "View Once" feature is a great way to send things you don't want living on your friends' devices. You can send voice messages, photos, and videos that will "self-destruct" after they're opened, limiting (if not eliminating) the risk of your friends keeping them forever. However, View Once has a major limitation: While WhatsApp will let you send voice memos and images that way, you can't use it to send texts, meaning every one you send will live on (unless you unsend it yourself).

That's now changing. As reported by WABetaInfo, WhatsApp is now beta testing View Once for text messages, too. Soon enough, you'll be able to send voice memos, photos, videos, and texts as one-time-only messages. That way, you can send sensitive information via text—say, a password or an important account number—without worrying about it persisting. Here's how it works: You craft your text message as you usually do, but rather than tap the send button, you hold it. You'll see the usual "Schedule message" option, but once the feature rolls out, you'll also find a new "View Once" option as well.

As mentioned above, this feature is currently in testing, so it's only available to WhatsApp beta testers. What's more, only the Android version of the beta has access at the moment, so iOS beta testers are out of luck. (That said, the WhatsApp iOS beta is perpetually full, so there's not much you could do even if WhatsApp made this test available on iPhone.)

If you have an Android device, you can enroll in the WhatsApp beta to try out "View Once" text messages today. According to WABetaInfo, the feature is live as of WhatsApp version 2.26.45.6. To enroll, open the WhatsApp beta page on the Google Play store and enroll your account in the beta. If you don't have WhatsApp on your phone already, download it here; if you do, reload the page and install the latest update. This will update your existing WhatsApp app to the latest beta version.

#3401. I Tested Pangram to See If It Can Really Detect AI-Generated Content Like It Claims

David Nield is a technology journalist from Manchester in the U.K. who has been writing about gadgets and apps for more than 20 years.

He has a bachelor's degree in English Literature from Durham University, where he also spent a term as editor of the award-winning student newspaper Palatinate. His journalism career started in print media, where he contributed to and edited several technology magazines and bookazines sold in the U.K. and internationally. More recently, he has worked as a freelancer for some of the biggest technology publications on the web, covering everything from on-the-ground reporting about product launches, to detailed explainers and how-to guides on apps, gadgets, and platforms. His expertise covers broad areas of consumer tech, including smartphones, laptops, wearables, and AI.

We know it can be difficult for human beings to spot AI-generated content, but can detection software fare any better? Pangram is one of the leaders in the field, promising a "near-zero false positive rate" by looking at "subtle cues" in the writing, based on a training and feedback model comparing human-made content with the AI equivalent.

You'll find arguments on both sides of the debate as to whether or not Pangram's claims stand up. After a short story was flagged by Pangram and then judged to be free from AI, the detection engine has been accused of bias against text from minority writers.

Proponents of Pangram would point to an ongoing reward offer—currently at $3,950—available to anyone who can find a pre-2019 (and pre-LLM) piece of writing that Pangram falsely flags as being AI-written. So far, the reward is unclaimed.

As the AI detector has recently added AI image and video detection to its capabilities, it seemed a good time to put Pangram's analysis skills to the test for myself. Here's how it performed in the three different content types.

On the human side, I picked out 10 of my most recent articles for Lifehacker, known to be written by a person because I personally wrote them—in the traditional way, I fretted over word choices, went back and changed sentences, and accidentally left in a variety of typos that editors thankfully fixed.

For the AI content, I rotated between ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude, and got the LLMs to write 10 articles with the same headlines and the same approximate number of words, for a tech-savvy audience. I even asked the AI apps to vary their language use, so that the output would "read less like an LLM has written it."

Pangram's AI text detector lets you upload files, but to make the task a little harder, I copied and pasted all of the text into the online article, so it wouldn't be able to rely on any metadata included in the file. The scans got the correct result each and every time: Human-written text came back as 100% human, and AI-written text came back as 100% AI.

What's more, Pangram was certain about its results. All of the human writing was marked as highly likely to be human, and the vast majority of the AI writing was marked as highly likely to have come from an LLM. There were only a handful of phrases or sentences across thousands of AI words that got a "medium" rather than a "high" ranking for AI.

Now, there have been some edge cases where Pangram has got it wrong—like a poem repeating the same six words thousands of times—but as far as this sample goes, it can't be faulted. Clearly, my writing is too idiosyncratic and too clunky to be confused for the smooth sheen of AI-produced prose.

To be fair, I do have another advantage over AI: I can actually test out devices and apps in a way that LLM bots can't. ChatGPT can't experiment with One UI 9 (at least not yet), though it can scrape the web for various experiments and tests that real people have done.

However, I was able to fool Pangram to some extent by alternating AI paragraphs with human-written paragraphs. The text was flagged as AI, but the percentage estimate was typically lower (20-25%) than what it actually was (around 50%). If you're offloading some but not all of your writing to AI, some of it might slip though as real.

Image and video detection is the new string to Pangram's bow, so I sifted through my phone's photo and video library for some pieces of content to test the AI on. Again, I used copy and paste to get the files into Pangram rather than uploading them, to limit how much information the AI detector could get from metadata.

Again, all the human-made content was recognized as such, with a very high level of certainty—whether it was complicated crowd shots or simpler images of natural scenes. Presumably, there are even more signals to go off than there are with writing, including camera movements, colors, style, consistency, and composition.

Next up, I generated a few images and videos in Google Gemini and ChatGPT, requesting results that would look as photorealistic and "non-AI" as possible—the resulting files covered people, animals, and buildings. As before, I used copy, paste, and a few screengrabs to try and limit the metadata Pangram had access to.

Here, too, the AI identification was spot on, with all of the artificial content recognized as such, to a high level of confidence. This is perhaps not surprising: I think AI images and especially AI video still have more "tells" than AI writing, especially if you've seen a lot of it, so I wasn't expecting Pangram to fail here.

I did try experimenting with real photos that had a little bit of AI in them, what with tools like Gemini and ChatGPT now so good at image editing, as well as creating pictures from scratch. These were marked as "unsure" by Pangram, though to cut it some slack, only a small amount of the images were altered.

As with the text, the best way to beat Pangram's detection systems seems to be to include some AI embedded in human-made content. It will most likely still fail the "100% human" test, but the tests I ran showed that Pangram is less certain in these cases, or underestimates the amount of AI there actually is.

Increase the level of AI, and the detection gets more reliable—but if you're only using AI for a small part of whatever it is you're making, it's less worthwhile using AI tools anyway. As far as these tests go, Pangram's claims about accuracy check out, making it a useful tool if you need to ensure something is AI-free.

#3400. Ken Urker's Mom Says He Injected Powerful Sedative He Thought Was Heroin

Ken Urker's mom says he didn't technically inject heroin on the night he died ... he injected a substance he thought was heroin -- something she says was actually even more dangerous.

In an interview with TMZ's Charlie Neff, Raina told us investigators in Louisiana have recently informed her that Ken took a combination of fentanyl and rhino -- a street name for medetomidine.

The substance is a powerful veterinary sedative which has slowly crept into the illegal drug supply. It causes prolonged sedation, slowed heart rate, and low blood pressure. Because it is not an opioid, naloxone -- the active ingredient in Narcan -- can't reverse its effects.

Raina says Ken took the substance because he thought it was heroin ... and it appears he was relapsing -- breaking a long streak of being clean.

She says the medical examiner told her it was the first time in a long while that Ken had used the substance, citing both the lack of injection marks and a clean toxicology screening. She adds authorities have told her Ken may have survived if he had taken just heroin.

#3398. New Fallout Game Leaks Ahead Of Fallout 5

Fallout has revealed two major games on the horizon, but those apparently aren't the only new adventures coming to the Wasteland. Plans for Fallout 5 have been established for a while now, and Microsoft announced this year that Fallout: New Vegas developer Obsidian Entertainment would also develop a new title in the universe. Remasters for Fallout 3 and Fallout: New Vegas have also been announced, further filling out an apparently crowded slate.

The latest news comes on top of all of that, and it's a lot more out of left field than any of the other games on the horizon. Made in partnership with Bethesda, A Wasteland Full of Cats looks like it may be the next return to the Fallout series.

The existence of A Wasteland Full of Cats was revealed in an Australian Classification rating, which was filed on October 22, 2026 and surfaced in the news cycle today. The board rates the game as PG for "Mild themes and violence" — a much more family-friendly classification than the typical Fallout offering — but the real details come from the description provided on the website.

Like a number of other titles from developer Devcats, A Wasteland Full of Cats is a hidden object game built around finding, you guessed it, cats. This time, those cats have escaped from a Vault into the Wasteland, forcing the protagonist to seek them out and bring them back to safety. A Wasteland Full of Cats consists of 14 locations and 33 rooms in total, along with some hidden levels that can be optionally uncovered through "light puzzle mechanics."

A Wasteland Full of Cats sounds like a surprising turn for both Fallout and the Full of Cats series, neither of which have taken a turn in such an odd direction before. Previous Fallout spin-offs have generally been more grounded in the typical style and lore of the series, and the Full of Cats games haven't previously attempted a game built around a franchise collaboration.

Nonetheless, there's no reason why this shouldn't be a good game in its own right. The Full of Cats games range between Very Positive and Overwhelmingly Positive review aggregates on Steam, and Fallout's vivid worldbuilding and sense of humor lend themselves to more lighthearted takes without much trouble. The greater question, really, is how this collaboration came about to begin with, a question that will hopefully get answered whenever the game is officially announced.

We likely won't have to wait long to learn more about A Wasteland Full of Cats, as the Australian rating suggests that an announcement could be just around the corner. One obvious window for a reveal would be The Game Awards 2026, with the ceremony coming up on December 10. Otherwise, Bethesda and Devcats could simply choose to drop the Fallout news in a dedicated Xbox showcase or on any random day of the week, since revealing the game on the next Fallout Day would mean waiting until October 2026.

#3397. Eight Hacks Every Tidal User Should Know

I recently switched from Apple Music to Tidal, and I'm happy I made the change. The main reason is AI-made music: Tidal has stricter AI filtering than any other major streamer. The second reason is audio quality. While all major music streaming services do basically the same thing, Tidal's focus has always been on streaming music at the highest possible quality. While other streaming services have more or less "caught up" in terms of pure sonic fidelity, Tidal still is better at getting that quality to your speakers, if you know a few tricks.

If you're switching from Apple Music or Spotify to Tidal, you probably want to bring your playlists with you. Tidal points new users toward third-party transfer tools like TuneMyMusic and Soundizz. They both have a free tier, but they only transfers a few hundred songs gratis. My playlists are way bigger than that. The easy solution is to grumble and sign up for a month, then cancel when your tracks are transferred, but that didn't sit well with me. A playlist is just a collection of song names, so why should I have to pay anything to transfer it? To solve the problem, I came up with a simple script that transfers playlists from Apple Music and Spotify to Tidal. I will not be charging a fee. Here's how it works:

Download your playlist as a .txt file. You can do this directly from Apple Music under File>Library>Export Playlist. You can't from Spotify, but the free site Exportify will download any of your playlists as a spreadsheet file you can save.

Install Python on your system. Double click "install certificates" in the folder that opens after installation.

Download this script. Save it in the same file as your playlist.

Run the script: (For Mac, open Terminal. For Windows, go to the Command prompt. Type python3 on a Mac or py on Windows.) Drag the script into the terminal window and press enter. It should ask you to drag your downloaded playlist into the window next.

Sign in to Tidal. Hit "Approve" to give permission for Tidal to run the script.

Have a banana. The script is going to search for all the songs on your playlist and match them to Tidal's library, so it can take a little while. I tested it with a playlist from Apple Music with 2,397 songs. It took about 20 minutes and found 2,362 of my tracks, a 99% success rate.

Fix the leftovers: The program creates two separate text files for "orphans." One is songs it couldn't find and one is songs it might be worth double-checking manually.

If everything goes well, your large playlist should be available on Tidal.

Note: The script uses a community-created library to talk to Tidal, so it could stop working if Tidal changes things up.

Like most streaming services, Tidal has a "heart" button called "add to my collection." You can click on any track, album, or playlist to "like" and saved it. But Tidal also has a separate, somewhat mysterious "Save for Later" option that puts songs, albums, and playlists into a separate collection. There are a couple reasons for this. First, it keeps a running list of new-to-you music waiting for you on a rainy day, and secondly, it (presumably) affects your recommendation algorithm differently. While Tidal isn't open about every detail of its recommendation algorithm, I assume "save for later" has less weight (if any) on your future recommendations than "add to my collection."

On Tidal, tracks that are 100% AI-generated get an "AI" badge, earn no royalties, and are never placed on a Tidal-curated playlist. Users can flip a switch in Settings to either allow or disallow AI content, too. Simple, but there's a bit of nuance that goes beyond the on/off switch. You have to set the AI-toggle separately on each device you use Tidal on, even if it's the same account. I guess this is so I can listen to AI music in my car but not at my desk? Sadly, AI detection is not a science, so some AI-made, and partly AI-made, tracks may still get through.

If you're streaming music from a music app through Bluetooth, the output is automatically compressed to a lower quality, and your phone stays in charge, so a phone call or a notification can interrupt your music. But Tidal's Tidal Connect feature skips the middleman. Music streams directly from your wifi to your speaker and your phone becomes a remote control, so you can take a call, go for a walk, and even run out of phone battery and the music will keep playing.

Have an external device with Tidal Connect compatibility.

Make sure your speaker or other output device and phone or computer are on the same wifi network.

Click the icon again to switch back to your phone.

Plenty of wifi speakers don’t support Tidal Connect, so check before you buy. Tidal keeps the full list of supported devices on its site. There's everything there from WiiM Mini—a $99 small box that adds Tidal Connect to speakers you already own—to dCS components that cost more than a car.

Tidal Connect isn't the only way to get the highest quality audio from Tidal. You can go for an old school, wired path like I have. I play audio from my desktop and route it directly to a mixer via USB. Here's the set-up:

Settings > Streaming > Audio Quality: Max.

Sound Output: choose your mixer as the output device instead of your computer’s speakers.

Exclusive Mode: On. It’s under Sound Output > More Settings. Tidal sends audio straight to the mixer at each track’s native sample rate, without your computer resampling it or mixing in system sounds.

Force Volume. It's in the desktop app next to Exclusive Mode, under Settings > Streaming > Sound Output > More Settings. Force Volume means Tidal will always output at the highest volume. You'll be controlling the actual volume from your mixer.

To check what your mixer can handle, look at its maximum sample rate:

Mac: Open Audio MIDI Setup (in Applications > Utilities), click your mixer, and open the Format menu. The highest number listed is your ceiling.

Windows: Go to Settings > System > Sound, click your mixer, and look under Output settings > Format.

My cheap-ass mixer tops out a 16-bit/48kHz which is CD quality, but not Tidal's top of 24-bit/192kHz, but at least I can control the EQ. Speaking of...

It's much cooler to turn dials than mess with computer settings. Tidal doesn’t have an equalizer, so if you’re using Tidal Connect or a wired connection, you'll need something to shape the sound. Here are some options:

Your computer: System-wide EQ apps, like Equalizer APO on Windows or SoundSource on Mac, can adjust Tidal’s output. They don’t work with Tidal Connect though, which bypasses your computer’s audio processing.

Your speaker’s app: If you use a Tidal Connect speaker or streamer, it probably has a companion app for EQ.

A mixer or audio interface: Channel EQ knobs let you adjust bass, mids, and treble by hand, in real time.

Your speakers: Many powered speakers and studio monitors have low and high controls on the back.

A stereo receiver or amp: Old-school bass and treble knobs still work in 2026.

Most of Tidal's catalog streams as "better-than-CD quality" FLAC files at every subscription tier, so you might be inclined to click "play music at highest quality on everything." but settings are only as good as the gear you're using, and there are times when lower quality is the right choice. Here's when to turn down the settings:

When you're in your car: CarPlay and Bluetooth cut audio down to CD quality or less before it reaches your speaker, and with road noises, it usually doesn't matter anyway, so turn the streaming down to "High" instead of "Max." Or download your playlist before you leave, if you must have "as good as possible" audio.

You have a data cap and are off wifi. Top quality audio requires huge file transfer, so set your mobile data to High or Low and save Max for wifi.

Your connection is spotty: To avoid buffering, a lower setting keeps the music playing.

This isn't a universal hack, but some Android phones have microSD card slots, which can save you a lot of hassle if you're downloading a lot of audio files—an album at high quality might top 1GB, so having an external source will save you a ton of hassle. If your phone has a microSD card slot, go to Tidal's settings, find "download destination" and choose the memory card.

#3393. ‘The Gilded Age’ Officially Gets Massive Expansion at HBO

Season 4 of The Gilded Age has now debuted on HBO, with all the social striving, romantic yearning, and vintage frocks that its fans have come to expect. However, now that HBO's parent company, Warner Bros., has become part of a massive merged conglomerate with Skydance and Paramount, will the series' large and lavish budget make this season the end of an era? The decision has been made, and fans will probably be excited.

The Gilded Age had a somewhat difficult conception. The series is the brainchild of Julian Fellowes, the creator of Downton Abbey; in fact, it was originally conceived of as an America-set prequel to that series, depicting the clash between the New World's old money and new money, and the latter's intermarriage with the aristocracy to gain prestige. It was also originally in development with NBC; however, the scope of the series soon grew to a point where it would not be sustainable on network TV. Instead, it moved to HBO, and the arrangement has proved to be a fruitful one.

In fact, it's so fruitful that HBO has renewed The Gilded Age, a mere three episodes into its fourth season. The series will now return for a fifth season next year, thanks to some excellent ratings. According to HBO's own numbers, the series is now averaging 5.9 million US cross-platform viewers per episode, a number that's still growing. That's enough to outpace last season by nearly 20%, and making this the show's highest-rated season yet.

Four love stories, four completely different ideas of what it means to be somebody's person. This is the one that matches how you actually fall, and what it would ask of you.

You do not fall for strangers. You fall for the person you have already been talking to for years, which is the slowest and by some distance the most durable way anybody has found to do this.

You want a partner, not an audience. Somebody who wants their own life as badly as you want yours, and who would never ask you to be smaller to make the relationship easier.

The intensity was never the problem. The secrecy is. You are drawn to a love that lives entirely in private, and to the particular ache of wanting somebody you are not supposed to want.

You do not do this cautiously. When it happens for you it is immediate and total and it rearranges everything, and you would not accept a smaller version of it.

The marriage of robber baron George Russell (Morgan Spector) and his social-climbing wife Bertha (Carrie Coon) is still fractured, but there's some new joy in their lives, as after a difficult delivery, their daughter, Gladys (Taissa Farmiga), gave birth to a healthy child. Bertha's now in a cold war with Agnes van Rhijn (Christine Baranski) over hosting US President Grover Cleveland; more consequentially, Agnes' niece Marian Brook (Louisa Jacobson) had a night of passion with Bertha and George's son, Larry (Harry Richardson), that seems to have derailed their on-and-off romance. Meanwhile, Marian's friend Peggy (Denée Benton) has married the man of her dreams, affluent doctor Dr. William Kirkland (Jordan Donica), despite some friction between their families.

The Gilded Age has been renewed for a fifth season; season 4 is currently airing on HBO. Stay tuned to Collider for future updates.

#3388. Eight Important Router Settings You Should Check (or Change)

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Your router is a key piece of your home network, as it connects all of your other devices to the internet. This also makes it a highly valuable target for attackers and can leave your data vulnerable—especially if you simply plug your router in with its default settings unchanged. Whether your router is brand new or it's been a while since you audited your existing setup, these are the key settings to check and change right now.

Your router's security protocol determines how encryption and authentication work to protect data that's transmitted over your network. WPA3 Personal is the newest standard and the most secure, so if it's available on your router, enable it. It's compatible with devices that support Wi-Fi 6. Some older devices may not work with WPA3, in which case the WPA2/WPA3 Transitional mixed mode is a good alternative. At minimum, set your router to WPA2 Personal (AES).

Some routers ship with factory default login credentials, which are the username and password you need to access your device's admin dashboard. (This is not the same as your network name or wifi password, which you set up later.) Default router passwords are searchable online, which leaves your router's admin settings open to anyone. Once you get into your dashboard for the first time, change the default credentials and enable two-factor authentication for your admin account if available.

While some newer routers do have unique, device-specific defaults, it's a good idea to check this setting and ensure it's secure. If you're prompted to create custom admin credentials during the setup process, do it.

Your network name, or SSID, is how your network appears when you search for available wifi. By default, this may be the name of the router brand or a short string of characters, but you should choose something unique to your network. Make sure there's no identifying personal information, such as your name or house number. While you may be tempted to hide your network and obscure your SSID, this may actually make your information less secure, so keep this setting disabled. You can, however, add "_nomap" to the end of your network name, which prevents your router's physical coordinates from being mapped by location databases.

The password to access your network should also be unique and secure and should not include obvious personal information. One option to keep it memorable and easy to type is to create a passphrase using five to seven unrelated words that, combined, have at least 16 characters.

Being able to log into your router's admin dashboard from anywhere may be useful if you have complex networking needs or troubleshooting issues that often have to be addressed when you're away from home, but it also leaves an entry point open for attackers. Turn off remote management to prevent anyone from accessing your dashboard unless they are on your network. (This is also a great reason to have strong, unique admin credentials.)

Two additional settings that leave your network vulnerable are Wi-Fi Protected Setup (WPS) and Universal Plug and Play (UPnP). The former lets users connect to your network with a PIN, which can be vulnerable to brute-force attacks. The latter allows smart devices to easily connect to your network—but this also allows malware to spread more readily. You may need to have UPnP on in order to connect devices initially but should disable it afterward.

Any easy win for your network security is segmenting traffic to different networks, so if one is compromised, the data on the others remain unaffected. Many wifi routers have a "guest mode," which creates a separate SSID and password that you can share with visitors instead of giving them your primary network credentials. You can also set up a separate network for all of your smart home and IoT devices so exploitable vulnerabilities in these devices don't put your computers, phones, and other connected devices at risk too.

Routers run a type of software—called firmware—just like any other device. Firmware controls the router's core functions and is not immune to vulnerabilities, which can be exploited by bad actors. And, just like other types of software, manufacturers occasionally push updates to patch these flaws. Check your router's dashboard to see if automatic updates are toggled on. Some devices require an opt-in for auto updates during setup, so you should enable them if they are off. Some routers may even require manual updates—in this case, set a monthly or quarterly (at minimum) calendar reminder to check for patches.
