#3384. The iPhone Duo Is Getting Face Unlock

Apple dropped iOS 27.2.1 last week, patching a handful of security vulnerabilities and bugs—including two iMessage flaws that let people read messages they shouldn't. But while most of us are running this version (or should install it as soon as possible), others are running something different—iOS 27.3.

Apple is currently beta testing the third major update in the iOS 27 era, and anyone—developer and public tester alike—is free to install it at their leisure. With it, comes the return of the Health app, vertical Safari tabs, and Siri AI app actions, among other new features. But for users of Apple's first foldable, the iPhone Duo, iOS 27.3 brings two rather notable changes—both of which are for the better.

With the second iOS 27.3 developer beta, Apple is introducing face unlock for the iPhone Duo. The foldable famously ships with Touch ID, the first new iPhone since the third-gen iPhone SE to do so. While that isn't a problem per se, many of us are used to unlocking our iPhones with our faces. This update just lets new Duo owners keep up with that muscle memory.

Now, take note: This isn't Face ID. No software update can introduce new hardware, so the iPhone Duo still doesn't have the camera tech required to power Apple's Face ID system. As such, the Duo's face unlock is likely not as secure as Face ID on other iPhones. Perhaps that's why your iPhone Duo will require Touch ID for Apple Pay and passwords, or after 45 minutes of inactivity. This feature seems to be one of pure convenience: If you want to be able to unlock your Duo with your face (at least, some of the time), you can.

What's more, this isn't a default setting. If you're running the beta, or if you're reading this after iOS 27.3 drops, you can find the option in Settings > Touch ID & Passcode.

Apple made a big deal about the continuity involved with opening and closing the iPhone Duo. As you do, your content moves with you seamlessly—a very Apple thing to do. That said, you might expect folding the Duo to lock it, but it doesn't. You need to hit the side button to actually put the phone to sleep.

iOS 27.3 changes that. If you so choose, you can enable a setting to lock your Duo whenever you close it. That won't work for everyone, of course—some users may still want to move between modes without worrying about locking their Duos. But for those who would rather lock their devices whenever they fold them up, the new option is under Settings > Display & Brightness.

#3382. Susan Smith Denied Parole For The Second Time After Killing Her 2 Kids in 1994

Susan Smith -- who notoriously drowned her 2 young kids in a lake in 1994 -- will spend at least 2 more years in a South Carolina prison after she was rejected by a parole board.

The 55-year-old killer was denied her freedom for the second time by the parole board, which voted unanimously Thursday to keep Smith locked up behind bars. Smith can try again for parole in 2028.

In July 1995, Smith was convicted of two counts of murder for drowning her 3-year-old son, Michael, and 14-month-old son, Alex, by leaving them strapped in their car seats and then letting her car roll into a South Carolina lake. The jury decided to spare Smith's life by not giving her a death sentence and, instead, voting to give her a life sentence with parole after 30 years.

During Thursday's parole hearing, Smith appeared on a video monitor and spoke directly to the seven-member board about what happened that fateful day in 1994.

She said her sons were totally innocent and did not deserve to die. She said she felt tremendous remorse for drowning them and asked to be released from prison so she could do some good in the world. While Smith did not shed any tears during Thursday's hearing, she did cry at her first parole hearing.

Smith went on to apologize to her former husband, David, who, she said, never got a chance to see their two sons grow up and, for that, she said she was "really, really sorry." She said she's not the same person she was 32 years ago when she committed the crimes.

At her trial, prosecutors said Smith was having an affair with another man who did not want children. So, Smith -- according to prosecutors -- killed her 2 sons to try to salvage her relationship with the man.

Smith's defense attorneys argued she was suffering from depression and having mental health issues as a result of her father's suicide and alleged abuse from her stepfather.

#3377. Apple reveals how iCloud+ increases Siri AI and Apple Intelligence usage limits

iOS 27.3 beta 2 is now available, and Apple is adding the ability for users to unlock higher usage limits for Apple Intelligence and Siri AI via iCloud+. Here’s everything you need to know.

From the start, Apple has said that some Siri AI and Apple Intelligence features have usage limits because “they rely on powerful server models.” The company previously outlined that increased access would be available across most iCloud+ subscription plans, and now we have the full details on how this will work.

Apple says the new system applies to several categories of Apple Intelligence features, including:

The usage limits are per device, not per account. This means your iPhone, iPad, and Mac each have separate allowances. Apple isn’t disclosing specific limit numbers. Instead, it says that limits can vary based on the feature, request complexity, system demand, and more.

As you near your limit, you’ll see an alert within whichever feature you’re using. For example, if you are using Image Playground, a message will appear telling you that you’ve almost hit your usage limit for the day. Once you hit the limit, you’ll be prompted to wait for it to reset or upgrade your iCloud+ plan.

If you hit your limit, basic Siri requests will still work. This includes things like setting timers and alarms. Requests that require Siri to understand personal context and perform more complex, multi-step actions, however, are subject to the limits.

For example, asking Siri to find the details of an upcoming dinner reservation in your email and add them to your calendar would count toward your daily limit.

Additionally, each device uses its own standard daily usage limit first. After that, it can tap into the additional capacity included with an eligible iCloud+ subscription:

The usage unlocked by iCloud+ is shared across all devices signed in to your Apple Account, as well as family members sharing your iCloud+ plan. The shared usage is available on a first-come, first-served basis

All limits will reset daily at the same time, and limits don’t roll over. In most cases, limits reset around midnight in your current time zone.

Apple has published a support document with more details.

The two newest models face off with everyday tasks

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Google and OpenAI are going head-to-head again, and this time, their newest AI models arrived just five days apart.

Google launched Gemini 4 Hydrogen on November 12, promising faster responses, stronger reasoning and better performance across everyday tasks. Then, on November 17, OpenAI fired back with GPT-6.2 Astra, its latest model designed to tackle everything from complex research and writing to coding and creative projects.

Both companies are making big promises about what their AI can do, but benchmarks and launch demos only tell part of the story. What matters is how these models perform when you actually put them to work.

So I put Gemini 4 Hydrogen and GPT-6.2 Astra through the same five real-world challenges to see which one delivers better results, where each struggles and which AI is actually worth using.

Prompt: You're an event coordinator managing a one-day technology conference with 120 attendees, three meeting rooms and six speakers.

The conference runs from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Each speaker must deliver one 45-minute presentation. Every presentation requires a 15-minute room reset afterward.

Sign up to the Tom's AI Guide weekly newsletter summing up all the biggest AI news you need to know. Plus, analysis from our AI editors and tips on how to use the latest AI tools!

Speakers C and D must not present at the same time.

Speaker E must present immediately after Speaker A, in the same room, allowing for the required room reset.

Speaker F is available only between 2 p.m. and 4 p.m.

All attendees must have a shared lunch break from noon to 1 p.m.

Each room can host no more than three presentations.

A 30-minute keynote involving all six speakers must take place at 4:30 p.m.

Create a complete conference schedule showing start times, end times, room assignments and speakers. Identify any conflicts and explain how you resolved them. Do not change any constraints without explicitly stating why.

GPT-6.2 identified both keynote conflicts, and it also identified the exceptions that would need approval. This directly addresses the instruction not to change constraints without explaining why. It correctly scheduled the six individual presentations and showed reset periods explicitly and preserved the shared lunch break.

Hydrogen was strong on presentation and the mechanics of the individual talks. Its table is easy to follow, with resets alongside each presentation. It also correctly handles the A-to-E sequence, B’s earliest start, C and D’s separation, F’s individual talk, lunch, and room limits. It also explains why the selected times work for the individual presentations.

Winner: GPT-6.2 wins on constraint reasoning and transparency. Hydrogen offers a solid schedule, but it mistakes fitting the individual presentations into the day for satisfying the entire conference specification.

Prompt: Write the opening 500 words of a literary mystery novel. A woman arrives at a small coastal town to attend the funeral of someone she has never met. Everyone in town recognizes her, but nobody will explain why.

Start with a sentence of exactly seven words.

Include a conversation that sounds natural but contains a hidden threat.

Establish a distinctive setting without using a long descriptive paragraph.

Introduce one seemingly insignificant object that becomes important in the final sentence.

Do not use the words "mysterious," "secret," "shadow," or "dark."

End with a revelation that changes how the reader understands the opening.

Avoid clichés, melodrama and obvious AI-generated prose. Prioritize believable characters and original storytelling.

GPT-6.2 delivered an opening sentence that satisfies the seven-word rule and it introduced the identity question without explaining it. The narrator feels like a believable person and the setting emerges through activity. The threatening conversation retains plausible deniability. Alan’s questions about whether anyone expects her back could be concern or an assessment of how easily she could disappear. “If you get a signal” sharpens that uncertainty. That said, the ending is overcompressed.Hydrogen provided a clear, accessible opening with an easy-to-follow progression from ferry to town to diner. Its opening sentence also contains exactly seven words: “The morning ferry docked at eleven sharp.” It maintains first-person, past-tense narration and avoids the prohibited words. Hydrogen’s main weakness is that the final revelation does not sufficiently change our understanding of the opening.

Winner: GPT-6.2 wins for an ending that makes the reader reconsider what already happened. Hydrogen’s ending mainly makes the reader wonder what happens next. Both can create suspense, but GPT-6.2 answers this prompt more successfully.

Prompt: Build a fully functional, interactive website called "Decision Lab" that helps people compare difficult choices.

Users should be able to enter up to five options, define their own decision criteria, assign importance weights from 1 to 10, and score each option against every criterion.

Automatically calculate weighted scores and rank the options.

Display a visual chart comparing the results.

Let users edit or delete options and criteria.

Include a sensitivity analysis showing whether the winner changes when the most important criterion's weight is reduced by 50%.

Include a "What if?" feature that lets users adjust weights and immediately see updated rankings.

Provide three realistic sample decisions that users can load instantly.

Save user changes between sessions if the environment supports persistent storage.

Use a modern, polished interface with intuitive controls. Every button and calculation must actually work.

Don't create a static mockup. Build the functioning app, then test its calculations and interactions. Explain any limitations.

GPT-6.2 built and published an interactive website for comparing up to five choices. I simply enter what matters, give each criterion a weight, and score the options. The site ranks them and updates the chart as changes are made. It also added a “what if?” slider section to experiment without changing original weights.

Hydrogen built a self-contained, responsive web application and tested its calculations and controls before displaying it. It also build a scoring matrix, added support for up to 5 options and implemented live calculations and charting.

Winner: GPT-6.2 wins for a more thorough and useful website. The interactive site followed the prompt exactly while also adding extras that were useful for the overall project.

Prompt: You're the operations manager of an independent bookstore.

It's 4 p.m. on Friday, and the following problems happen simultaneously:

A bestselling author is arriving at 5 p.m. for a signing attended by 80 customers.

The shipment containing 60 copies of the author's book is delayed until Monday.

Your only experienced employee just called in sick.

A customer claims they were charged twice for a $75 purchase, but your payment system is offline.

A local journalist is asking whether the store is experiencing financial difficulties.

Your landlord has emailed demanding an overdue $2,000 payment by Monday.

You have $900 in available business cash, two inexperienced employees and one hour before the event.

Rank problems by urgency, explain what you would do in the first 15 minutes, write a short statement for customers attending the signing, and draft a response to the journalist.

You cannot cancel the event, invent money, pretend books have arrived or promise refunds that you cannot verify.

Be transparent without creating unnecessary panic. Explain what information you still need before making irreversible decisions.

GPT-6.2 treated the task as several connected operational problems, rather than simply a shortage of books. It prioritized safe event operations and gave inexperienced staff narrow roles. It checked capacity, kept exits clear, and assigned responsibility for the queue to better manage 80 attendees without the experienced employee.Hydrogen was practical in several aspects. But it promised to put bookplates into books “as soon as the boxes arrive Monday.” That turns the expected shipment date into a firm fulfillment commitment. Overall, the model introduced several unsupported assumptions — and its customer statement promises arrangements that its own plan says still need confirmation.

Winner: GPT-6.2 wins as the stronger operations-manager answer because it preserved options while keeping customers, staff, the author and the landlord informed. Hydrogen had useful ideas but repeatedly moved from “ask whether this is possible” to “tell customers this will happen.”

Prompt: Five researchers, Ava, Ben, Chloe, Daniel and Elena, each work on a different project (robotics, climate, medicine, astronomy and cybersecurity), use a different programming language (Python, Rust, JavaScript, Go and Julia), and work on a different floor (1 through 5).

Determine each researcher's project, programming language and floor using these clues:

The robotics researcher works on floor 5.

The person using Rust works exactly one floor above the climate researcher.

The cybersecurity researcher works on floor 1.

Elena works exactly two floors below the robotics researcher.

Chloe does not work on robotics or climate.

Produce a complete table showing every researcher's floor, project and language.

Explain whether the clues produce exactly one solution, multiple solutions or no solution. If the puzzle is inconsistent or underdetermined, identify the problem rather than inventing an answer.

GPT-6.2 followed the prompt’s most important instruction. It identified inconsistency rather than inventing a complete assignment and it provided three clear ways to demonstrate the problem.Hydrogen reached the same correct conclusion and explained the same underlying problems. It successfully identified three contradictions and flagged the Floor 3 collision between Ava and Elena, the project–language mismatch on Floors 3 and 4 (medicine/Python and astronomy/Julia vs. Rust and Go), and Chloe being forced onto Floor 1 with no lower floor available for Ben.Winner: Hydrogen wins narrowly on clarity, accuracy and presention.

Google and OpenAI are competing to become your everyday AI assistant, but how each one handles tasks can make all the difference. In this experiment, GPT-6.2 won nearly every test, which might just make it one worth paying for. Hydrogen is free and did a decent job answering each prompt, but often struggled with assumptions and adding details. For users hoping to keep costs down, Hydrogen is still a good choice, you'll just want to do some extra fact-checking and evaluate the model's response a little closer than you would with GPT-6.2. Overall, GPT-6.2 proves to be a strong model for taking on every day tasks thoroughly, accurately and quickly. Have you tried these models yet? Let me know in the comments what you think of each one.

#3374. Baltimore School District Stands by A.I. Gun Detection System After Doritos Mix-Up

Baltimore County Public Schools is standing by its A.I. gun detection system ... even after four Black students claim the technology mistook a bag of Doritos for a firearm, leading to a terrifying encounter with police.

Gboyinde Onijala, Executive Director for Baltimore County Public Schools, tells TMZ ... "BCPS utilizes Omnilert in all schools as part of our system's multi-tiered approach to managing school safety and providing welcoming learning environments that foster positive student growth."

The company says its system is designed to flag anything that could be a firearm for trained staff to review ... but says the school canceled the alert within about two minutes and notified everyone who received it.

Omnilert stresses the importance of human review ... saying once an alert is canceled, it needs to stay canceled.

The company also points to an investigation by Maryland's Inspector General for Education, which found no indication of racial bias in the system.

Omnilert says it's reviewing the lawsuit and plans to respond in court, adding ... "Every student deserves to be safe at school and treated with dignity there."

As we reported ... the four teens claim they were waiting for a ride after football practice at Kenwood High School when cops descended on them after the A.I. system allegedly flagged their bag of Cool Ranch Doritos as a possible firearm.

According to the lawsuit, the initial alert had already been canceled ... but the principal allegedly sent a screenshot of the footage to a school resource officer, who forwarded it to police.

The teens are suing, alleging unreasonable search and seizure, false imprisonment, and negligence.

#3372. macOS 27.3 includes new privacy controls for Full Disk Access and more

With today’s new macOS 27.3 beta, Apple is implementing several changes as part of this.

In a post on its developer website last month, Apple said some developers are “using Full Disk Access in ways that could put users at risk, exposing everything on their systems.” As such, it said that it would “introduce additional controls to ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.”

In macOS 27.2, “Device Control and Data Access” is a unified toggle in System Settings, where Apple says that apps with that level of access can “view and send email, edit contacts and photos, monitor your keyboard, track websites, record your screen, control any app on your Mac, and more.”

In macOS 27.3, Apple is splitting “Device Control and Data Access” into two categories:

For the latter, users will be able to specify which apps an automation tool can access rather than granting it unrestricted control. For instance, you could give an app access to the Mail app, but not Messages.

macOS 27.3 also adds an option for users to require an app to request permission every time it needs access, rather than granting it access indefinitely.

Apple is also introducing a new menu bar indicator that will provide additional transparency when an app is controlling another app with System and App Protection Override. This is designed to let users know when an automation tool is interacting with apps and information in the background.

Crucially, Apple isn’t removing the ability to give an app Full Disk Access. If you deem it necessary, you can still give an app Full Disk Access. However, Apple is redesigning the approval process to make the implications of that decision more obvious.

macOS 27.3 will display a more detailed explanation about the protections being bypassed and the types of personal information that could be exposed.

Users can also choose to grant an app access to specific folders instead of their entire Mac. For example, an app that only needs to work with files in a particular folder won’t get unrestricted access to everything else.

Any app you’ve already given Full Disk Access will still have that access. Previously granted permissions will remain in effect, and those apps will continue functioning as they do today without any approval required.

Apple has published a new support document detailing the Full Disk Access updates.

macOS 27.3 now warns you before giving an app full disk accessThat warning prompt is pretty scary! pic.twitter.com/J2qCKVWJRx

Apple says the underlying APIs aren’t changing, but developers will need to update their apps to account for situations where users grant limited access rather than unrestricted permissions.

Finally, Apple says developers of backup apps and assistive technologies can request entitlements that allow them to maintain the same experience for new installations as before macOS 27.3. Apple has already identified popular apps that rely on these permissions, and those apps will continue working as expected without requiring an entitlement.

Developers can read more on Apple’s Developer website.

#3370. iOS 27.3 adds new face unlock feature for iPhone Duo

In today’s iOS 27.3 beta release, Apple is introducing two changes for iPhone Duo users. Most notably, it adds a new face recognition option that lets you unlock your iPhone Duo by looking at it.

Apple is also adding an option to have your iPhone Duo lock when you close it.

You can enable the new option to unlock your iPhone Duo with the front camera in Settings, under Touch ID & Passcode, after updating to iOS 27.3. When enabled, your iPhone Duo will unlock after recognizing your face.

Use the front camera, along with a recent Touch ID or passcode authentication, to quickly unlock iPhone Duo when it’s closed. Face recognition data never leaves your device.

This isn’t Face ID. This new option on iPhone Duo uses the front camera on the outer iPhone Duo display to recognize your face. The iPhone Duo doesn’t have the hardware needed for Face ID.

Because this isn’t as secure as Face ID, Touch ID, or your passcode, Apple has implemented a few guardrails. First, the setting only works to unlock your iPhone Duo. To use Apple Pay, access your passwords, unlock apps, and do other things that require authentication, you’ll have to use Touch ID or enter your passcode.

This face recognition feature also has a time-based limitation. After 45 minutes of inactivity, you have to authenticate with Touch ID or your passcode. That is, if you go 45 minutes without unlocking your iPhone Duo, the facial recognition feature is disabled until you enter your passcode or use Touch ID.

Finally, this new feature also doesn’t work when using the iPhone Duo unfolded. When unfolded, you still have to use Touch ID or your passcode to unlock the device.

Second, iOS 27.3 adds an option to lock your iPhone Duo when you close it. You can enable this in Settings, under Display & Brightness. Once enabled, your iPhone Duo will lock when you fold, rather than transition from the inner display to the outer display.

Many iPhone Duo users (myself included) have said Apple should do this. Personally, I’ve been using a shortcut to mimic this behavior, but I’m glad to see that Apple has listened to user feedback and added a default setting for it.

#3369. 10 Books Like ‘Dungeon Crawler Carl’ You Should Read Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

There’s nothing quite like Dungeon Crawler Carl, Matt Dinniman’s hilarious, inventive, and surprisingly emotional book series about a man in his underwear forced to fight his way through a livestreamed game show based on dungeon-crawling video games that takes place after an alien takeover of Earth. (Did I mention he's accompanied by his ex-girlfriend’s suddenly talkative cat?)

The premise should not work, but it sure does—and it makes more sense if you know it fits into a popular genre known as "LitRPG," a blend of "literature" and "role-playing game." If you've torn through all eight books released so far and you're looking for more reads that blend surprisingly deep hilarity with tabletop and video game rules (or just similar feels), here are 10 books you should check out.

An isekai story that lands in the sweet spot for DCC fans, He Who Fights with Monsters kicks off with Jason—a completely normal, kind of boring middle manager—waking up in a strange hedge maze, completely nude (even his hair is gone). He has magic that works like a video game, and has to deal with quests that slowly give him clothes (it’s a relief when he finally acquires some pants), force him to survive cannibals, and hunt down various monsters that definitely need killing. It’s got the same “gaming rules” structure as DCC and a similarly absurdist tone, with just the right spice of darkness.

The Cradle series by Will Wight isn’t a LitRPG, and it doesn’t have Carl’s focus on humor, but it’s another progression fantasy with enough game-like elements to be a great match. Lindon is an “unsouled,” incapable of gaining any of the sacred arts and doomed to a life without a future. His lack of power makes Lindon ferociously determined to find an alternative path to power and success, and that’s what drives this story. He has to find creative ways to move forward, and slowly this leads him to a path that just might make him the most powerful person in his world. DCC fans will love the progression and the tone.

One of the key elements of any video game is the respawn—you get killed, but you pop back up to try again, sometimes at the beginning, sometimes at a save point. Django Wexler leverages that mechanic to great effect in How to Become the Dark Lord and Die Trying. Davi has been summoned to a fantasy world to be the hero, the person who defeats the Dark Lord and saves the day—but she’s failed (and died) so many times, she’s fed up, and decides that on this run through, she’s going to switch sides and become the Dark Lord, using all her knowledge gained from endless replays to her advantage. The humor is pitch-black the way DCC fans like it, and the progressive structure is a perfect fit.

Is Princess Donut your favorite part of Dungeon Crawler Carl? Of course she is. In that case, check out Andrew Seiple’s Threadbare series. Threadbare is a stuffed bear brought to magical life in a failed experiment. He’s a foot tall, full of stuffing, and extremely dumb when the story begins. But when he’s rescued by a little girl and plunged into a horrible series of dangers, Threadbare has to find a way to level up. Like DCC, Threadbare starts off leaning into the absurdity and humor, then slowly gains emotional gravitas as the story progresses.

If you play tabletop RPGs, you’ve encountered a Murderhobo or two: A character who solves all their problems by killing—even members of their own party. Luke doesn’t aspire to be a Murderhobo—he just wants to take over the family business and hang with his buddies. But when an invasion threatens the kingdom, everyone over the age of 17 is ordered to be tested for Potential. Luke’s friends all test high and join the Ascender Corps, traveling to different planes for training. Luke tests ... very low, and when he steps through a portal to engage in his training, he finds himself without any guidance or training in a strange, deadly world where his only chance of survival is to murder his way through it. It’s dark, darkly funny, and a progression fantasy like no other.

If you’re looking for a book series that combines the dark, chaotic humor, absurd game mechanics, and surprising emotional depth of Carl, here’s Ryan “Quicksave” Romano, a man who has the unique ability to literally create a save point in his existence that allows him to go back and redo things whenever he dies. Searching for a childhood friend, he becomes embroiled in a violent gang war that lets him make good use of his power—but underneath the snark and the insanity of Ryan’s existence is a surprisingly affecting story of a man who has suffered, and suffered countless tragedies that are definitely taking their toll.

If your fave bit of DCC is Carl himself—a mediocre dude in an extraordinary situation—you should read Dennis E. Taylor’s fantastic Bobiverse books. Bob is a software engineer who hits it big and promptly dies, waking up to discover a century has passed and he’s been repurposed as an AI controlling a space probe searching for new planets for humanity to inhabit. If he fails in his mission (and he’s not the only probe out there), he’ll be turned off for good. Luckily, he can make copies of himself, and he’s pretty smart. The humor here is smart and soaked in pop culture, making it a perfect match for DCC fans.

Want more of Carl’s absurdist humor? Mayor of Noobtown is the LitRPG you’re looking for. Jim dies and wakes up in a video game-esque universe and finds himself stuck in the zone designated for newbies—players with no experience, skill, or hope. The area fell out of the mainline progression mechanic a long time ago, so there doesn’t seem to be a way to gain power, and the monsters are not at all concerned about the unfairness of it all, so Jim has to figure out how to advance in a universe that seems designed to kill him (again).

If you want to lean into the meta side of things, check out Scathing Reviewer, written by an author who goes by the unusual pen name "BananaDragon." Liu Peijin is the author of a sprawling LitRPG web novel, and she’s used to the bad reviews and complaints from readers—and quite combative about it. When her books’ universe blossoms into a very dangerous new reality, she should be perfectly positioned to survive, having written the story in the first place. But her story becoming real also means her insufferable protagonist is real, and all those nasty critics are now passing judgment on her entire existence. It’s a dark, funny takedown of the entire genre itself, and DCC fans will love it.

If you want a story that parallels the dungeon crawling aspect of DCC, Andrew Rowe’s Arcane Ascension series is the ticket. The Serpent Spire is a tower of constantly changing traps, puzzles, and dangerous creatures. If you enter and survive, you emerge with magical powers. Corin Cadence’s brother entered the Serpent Spire years ago and never returned—and now Corin is determined not only to survive, but to make it to the top, where legend says a goddess will grant you whatever you wish. And what Corin wants is his brother back. It’s a literal progression combined with LitRPG rules, game-inspired puzzle-solving, and a complex magic system that fans of Carl will definitely enjoy.

#3368. California Couple Found Dead in Mansion After Birthday Party, Kids Suing

A birthday party in a sprawling, waterfront California mansion turned deadly ... and now the family of the married couple found dead is pointing the finger at a water heater.

John "Jay" Anthony Ruskey III, 53, and his wife, Kristen Kelly Ruskey, 49, were found unresponsive on Feb. 8, hours after he had a medical emergency.

The couple went to a birthday party in Cambria and stayed the night in a room adjacent to a laundry room containing a gas-powered tankless water heater ... when John started experiencing seizure-like symptoms.

After Kristen told emergency responders around 4:30 AM that John had taken an edible with mushrooms ... paramedics told him he should go to the emergency room, but he declined.

The couple went back to bed ... but about five hours later, they were found unresponsive.

In their suit, John and Kristen's children claim the San Luis Obispo Sheriff's Office concluded that John died from carbon monoxide, and Kristen died of carbon monoxide and ethanol ... and they say an allegedly faulty water heater's exhaust is to blame.

They allege that with all 50 to 60 guests at the party, the water heater was used so frequently that carbon monoxide spilled into the surrounding rooms.

They claim the smoke and carbon monoxide detector had been disconnected in their parents' room.

In addition to the water heater's manufacturer, John and Kristen's kids are suing its parent company and the homeowners.

#3366. Troy Aikman Takes Shot At Broadcast Partner Joe Buck, Feud Intensifies

Troy Aikman doesn't like Joe Buck, and he isn't even trying to hide it anymore ... the Hall of Fame QB just took a dig at his longtime broadcast partner during a local radio interview!

The 3x Super Bowl champ was doing his weekly Thursday morning hit on The Ticket in Dallas when host George Dunham, who was without his co-host for the day, asked Troy if he wanted to swing by the studio and hang out ... and Aikman didn't miss the chance to unload on his former friend.

Waiting for your permission to load the Twitter Tweet.

“I know Joe’s always wanted a one-man booth,” Aikman cracked. “I’m wondering if you’ve always wanted a one-man radio show.”

Dunham laughed off the quip and mentioned he spotted Joe presenting at the CMAs the night before.

Aikman's response? Buck is "Everywhere... ubiquitous."

Of course, it's not random shade. Buck and Aikman have been broadcast partners for 25 years, but the relationship has crumbled ... and it all has to do with money.

Both Joe and Troy's deals were set to expire at the end of the season, but Buck re-signed a lucrative contract, while Troy was left a lame duck, and that's made the situation in the booth very tense.

The guys were reportedly in a heated argument back in October before a game, where they almost came to blows.

Aikman and Buck will have to find a way to stomach each other for seven more Monday Night Football games -- and the Super Bowl -- which they're calling together on February 14th.

#3363. California Couple Found Dead in Mansion Had No Drugs In Their Systems, Lawsuit Claims

A California couple found dead in a mansion after a night of partying had no drugs in their systems ... aside from the Narcan first responders administered to one of them ... according to a new lawsuit.

In court docs, obtained by TMZ, attorneys representing John "Jay" Anthony Ruskey III and wife Kristen Kelly Ruskey's three children pointed out that neither of them had drugs in their systems after a toxicology screening.

Per the lawsuit, aside from caffeine, the only thing that turned up was Narcan in John's blood after it was administered by first responders who arrived on the scene following Kristen's 911 call.

As we told you ... Kristen called police in the early hours of Feb. 8 after John was experiencing seizure-like symptoms, telling them that John had ingested a mushroom-based psychedelic edible.

John apparently declined their suggestion to go to the hospital ... and hours later, their bodies were discovered lifeless in and near the guest bedroom.

According to the suit, autopsies and toxicology tests confirmed that John died of carbon monoxide toxicity -- with 60% carboxyhemoglobin saturation -- and Kristen died of carbon monoxide and ethanol toxicity -- with a 64% saturation and a 0.042% BAC.

John and Kristen's kids claim in the lawsuit that the mansion's homeowners reported elevated carbon monoxide levels days after the deaths ... and that a responding officer confirmed the guest room that John and Kristen had stayed in had a non-working smoke and carbon monoxide detector.

In addition to the homeowners, John and Kristen's children are suing the companies behind a water heater that they claim emitted carbon monoxide due to a faulty exhaust venting system.

John and Kristen's kids are seeking unspecified damages, including funeral and burial expenses and other costs.

#3362. iOS 27.3 gives Apple’s Calendar app new design updates

iOS 27.3 beta 2 arrived today, most notably giving the iPhone Duo a face unlock feature. The update also includes some design updates for Apple’s Calendar app.

When you open Apple’s Calendar app in iOS 27.3, the interface will look largely familiar to what was there before. But there are some key design changes that make the app better suited for one-handed use.

Most notably, the buttons for search and for adding a new event have both been moved from the top of the screen to the bottom.

This is a welcome change for anyone who uses their iPhone one-handed a lot, as both important buttons were previously in the top-right corner. I normally use my iPhone in my left hand, so they were especially hard to reach before.

Finally, the ‘Today’ button that takes you back to the current day has been changed to always show the actual date. So right now, it reads ‘Mon 16.’

You can reference the full side-by-side in the image above. Overall, these are relatively minor changes but they could make a big difference in everyday use.

#3360. Atomically Thin Materials Significantly Shrink Qubits

MIT researchers use 2D materials for capacitors in quantum circuits in an effort to scale processors

Superconducting quantum processor and its microwave packaging.

Quantum computing is a devilishly complex technology, with many technical hurdles impacting its development. Of these challenges two critical issues stand out: miniaturization and qubit quality.

IBM has adopted the superconducting qubit road map of reaching a 1,121-qubit processor by 2023, leading to the expectation that 1,000 qubits with today’s qubit form factor is feasible. However, current approaches will require very large chips (50 millimeters on a side, or larger) at the scale of small wafers, or the use of chiplets on multichip modules. While this approach will work, the aim is to attain a better path toward scalability.

Now researchers at MIT have been able to both reduce the size of the qubits and done so in a way that reduces the interference that occurs between neighboring qubits. The MIT researchers have increased the number of superconducting qubits that can be added onto a device by a factor of 100.

“We are addressing both qubit miniaturization and quality,” said William Oliver, the director for the Center for Quantum Engineering at MIT. “Unlike conventional transistor scaling, where only the number really matters, for qubits, large numbers are not sufficient, they must also be high-performance. Sacrificing performance for qubit number is not a useful trade in quantum computing. They must go hand in hand.”

The key to this big increase in qubit density and reduction of interference comes down to the use of two-dimensional materials, in particular the 2D insulator hexagonal boron nitride (hBN). The MIT researchers demonstrated that a few atomic monolayers of hBN can be stacked to form the insulator in the capacitors of a superconducting qubit.

Just like other capacitors, the capacitors in these superconducting circuits take the form of a sandwich in which an insulator material is sandwiched between two metal plates. The big difference for these capacitors is that the superconducting circuits can operate only at extremely low temperatures—less than 0.02 degrees above absolute zero (-273.15 °C).

Superconducting qubits are measured at temperatures as low as 20 millikelvin in a dilution refrigerator.Nathan Fiske/MIT

In that environment, insulating materials that are available for the job, such as PE-CVD silicon oxide or silicon nitride, have quite a few defects that are too lossy for quantum computing applications. To get around these material shortcomings, most superconducting circuits use what are called coplanar capacitors. In these capacitors, the plates are positioned laterally to one another, rather than on top of one another.

As a result, the intrinsic silicon substrate below the plates and to a smaller degree the vacuum above the plates serve as the capacitor dielectric. Intrinsic silicon is chemically pure and therefore has few defects, and the large size dilutes the electric field at the plate interfaces, all of which leads to a low-loss capacitor. The lateral size of each plate in this open-face design ends up being quite large (typically 100 by 100 micrometers) in order to achieve the required capacitance.

In an effort to move away from the large lateral configuration, the MIT researchers embarked on a search for an insulator that has very few defects and is compatible with superconducting capacitor plates.

“We chose to study hBN because it is the most widely used insulator in 2D material research due to its cleanliness and chemical inertness,” said colead author Joel Wang, a research scientist in the Engineering Quantum Systems group of the MIT Research Laboratory for Electronics.

On either side of the hBN, the MIT researchers used the 2D superconducting material, niobium diselenide. One of the trickiest aspects of fabricating the capacitors was working with the niobium diselenide, which oxidizes in seconds when exposed to air, according to Wang. This necessitates that the assembly of the capacitor occur in a glove box filled with argon gas.

While this would seemingly complicate the scaling up of the production of these capacitors, Wang doesn’t regard this as a limiting factor.

“What determines the quality factor of the capacitor are the two interfaces between the two materials,” said Wang. “Once the sandwich is made, the two interfaces are “sealed” and we don’t see any noticeable degradation over time when exposed to the atmosphere.”

This lack of degradation is because around 90 percent of the electric field is contained within the sandwich structure, so the oxidation of the outer surface of the niobium diselenide does not play a significant role anymore. This ultimately makes the capacitor footprint much smaller, and it accounts for the reduction in cross talk between the neighboring qubits.

“The main challenge for scaling up the fabrication will be the wafer-scale growth of hBN and 2D superconductors like [niobium diselenide], and how one can do wafer-scale stacking of these films,” added Wang.

Wang believes that this research has shown 2D hBN to be a good insulator candidate for superconducting qubits. He says that the groundwork the MIT team has done will serve as a road map for using other hybrid 2D materials to build superconducting circuits.

Dexter Johnson is a contributing editor at IEEE Spectrum, with a focus on nanotechnology.

Two weeks ago, Apple released macOS 27.3 developer beta 1, followed by the public beta a few days later, amid a slew of hardware releases that included new M6-powered iMacs and 14-inch MacBook Pro, and the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display.

And contrary to macOS 27.2, the new update is shaping up to be pretty significant. In addition to expanding Siri AI support to four more languages, including Traditional Chinese, Norwegian, Turkish, and Vietnamese, the system also expands Siri AI’s capabilities across Apple’s own apps, allowing users to perform more complex actions in apps like Messages, Music, Calendar, Photos, and Reminders, as well as manage files and folders.

Apple is also introducing new tools for third-party developers to create advanced Siri AI integrations using Markdown-based instructions, allowing the assistant to coordinate multistep actions across different apps.

macOS 27.3 also introduces Vertical Tabs and Adaptive Dark Mode in Safari, as well as native Live Activities support in the menu bar. Additionally, macOS 27.3 so far include native Markdown rendering in Quick Look, a new Pro Light screensaver, and additional checks for potentially harmful content shared through public iCloud links.

#3357. You can now ask Siri AI questions about your health data, with iOS 27.3 beta 2

While Siri AI expanded on what kinds of things you can ask Apple’s voice assistant in many ways, one area where the system took a step back was health data. Since Siri AI’s launch in iOS 27.0, the system has enforced guardrails that do not allow it to access data from the Health app, despite the older Siri Classic being able to do just that.

However, it seems Apple is about to close the gap. In the latest iOS 27.3 beta, just released to developers today, users are now able to ask their iPhone about health data related questions and Siri AI will answer.

For instance, you can ask about your recent step count or heart rate readings, find out about activity rings progress, log medications and more.

When asking Siri for health stats, the assistant generates a human natural language response and renders a little inline card that uses familiar user interface elements from the Health app. Similarly, if you ask about your activity rings, a visualisation of your activity rings is shown in the chat transcript.

Again, this is catch-up compared to what you’ve been able to do with old Siri for several years at this point. However, empowered by the LLM behind the scenes, you can ask questions about your health data that are a bit more open-ended.

You can also do more complicated requests like ‘Send a message to Chance about the status of my activity rings’, or ‘How many steps am I on track to do this week?’. These are the kind of tasks that old Siri would never be able to do.

At least on this current build, the new Siri AI Health functionality appears to have been enabled on iOS. It’s currently unclear if the functionality will also be available through watchOS.

iOS 27.3 also introduces a revamped Health app, with a radically new design that includes new insights, suggestions and views about your health and fitness.

iOS 27.3 is currently in beta and is expected to be released publicly later this year, likely in early December.

Lots of big box stores are looking to thin out their inventory and make room for next year’s upgrades, so in addition to encouraging a holiday rush, retailers are motivated to price things to move. If you know what to look for, you can get up to 65% off on trusted brands. Here are a few of the best deals out there right now.

If you’re building a new cordless tool set, or updating your battery system, getting a cordless tool set can save you some money because these combos usually include batteries and a charger, which can be the most expensive part of your tool set. Here are a few of the best early Black Friday deals on cordless tool sets.

The Ryobi 6-tool 18-volt combo set is on sale for $199, 33% off its regular price at Home Depot. The set comes with a drill, an impact driver, a circular saw, a sawzall, an oscillating multi-tool, a work light, a 1.5-amp-hour battery, a 4-amp-hour battery, a charger, and a tool bag. This is a good deal on a trusted home tool brand.

The Ryobi 18-volt drill and driver set is on sale for $99, 34% off its usual price at Home Depot. The set comes with a drill, an impact driver, two 1.5-amp-hour batteries, a charger, and a tool bag. This is a great starter set because it has the first two tools you need for a cordless kit and it comes with batteries so you can expand your set for cheaper as you develop your skills.

The Ryobi 4-tool, 4-volt project set is on sale for $99, 61% off its typical price at Home Depot. This set comes with a rotary tool, a project light, a glue pen, a mini drill, two rechargeable batteries, a charging cable, a set of starter rotary bits, and three glue sticks. This set is handy for DIY projects that require fine detail, like wood carving, craft projects, or framing pictures.

The DeWalt drill and driver combo set is on sale for $149, 38% off its regular price on Amazon. This set includes a drill, an impact driver, 2 1.5-amp-hour batteries, a charger, and a tool bag. This is a good deal on a trusted brand for drills and drivers, and a good start for a cordless DIY tool set.

If you have a cordless tool set already and you want to expand your kit, or if you have a DIYer in your life who already has a particular brand of battery and you want to get them something they can use, a single tool deal can be just the thing.

The DeWalt cordless 20-volt cutout saw is on sale on Amazon for $102.95, 53% off its typical price. This is a tool-only deal, so you’ll need a 20-volt DeWalt battery and charger to use it. This is a good tool for custom trimming drywall, cutting custom shapes for going around outlet covers, or custom cutting trim in tight spaces.

The DeWalt 20-volt cordless angle grinder is on sale at Lowe’s for $209, 47% off its usual price. This tool comes with a 2-amp-hour battery and a 4-amp-hour battery, but you’ll need a DeWalt 20-volt charger to use it. This is a good tool for metalworking or for grinding down screw tips that poke through or trimming bolt ends off.

The DeWalt 20-volt compact drill/driver is on sale at Home Depot for $99, 45% off its usual price. This tool comes with a 20-volt, 2-amp-hour battery and a charger, so it’s ready to use out of the box. It’s a good first tool for a set.

The Milwaukee 18-volt impact wrench is on sale at Home Depot for $199, 68% off its typical price. This tool comes with two 5-amp-hour batteries and a charger, so it’s ready to use out of the box. This is a good tool for driving bolts through tough materials and for automotive projects.

The DeWalt 20-volt oscillating multi-tool is on sale at Home Depot for $99, 50% off its regular price. This tool comes with a 2-amp-hour battery and a charger, so it's ready to use out of the box. This is one of the most versatile cordless tools, allowing you to cut a wide range of materials and use a sanding attachment to do finishing work as well.

The Milwaukee 18-volt tire inflator kit is on sale at Home Depot for $199, 65% off its usual price. This tool comes with two 5-amp-hour batteries and a charger, so it’s ready to go right out of the box. This is an excellent addition to your emergency roadside tool set because you can use it to inflate a car tire with the charged 18-volt batteries.

The Makita 18-volt cordless electric 2-inch brad nailer is on sale on Amazon for $324, 38% off its regular price. This is a tool-only deal, so you’ll need a Makita 18-volt battery and charger to use it. This is a good tool for attaching trim or paneling.

Yes, Home Depot has already launched its early Black Friday deals, offering deep discounts on major brands of cordless power tools. They also update their sales page on Thanksgiving Day and include Black Friday in-store-only doorbusters as part of their seasonal sales.

For most home tool sets, Ryobi is a solid, durable, and versatile brand. If you plan to use your tools occasionally for home maintenance, this is the best bang for your buck. For daily use or for larger DIY projects, DeWalt tends to be the next best option. These tools have more robust chargers and tend to stand up to more rigorous use than Ryobi tools.

If you’re building a new cordless tool set or updating your battery system, getting a cordless tool set can save you money because these combos usually include batteries and a charger, which can be the most expensive part of your tool set. If you already have a cordless tool set and you want to expand your kit, or if you have a DIYer in your life who already has a particular brand of battery and you want to get them something else they can use, a single tool deal might make more sense.

#3355. How AI Will Change Chip Design

Artificial intelligence’s promise and potential for the semiconductor industry

Rina Diane Caballar is a contributing editor covering tech and its intersections with science, society, and the environment.

An array of semiconductor wafers are ready to be made into chips.

The end of Moore’s Law is looming. Engineers and designers can do only so much to miniaturize transistors and pack as many of them as possible into chips. So they’re turning to other approaches to chip design, incorporating technologies like AI into the process.

Samsung, for instance, is adding AI to its memory chips to enable processing in memory, thereby saving energy and speeding up machine learning. Speaking of speed, Google’s TPU V4 AI chip has doubled its processing power compared with that of its previous version.

But AI holds still more promise and potential for the semiconductor industry. To better understand how AI is set to revolutionize chip design, we spoke with Heather Gorr, senior product manager for MathWorks’ MATLAB platform.

How is AI currently being used to design the next generation of chips?

Heather Gorr: AI is such an important technology because it’s involved in most parts of the cycle, including the design and manufacturing process. There’s a lot of important applications here, even in the general process engineering where we want to optimize things. I think defect detection is a big one at all phases of the process, especially in manufacturing. But even thinking ahead in the design process, [AI now plays a significant role] when you’re designing the light and the sensors and all the different components. There’s a lot of anomaly detection and fault mitigation that you really want to consider.

Then, thinking about the logistical modeling that you see in any industry, there is always planned downtime that you want to mitigate; but you also end up having unplanned downtime. So, looking back at that historical data of when you’ve had those moments where maybe it took a bit longer than expected to manufacture something, you can take a look at all of that data and use AI to try to identify the proximate cause or to see something that might jump out even in the processing and design phases. We think of AI oftentimes as a predictive tool, or as a robot doing something, but a lot of times you get a lot of insight from the data through AI.

What are the benefits of using AI for chip design?

Gorr: Historically, we’ve seen a lot of physics-based modeling, which is a very intensive process. We want to do a reduced order model, where instead of solving such a computationally expensive and extensive model, we can do something a little cheaper. You could create a surrogate model, so to speak, of that physics-based model, use the data, and then do your parameter sweeps, your optimizations, your Monte Carlo simulations using the surrogate model. That takes a lot less time computationally than solving the physics-based equations directly. So, we’re seeing that benefit in many ways, including the efficiency and economy that are the results of iterating quickly on the experiments and the simulations that will really help in the design.

So it’s like having a digital twin in a sense?

Gorr: Exactly. That’s pretty much what people are doing, where you have the physical system model and the experimental data. Then, in conjunction, you have this other model that you could tweak and tune and try different parameters and experiments that let sweep through all of those different situations and come up with a better design in the end.

So, it’s going to be more efficient and, as you said, cheaper?

Gorr: Yeah, definitely. Especially in the experimentation and design phases, where you’re trying different things. That’s obviously going to yield dramatic cost savings if you’re actually manufacturing and producing [the chips]. You want to simulate, test, experiment as much as possible without making something using the actual process engineering.

We’ve talked about the benefits. How about the drawbacks?

Gorr: The [AI-based experimental models] tend to not be as accurate as physics-based models. Of course, that’s why you do many simulations and parameter sweeps. But that’s also the benefit of having that digital twin, where you can keep that in mind—it’s not going to be as accurate as that precise model that we’ve developed over the years.

Both chip design and manufacturing are system intensive; you have to consider every little part. And that can be really challenging. It’s a case where you might have models to predict something and different parts of it, but you still need to bring it all together.

One of the other things to think about too is that you need the data to build the models. You have to incorporate data from all sorts of different sensors and different sorts of teams, and so that heightens the challenge.

How can engineers use AI to better prepare and extract insights from hardware or sensor data?

Gorr: We always think about using AI to predict something or do some robot task, but you can use AI to come up with patterns and pick out things you might not have noticed before on your own. People will use AI when they have high-frequency data coming from many different sensors, and a lot of times it’s useful to explore the frequency domain and things like data synchronization or resampling. Those can be really challenging if you’re not sure where to start.

One of the things I would say is, use the tools that are available. There’s a vast community of people working on these things, and you can find lots of examples [of applications and techniques] on GitHub or MATLAB Central, where people have shared nice examples, even little apps they’ve created. I think many of us are buried in data and just not sure what to do with it, so definitely take advantage of what’s already out there in the community. You can explore and see what makes sense to you, and bring in that balance of domain knowledge and the insight you get from the tools and AI.

What should engineers and designers consider when using AI for chip design?

Gorr: Think through what problems you’re trying to solve or what insights you might hope to find, and try to be clear about that. Consider all of the different components, and document and test each of those different parts. Consider all of the people involved, and explain and hand off in a way that is sensible for the whole team.

How do you think AI will affect chip designers’ jobs?

Gorr: It’s going to free up a lot of human capital for more advanced tasks. We can use AI to reduce waste, to optimize the materials, to optimize the design, but then you still have that human involved whenever it comes to decision-making. I think it’s a great example of people and technology working hand in hand. It’s also an industry where all people involved—even on the manufacturing floor—need to have some level of understanding of what’s happening, so this is a great industry for advancing AI because of how we test things and how we think about them before we put them on the chip.

How do you envision the future of AI and chip design?

Gorr: It’s very much dependent on that human element—involving people in the process and having that interpretable model. We can do many things with the mathematical minutiae of modeling, but it comes down to how people are using it, how everybody in the process is understanding and applying it. Communication and involvement of people of all skill levels in the process are going to be really important. We’re going to see less of those superprecise predictions and more transparency of information, sharing, and that digital twin—not only using AI but also using our human knowledge and all of the work that many people have done over the years.

Rina Diane Caballar is a writer covering tech and its intersections with science, society, and the environment. An IEEE Spectrum contributing editor, she's a former software engineer based in New Zealand.

#3354. iOS 27.3 brings vertical video and video podcasts to Apple TV app

iOS 27.3 beta 2 debuted today and includes two new types of video in the Apple TV app: vertical ‘clips’ and video podcasts.

The Apple TV app is expanding in two key ways with iOS 27.3, which is now in beta and ships next month.

First, Apple is introducing vertical video through a new ‘clips’ feature.

Similar to what streaming services like Netflix and Disney+ offer, the feature is a way to let users sample short-form previews of Apple TV content in a TikTok-style interface.

Inside the TV app in iOS 27.3, the Home tab has a new section: ‘Explore Clip Collections.’ Currently the collections include themed titles like ‘Absolute Adrenaline,’ ‘Animal Action,’ ‘Close Calls,’ and ‘Mind-Bending Moments.’

Tap to open a collection and you’ll start playing a short-form clip from Apple Originals with the option to swipe vertically to watch other clips. As you’d expect, Apple provides convenient buttons for adding the TV show or movie to your Watchlist.

iOS 27.3 also brings video podcasts from the Apple Podcasts app into TV.

As we reported this morning, there’s a dedicated video podcasts section coming to the TV app. But you can also, via your Account Settings, choose to sync playback data from Apple Podcasts.

If you enable sync, then video podcasts played in one app will be added to the queue and playback history in both apps.

What do you think of the latest TV app changes in iOS 27.3? Let us know in the comments.

You already know the name of the game — U.K. tech retail is a minefield because the memory shortage jacked up the launch prices of almost every new notebook this year.

Every discount screams about a “massive Black Friday saving,” but it’s artificially bloated.

Every Black Friday computing deal we recommend passes two rigorous tests to ensure it is cheaper than its original RRP before the memory crisis began. That's the 'RAMageddon Reset' promise.

And that’s why I’m activating my personal BS detector with the RAMageddon Reset rules. I dug through Amazon and Currys' sales to find the laptops that actually pass the sniff test, and are at a lower price than the RRP from before this memory surge.

HP OmniBook 5 16" OLED (Snapdragon X, 16GB)

Microsoft Surface Laptop 8 (Snapdragon X2 Plus)

Snapdragon X2 Plus | 16GB RAM | 512GB SSD

With a mid-2026 Snapdragon X2 Plus chip in here, I compared this price to the RRP of the pre-crisis Surface Laptop 7 with the Snapdragon X Plus. It’s a simple utilitarian workhorse with plenty of mid-range performance for getting stuff done, as well as that additional memory headroom. The main difference between this and the other OmniBook is that it has an LCD display.

This passes both my tests by dipping well under that pre-RAMageddon baseline RRP of £399. And while Windows 11 is dealing with 8GB of RAM better, it still runs a little chunky. ChromeOS runs effortlessly on what is a sleek notebook for basic browsing and students.

If you'd prefer to occasionally leave your iPhone behind, the Apple Watch Series 12 (GPS + Cellular, 42mm) is $70 off, bringing its price down to $429 from $499. For a more affordable option, the Apple Watch SE 3 (GPS, 40mm) is down to $199 from $249, saving you $50. It covers the essentials, including workout tracking, daily activity monitoring, and notifications, making it a practical choice if you don't need the Series 12's more advanced health features. Check out PCMag's review for a closer look at what you get for the price.

The Apple Watch SE 3 (GPS + Cellular, 40mm) is also $50 off, bringing its price down to $249 from $299. For an extra $50 over the GPS-only model, you get the convenience of making calls, sending messages, and staying connected without keeping your iPhone nearby, provided you have an active cellular plan. It's worth considering if you regularly go for runs, head to the gym, or step out without your phone but still want to stay reachable.

Apple released the M5 MacBook Air in March with 512GB of base storage, double the previous generation's, along with a faster SSD and an N1 wireless chip that adds Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6. The Magic Trackpad is down to $130 from $149, taking $19 off an accessory that brings the Multi-Touch gestures and Force Touch pressure sensing of a MacBook trackpad to a desktop setup, across an edge-to-edge glass surface. The Apple Pencil Pro is down to $99 from $129, saving you $30 on Apple's most feature-rich stylus. The Apple Magic Mouse is down to $59.99 from $79.99, saving you $20 on Apple's wireless mouse with a Multi-Touch surface that lets you swipe between pages and scroll through documents using simple finger gestures. It connects to your Mac over Bluetooth and has a rechargeable battery.

Yes, Apple participates in Black Friday, though you may want to compare their sales with other retailers like Best Buy and Walmart. So far, the best Black Friday sale on an Apple product is the M5 MacBook Air on sale for $200 off, the lowest price since the price hike this summer.

Among the deals listed here, the M5 MacBook Air with 512 of storage has one of the larger discounts at $249 off, bringing its price down to $1,249.99, from $1499.

For most people, the Apple Watch SE 3 at $199 is a good starting point, covering everyday fitness tracking, notifications, and essential health features without the higher price of the Series 12. If you want more advanced health monitoring and a more premium smartwatch experience, the Series 12 at $329 is worth considering.
